# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

5	1967). With this method, speed of movement increases with and without loads, and experiments have shown that 
6	the general increase in speed can reach 146% of the initial level. Movements should be executed with maximal 
7	effort and the apparatus should be accelerated as rapidly as possible.
8	To promote muscle recruitment in the active state, exercises with light and heavier weights (up to 40% of 
9	IRM) should be combined (the variable method) and the load should be lifted with the emphasis on acceleration at 
10	the beginning of the movement. Plyometric exercises (see 5.2.4), as well as exercises where isometric tension is 
11	generated quickly using 60-80% of 1 RM, should also be included. The optimal combination o f the volume of 
12	exercises with light weights and relatively heavy weights should be in a ratio of 5:1. Regarding sequencing, it has 
13	been found that the alternation of exercises is most effective for the ranked athlete.
14	To develop speed-strength in acyclic movements, plyometric or throwing exercises should be selected on the 
15	basis of their relevance to the sports activity. For example, to develop strength for the waterpolo throw, better 
16	results are obtained by throwing a medicine ball of 2 kg weight rather than one of 4 kg, the increases in throwing 
17	distance being 13.6% and 8.9%, respectively. 
18	Moreover, throwing a 4 kg ball is detrimental to technique 
19	(Rogener, 1961).
20	Training with a light (57 grams) and a heavy (184 gm) baseball for throwing ability results in improvements 
21	with both of them, where the mass of a regulation ball is about 148 gm. However, the transfer of specific fitness 
22	is not uniform: throwing the light ball improves precision for throwing the heavier ball, but the reverse effect does 
23	not occur (Egstrom et al, 1960). The optimal weight for javelin training which does not disrupt technique is 3 kg 
24	(Matveyev, 1967).
25	The progressive development o f speed-strength is the result of combining means for exploiting the after- 
26	ejfect phenomenon of preceding work to increase the effectiveness of subsequent work. In devising training means 
27	and methods for perfecting sporting performance, modelling is of central importance, where sports modelling 
28	refers to the formulation of descriptive models of sporting activities on the basis of biomechanical, kinesiological, 
29	physiological and other scientific measures.
30	Exercise modelling experiments show that the working effect of an explosive movement, as measured by the 
31	height to which a load was thrown (Fig 5.4), increases by an average of 38-40% after execution of barbell presses 
32	for 3 sets of 3 repetitions with 80% of the 1 RM (with a rest interval of 10 minutes between the pressing and the 
33	throwing). Movement time decreases, there is an increase in the length of the working path, the average speed, the 
34	driving force and power output (Table 5.3). Thus, the repetition of the same stimulus evokes a more pronounced 
35	reaction by the body and greater development of strength and speed.
36	Research shows that speed of movement increases significantly by use of the variation method: for example, by 
37	putting the shot directly after muscular contraction has been produced by putting a lighter object. 
38	In one 
39	experiment, lighter and heavier shots differing in mass by 250 grams were thrown at different velocities. A 
40	statistically significant difference was not found in the mean results of alternately putting standard shots of 
41	different mass. However, distances close to the mean were obtained with a difference in mass of 250 grams,

46	SUPERTRAINING
47	whereas this closeness to the average was not achieved with a difference of 500 grams (Ivanova, 1964; Vasiliev,
48	1975).

78	Thus, the transference of throwing speeds from a lighter to a heavier mass (i.e. the normal mass) apparently is 
79	possible only by alternating the throwing of shots of different mass. The effectiveness of the variable method of 
80	developing speed of movement was confirmed in the training of hockey players who successively hit a normal and 
81	a heavier puck. The optimal mass o f the heavier puck was found to be between 0.6-0.8 kg. However, it is 
82	necessary to select the mass for each player individually, based on the athlete's ability to hit the heavier puck effi­
83	ciently (Savin, 1974).
84	It should be pointed out that certain Eastern European and Chinese athletes train with heavier implements in 
85	their own sports and maintain that this method contributes to their impressive results. For instance, some table 
86	tennis competitors will eventually train with as much as 2kg bats, which is considerably heavier than typical bats 
87	of about 100 grams mass. Their coaches stress that this type of training is done only with carefully balanced bats 
88	by elite athletes about once a week before the competition phase, with less advanced competitors gradually 
89	increasing the weight of their bats over a prolonged period. 
90	This method should not be emulated by less 
91	experienced coaches, as the untutored use of this extraordinary approach can lead to overload injuries and altered 
92	neural control patterns.
93	Attempts must be made to resolve the conflict between the magnitude of the load and speed of movement in 
94	developing speed-strength. In this instance, this may be achieved if strength is used to oppose not the weight 
95	(gravitational force), but its inertia (acceleration force). Unfortunately this method is very seldom used in practice 
96	and its potential for enhancing strength is largely unexplored (see Fig 4.4), so that it is difficult to give specific 
97	recommendations for its application.
98	The next issue is the rest interval between sets of exercises. This interval is determined by level of fitness, 
99	the level of special endurance to repeatedly produce maximal tension and the degree of strength exerted. 
100	Experiments show that, with an optimal pause of 0.5-1 minute, speed-strength output can be maintained at a high 
101	level for a fairly long period without serious deterioration. The possible gradual decrease of speed-strength with 
102	exhausting, monotonous work can be largely eliminated by creating a favourable emotional state.
103	Spced-strength as displayed in rapid cyclical movements is characterised by repetitive contractions 
104	separated by relaxation phases. Depending on the special exercise, the effect of speed-strcngth can be determined 
105	by the ability of the neuromuscular apparatus to maintain the strength output for a long period at a specific work 
106	rate.
107	Thus, the movement tempo and the duration of work are of great significance in the development of speed- 
108	strength in speed-cyclic exercises. The resistance and the movement tempo are inversely proportional to one 
109	another. In other words, an increase in the resistance decreases the movement tempo and promotes the rapid 
110	onset of fatigue. Therefore, the optimal combination of resistance and tempo should be selected in each specific 
111	case, based on the kinesiological structure of the given exercise. It should be remembered that speed of movement 
112	decreases over a long period of training done at a slow tempo and increases through training at the optimal speed 
113	(Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958).
114	The ability to correctly execute the full movement cycle, including the appropriate phases of tension and 
115	muscular relaxation, should serve as a criterion. The movement tempo should gradually approach the tempo of the 
116	special exercise and even exceed it, while the working time should lengthen (Diachkov, 1961).
117	All that has been stated concerning the development o f speed-strength is related primarily to exercising 
118	functionally the relevant muscle groups by means of the special exercise. However, good results are achieved by 
119	making the special exercise more demanding. Thus, the use of water resistance in rowing or very small loads on
120	266
121	
122	
123	######## PDF idx 278 (printed 267)
124	SUPERTRAINING
125	the limbs of track-and-field athletes and gymnasts can enhance speed-strength under conditions that are very close 
126	to those of the special exercise.
127	In certain cases, power can be increased without using additional loads. For example, with jumps from one leg 
128	to the other, the push-off displays values of power which are greater than in running. Therefore, these jumps are 
129	excellent for the special strength training of sprinters. It is only necessary to execute them correctly by not 
130	accentuating the push-off of the body (which does not happen in sprinting), but by active gathering-in of the 
131	planted leg (i.e. via hip flexion). These jumps should be executed repetitively over distances of 50-100 meters as 
132	fast as possible. The addition of small cuffs weighing from 100-150 grams on each thigh can makes such exercises 
133	more effective in experienced athletes (based on Verkhoshansky’s experience with top Russian sprinters, such as 
134	Zubov).
135	Thus, to develop speed-strength one should use exercises, primarily with small resistance (20% of 1 RM) and, 
136	for acyclic activities of brief duration, a combination of these exercises with weights up to 40% of 1 RM in a ratio 
137	of 5 to 1. The work regime should correspond to the special exercise (cyclic or acyclic) and take into account the 
138	initial conditions from which force is developed (i.e. with the muscles relaxed, in a state of preliminary tension or 
139	stretched).
140	Perfecting the methods of developing speed-strength is a result of the search for a specific combination of 
141	means that exploit:
142	• the positive after-effect of preceding work on the subsequent activity
143	• the use of exercises in which muscular force opposes the inertia of the load and not its weight.
144	Fatigue must be avoided when one is trying to develop speed-strength for acyclic movements. However, fatigue is 
145	a necessary component of training for spced-strength in cyclic movements which require speed-endurance. Precise 
146	implementation of these findings is possible only under specific training conditions so, for the present, one has to 
147	rely on empirical methods.
148	5.2.4 Developm ent of Explosive Strength and R eactive Ability
149	The development of effective methods to develop explosive strength and reactive ability logically begins with an 
150	analysis of the speed-strength methods traditionally used for this purpose. For instance, athletes often attempt 
151	to develop explosive strength in the legs by using heavy barbell squats. In this case the musclcs work very slowly 
152	(quasi-isometrically) with a relatively constant tension produced by the load. 
153	Consequently, the muscles 
154	primarily develop isometric strength, but this does not mean that it is impossible for them to execute fast dynamic 
155	contractions. It should be added that increase in the weight of the barbell, which is frequently considered a basic 
156	indicator of special strength fitness, places a large and generally unnecessary load on the spine.
157	However, to solve the task of speed-strength preparation, athletes use smaller loads. For example, doing 
158	squat thrusts with a 60kg barbell on the shoulders produces a large dynamic maximum force. Therefore, exercises 
159	with heavy weights tend to increase the strength potential of the muscles, while fast exercises with light weights 
160	improve speed. Nevertheless, these means are not the only way of developing explosive strength.
161	Explosive strength is a motor quality requiring specific movements and training means. The above- 
162	mentioned means of strength training do not adequately enhance specific components of explosive movements 
163	such as the rapid excitation of muscles and the rapid changing from eccentric to concentric work.
164	These and allied skills require a specific training regime which is impossible to imitate with only one 
165	resistance exercise. Indeed, stimulation of muscular activity with slow resistance movements, and lifting a barbell 
166	in preparation for squatting or jumping with it, removes the possibility of controlling the mechanisms which are 
167	crucial to the rapid switching of muscles to the active state. At the same time, a decrease in the resistance 
168	diminishes the dynamic effort required and creates a vicious cycle from which there is no apparent escape.
169	Thus, if the athlete successfully develops a high level of explosive strength, then it may be attributed to 
170	certain means in his training. Consequently, the problem amounts to singling out those means and organising them 
171	so as to systematise the special strength training.
172	The Plyometric Method
173	Prolonged research in the direction discussed above led to the development of the so-called 'shock' (plyometric) 
174	method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability (see 1.5). Basically it consists of stimulating the 
175	muscles by means of a sudden stretch preceding any voluntary effort (see 4.2.3). Kinetic energy and not heavy
176	2 6 7
177	
178	
179	######## PDF idx 279 (printed 268)
180	SUPERTRAINING
181	weights should be used for this, where the kinetic energy may be accumulated by means o f the body or loads 
182	dropping from a certain height (see 4.2.3). Depth jumps and medicine ball rebounding are two of the exercise 
183	regimes commonly used in plyometrics.
184	The increase in popularity of plyometrics in the West deems it necessary that the concept be more rigorously 
185	defined. Plyometrics or the 'shock method' means precisely that - a method of mechanical shock stimulation to 
186	force the muscle to produce as much tension as possible. This method is characterised by impulsive action of 
187	minimal duration between the end of the eccentric braking phase and initiation o f the concentric acceleration 
188	phase. It relies on the production of a very brief explosive-isometric and eccentric-isometric phase which pre­
189	cedes the release of the elastic energy stored in the tendons and other components of the scries elastic component 
190	of the muscle complex during the eccentric deceleration phase (see 1.9, 3.1 and Fig 4.11). If the transition phase 
191	(or, coupling phase) is prolonged by more than about 0.15 second, the action may be considered to constitute 
192	ordinary jumping and not classical training plyometrics. A useful visualisation is to imagine that the surface being 
193	touchcd by the hands or the feet during the plyomctric contact phase is red hot, so that any prolonged contact 
194	would be dangerous.
195	It is important to note that the activity is not accurately plyometric if the athlete relies upon ongoing 
196	feedback processes to control the isometric and concentric actions instead of upon feedforward programmes 
197	established before any movement begins (see 1.8 and 1.12). True plyometric training usually involves ballistic 
198	rather than cocontraction processes, a concept discussed earlier (see 1.8).
199	Plyometrics as a Discrete Training System
200	A thorough discussion of what is meant by the term plyometrics is essential, bccause one must distinguish clearly 
201	between plyometric actions, which occur as part of many 
202	running, jumping, hurdling, striking and other 
203	rebounding movements in sport, and plyometric training, which applies plyometric actions as a distinct training 
204	modality according to a definite methodology.
205	The fairly recent adoption of plyometrics by Western coaches as a so-called 'Russian training secret’ has 
206	created an unwarranted mystique about a method that has been used extensively in Russia since its scientific 
207	formalisation in the early 1960s as a discrete training system by Verkhoshansky. In recognising that plyometric 
208	actions are widespread in most sport, Verkhoshansky has always consistently favoured the use of the term 'shock 
209	method' instead of'plyometrics' to distinguish between naturally occurring plyometric actions in sport and the 
210	formal discipline he devised as a discrete training system to develop speed-strength in particular. This is why the 
211	term powermetrics has been suggested elsewhere in this text to refer to plyometric training, as opposed to 
212	plyometric actions which occur quite naturally in many natural ballistic movements. The earliest published use of 
213	the word plyometrics seems to have been in a Soviet publication (Zanon, 1966).
214	Popular adoption of the term 'plyometrics' in the place of'shock method' has produced this confusion, just as 
215	popular use of the term 'aerobics' has caused widespread confusion between aerobic (cardiovascular) conditioning 
216	and acrobics as a form of exercise to music. Consequently, it is probably better to refer to plyometric action as 
217	stretch-shortening action, as has been done in much of the scientific literature, and to redefine 'plyometrics' as a 
218	specific training system in its own right, or, powermetrics.
219	Possibly the easiest way of showing that the shock method can indeed be regarded as a separate, goal-directed 
220	training system is to examine the concept of resistance training. Resistance to movement is encountered in all 
221	sport, so the critics of plyometrics as a definite training method should then agree that it is equally logical to 
222	conclude that resistance training must not be regarded as a distinct training system. On this basis one might also 
223	conclude that distance running or cycling are resistance training methods, because the athlete certainly experiences 
224	resistance and produces high levels of muscular tension in these sports.
225	One might extend this argument further and conclude that all human movement is really resistance training. 
226	After all, it is somewhat artificial to refer to weight training as resistance training and to ignore other sports that 
227	also involve work against significant resistance, simply because the loads superficially appear to be heavier in 
228	weight training. Basic biomechanical analysis of the forces and tensions involved show clcarly that the high levels 
229	of resistance and muscle tension involved in sports such as gymnastics, swimming, rowing and wrestling easily 
230	justify any objections to regarding resistance training as a separate training system.
231	Just as resistance training has adopted means, methods and apparatus from other sports and physical 
232	activities to create a discrete training discipline, so has plyometric training or powermetrics (as distinct from 
233	plyometric action) done the same to create its own methodology.
234	268
235	
236	
237	######## PDF idx 280 (printed 269)
238	SUPERTRAINING
239	Plyometric Training and Safety
240	Piyomctric training (powermetrics) is not without its vociferous opponents, all of whom believe that high impact 
241	loading of the joints in jumping or other impulsive activities is harmful to the joints and unproven in enhancing 
242	explosive performance. As yet, the opinion that plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not 
243	been proved experimentally or clinically, especially since it is very difficult to design an experiment which isolates 
244	piyomctric effects from the accompanying effects of other activities associated with a given sport and which 
245	includes control groups who are exposed to comparable overall intensity, duration and complexity of loading. 
246	Hiusfar, the dangers of plyometrics are inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been 
247	measured via force plate research during jumping activities, in particular. The opponents of plyomctrics who use 
248	this research or theoretical calculations of force from Newton’s Second Law to proclaim an unqualified 
249	condemnation of all piyomctric training (powermetrics) or any other types of ballistic training, for that matter, 
250	seem to overlook the obvious fact that running, jumping and other ballistic activities are an integral part o f most 
251	sports. In other words, they are implying that these activities in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, 
252	but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous.
253	They also arc implementing the unproved hypothesis that impulsive loading is far more dangerous for the 
254	joints than any other forms of less stressful loading. Moreover, they seem to be assuming that the joints do not 
255	follow the principle o f Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands (SAID) and that they can do little else than 
256	deteriorate in response to impulsive and ballistic loading.
257	In this regard it is relevant to point out that joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from 
258	osteoarthritis in old age and that those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of 
259	osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; 
260	Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977). 
261	Siff s former colleague, Dr Mark Swanepoel, at the University 
262	of the Witwatersrand in South Africa, pointed out that, as one progresses up the lower extremity from the ankle, 
263	to the knee, the hip and finally to the lumbar spine, so the extent of fibrillation increases at any given age.
264	It appears that the cartilages of joints subjected to regular impulsive loading with relatively high contact 
265	stresses is mechanically much stiffer and better adapted to withstand the exceptional loading of running and 
266	jumping than the softer cartilage associated with low loading. Thus, joint cartilage subjected to regular repetitive 
267	loading remains healthy and copes very well with impulsive loads, whereas cartilage that is heavily loaded 
268	infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production, the collagen network loses its cohesion and the 
269	cartilage deteriorates (Swanepoel, 1998).
270	This discussion does not dismiss the risks posed by inappropriate or excessive use of plyometric training 
271	lpowermetrics), but it stresses that it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the 
272	manner in which it is used, as is the case with all forms of training. In the case of plyometrics, the zealous way in 
273	which this so-called Russian training secret has been modified, extended and implemented in the West certainly 
274	does warrant a great deal of the criticism that has been levelled at it. Virtually every Western book or article on 
275	the subject presents encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms 
276	which often create the impression that quantity is more important than quality. 
277	Complexity of drills and 
278	apparatus often seems to replace optimal simplicity, technical correctness and elegance. Many repetitions of 
279	plyometric drills frequently are prescribed for some sports because of assumptions that this sort of training will 
280	improve fatigue resistance in repeated actions such as rebounding in basketball, yet research has shown this to be 
281	untrue (Nicol ct al, 1997).
282	Often, plyometric drills are prescribed without adequate attention being paid to the entire context of training, 
283	including the interaction with other physical activities, loading imposed by other work or play, the psychological 
284	modification of reflexes or the use of formal restoration. More often than not, plyometric enthusiasts do not 
285	consider the possibility that the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most o f the piyomctric training that is 
286	accessary and that adding more of this type of loading may be excessive or unwarranted. All exercise has to be 
287	offered in a way which is concordant with its advantages, disadvantages, scope and limitations - and plyomctrics 
288	are no exception.
289	Thus, any lack of safety in plyometric training has more to do with inappropriate and ineffective prescription 
290	than this mode of exercise itself, with overtraining being a major contributory factor (see 8.8). In this regard, 
291	overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) 
292	and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise). 
293	Thus, the prescription of an individually 
294	appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height) of plyometric exercises according to the principle
295	269
296	
297	
298	######## PDF idx 281 (printed 270)
299	SUPERTRAINING
300	of gradual progressive overload integrated periodically into an overall training programme with adcqutil 
301	restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running « 
302	jumping. Finally, in designing a training programme, it might be preferable to avoid use of the popular tenu 
303	plyometric drills, because drills tend to be associated with militarism and authoritarianism rather than wi&l 
304	individual flow, sensitivity, flair and nuances of personal interpretation. 
305	I
306	The Fundamental Theory of Plyometrics
307	Plyometric activity is characterised by the following phases of action between initiation and termination of ihel 
308	sequence of events (Fig 5.5):
309	1. An initial momentum phase during which the body or part of the body is moving because of kinetic energy] 
310	(KE) it has accumulated from a preceding action.
311	2. An electromechanical delay phase which occurs when some event such as contact with a surface prevents il 
312	limb from moving further and provokes the muscles to contract. This delay refers to the time elapsing] 
313	between the onset of the action potential in the motor nerves and the onset of the muscle contraction. Some 
314	workers define this phase to include the lengthening of the SEC (Series Elastic Component) of the muscic 
315	complex, but the name electromechanical was coined to mean the start of the electrical signal to the start of 
316	the mechanical contraction in a muscic, which does not include the passive stretching of connective tissue.
317	3. An amortisation phase when the ICE produces a powerful myotatic stretch reflex which leads to eccentric 
318	muscle contraction accompanied by explosive isometric contraction (see Fig 3.33) and stretching of the SEC 
319	(Series Elastic Component, e.g. tendons) o f the muscle complex (sec Figs 1.14, 1.18). 
320	The explosive 
321	isometric phase between the end of the eccentric action and the beginning of the concentric action lasts for a 
322	period known as the coupling time (Fig 5.5), which will be discussed shortly in greater detail.
323	4. A rebound phase involving the release of elastic energy from the SEC, together with the involuntary 
324	concentric muscle contraction evoked by the myotatic stretch reflex, as well as possible local change in the 
325	muscle fibre mechanics. This phase may include the contribution added by voluntary concentric contraction.
326	5. A final momentum phase which occurs after the concentric contraction is complete and the body or limb 
327	concerned continues to move by means of the kinetic energy imparted by concentric contraction and the 
328	release of elastic energy from the SEC.
329	Figure 5.5 The different phases o f a plyometric action. EM delay = Electromechanical delay between signal to terminate initial 
330	momentum phase and instant when eccentric contraction begins.
331	Discussion of the coupling time is of great importance because it has a fundamental bearing on whether or not any 
332	action may be accurately classified as classical plyomctrics. Earlier it was stated that classical plyometrics arc 
333	characterised by a delay o f no more than approximately 0.15 second between the eccentric and subsequent 
334	concentric contractions, a statement which requires some qualification. For instance, research by Wilson et al 
335	(1990) examining different delay times in the bench press showed that the benefits of prior stretch may endure for 
336	as long as 4 seconds, at which stage it is suggested that all stored elastic energy is lost (see Fig 5.6).
337	270
338	
339	
340	######## PDF idx 282 (printed 271)
341	SUPERTRAINING
342	Chapman and Caldwell (1985), on the other hand, found that the benefits of prior stretching during forearm 
343	movement were dissipated within 0.25 second, a figure which agrees with S iff s analysis of explosive rebound 
344	elbow flexion without additional loading (Fig 5.7). Other work by Wilson et al (1991) examining rebound action 
345	of the chest/arms concluded that no benefits of prior stretching arc evident after 0.37 second.
346	This research seems to suggest that delays of as long as a sccond or two can still produce significant 
347	augmentation of the subsequent concentric phase for some activities, but delays as short as 0.2 second are 
348	sufficient to dissipate the benefits of prior stretch during other activities. Research by Bosco et al (1982a) offers 
349	a partial solution to this apparent contradiction. They proposed that individuals with a high percentage of FT 
350	fibres in the leg muscles exhibit a maximum plyometric effect when the eccentric phase is short, movement range 
351	is small and coupling time is brief. On the other hand, subjects with a high percentage of ST fibres apparently 
352	produce their best jumping performance when the cccentric phase is longer, movement range is greater and the 
353	coupling time is longer, since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration.
354	It is also tempting to attribute these major differences in coupling times to the existence of specific maximum 
355	delays for each joint action. While this probably is true for different simple and complex joint actions, it is also 
356	important to note that the human body exhibits many different reflexes, each of which acts under different 
357	conditions and at different rates (see 3.5.3).
358	In particular, there are tonic (static) and phasic (dynamic) stretch reflexes and very rapid receptors such as 
359	pacinian corpuscles in joint capsules that detect the rates of movement and allow the nervous system to predict 
360	where the extremities will be at any precise moment, thereby facilitating anticipatory modifications in limb 
361	position to ensure effective control and stability (Guyton, 1984). Loss of this predictive function apparently 
362	makes it virtually impossible for one to run, jump, throw or catch. Other receptors such as the Ruffini endings

370	In addition, weightlifters and sometimes bodybuilders use the so-called pre-stretch principle to produce a 
371	more powerful concentric muscle contraction to enable them to lift heavier loads. In doing so, they begin a 
372	movement from a starting position which imposes an intense stretch on the relevant muscles, hold it for a couple 
373	of seconds and then thrust as strongly as possible from that position. It would seem that this longer delay would 
374	implicate the more tonic type of reflex with a characteristically greater coupling time. The action could certainly 
375	not be called plyometric, despite the fact that prior stretch had contributed to the subsequent concentric action. 
376	Conversely, phasic reflex activity would more likely be implicated in the explosive movements which typify 
377	classical plyometrics and the type of activity described graphically in Figure 5.7.
378	This explanation also serves to further distinguish between piyomctric action and piyomctric training, an issue 
379	discussed earlier in this section. One cannot simply distinguish between plyometric and non-plyomctric solely on 
380	the basis of coupling times, otherwise one would have to classify jogging or even brisk walking as classical 
381	plyometrics, because the time taken for the ground reaction force to reach a maximum can be less than 0.15 
382	second. One also has to take the force-time pattern and the rate of force development (RFD) into account (see Fig 
383	2.13).
384	On this scicntific basis, the argument as to whether a given action is classically plyometric or not becomes 
385	complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training. It is better to recognise the 
386	existence of different types of plyometric training {powermetrics). At the outset, a distinction should be made 
387	between maximal plyometrics training and sub-maximal plyometric training. In doing so, it is valuable to apply a 
388	powermetrics intensity scale similar to that used in weightlifting, where exercises arc ranked in terms of 
389	percentages of one’s 1 RM.
390	The concept of 1 RMs is meaningless in plyometric training, so one must rely on estimates of muscle tension 
391	produced by a given drill or on estimates of the impulse (see 5.1) produced during the contact phase of body with 
392	the ground or projectile. Impulse is equivalent to the change of momentum (m.AV) during the amortisation phase, 
393	so that its magnitude for a falling body depends on the height from which the body drops. Thus, the momentum 
394	just before contact (estimated from height of the drop jump or distance fallen by the object) may serve as a 
395	measure o f intensity. At one end o f the scale lies maximal plyometrics (the equivalent of the emotionally 
396	demanding competitive maximum, CFmax) and at the other end lies preparatory non-impact plyometrics (see Fig 
397	5.8). Maximal, submaximal and non-plyometrics are depicted in the same box in this diagram as a reminder that 
398	there is really a continuum of intensities, rather than an abrupt difference between each type of plyometric 
399	training.
400	Maximal plyometrics essentially are low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or 
401	rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced in the relevant muscles. Just 
402	like maximal strength training with weights, these powerful impulses are not meant to be imposed on the 
403	musculature every workout, nor are multiple repetitions even possible or advisable. Moreover, a rest interval of 
404	2-4 minutes is recommended between successive repetitions and as much as 10-12 minutes between sets.
405	Sub-maximal plyometrics involve mechanical impulses which do not produce maximal muscular tension, 
406	although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase with the floor or projected object. For 
407	example, lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound 
408	height. Rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot are other typical sub-maximal exercises.
409	Two broad classes of plyometric training may be recognised: impact plyometrics and non-impact plyometrics 
410	(Fig 5.8). During impact plyometrics the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object, whereas the 
411	recoil in non-impact plyometrics is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement 
412	not terminated by contact with a surface. Depth jumps are a typical example of impact plyomctrics, while snap 
413	kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts exemplify non-impact plyometrics. Depending on 
414	the power of the movements, non-impact plyomctrics may also be maximal or submaximal.
415	Plyometric training, in turn, involves several distinct categories of activities: classical plyometric exercises, 
416	supplementary plyometrics and preparatory drills for plyomctrics (Fig 5.8). Classical plyometric exercises are 
417	either functional or non-functional, the former referring to activities which arc matched as closely as possible to 
418	the specific explosive actions of the particular sport with respect to movement pattern, muscle involvement, 
419	timing and direction o f motion. Non-functional plyometrics are exercises intended to offer general training of the 
420	explosive qualities required by the sport. For example, functional plyometrics in long jump would use forward

442	Plyometrics may be better understood by applying Newton's Second Law in its simplest form: F = ma. In normal 
443	resistance training, the mass is increased, whereas the acceleration is increased in plyometrics. Plyometrics is a 
444	system of explosive training using relatively low inertial loading, but weight training usually relies on high inertia 
445	loading. One may produce the same force by moving a heavy load with low acceleration or a light load with a 
446	large acceleration, but the training effect is very different. Explosive, low inertia training targets involuntary, 
447	neuromuscular and central nervous processes more strongly than high inertia training, which has a greater effect on 
448	static strength development and muscle hypertrophy.
449	To ascertain whether an athlete needs plyomctric or heavy resistance training depends on measuring the 
450	strength deficit, or the difference between the absolute (involuntary) strength maximum and the voluntary strength 
451	maximum (see Ch I). Without such testing, prescription of plyometric training tends to remain hit-and-miss. The 
452	opposition to plyometric training by some experts is largely the result of this type of guesswork training, which 
453	can hinder performance and increase the risk of injury.
454	Correct breathing is important during plyometric training. It is vital that the athlete holds the breath during 
455	the amortisation and early propulsion phase to stabilise the body, offer pneumatic shock absorption and to 
456	increase the rebound force. Forced exhalation may accompany the remainder of the propulsion phase. Footwear 
457	or the floor covering should not be very soft or excessively shock absorbent, since this may impair ankle stability, 
458	diminish the storage of elastic energy in the SEC (e.g. tendons) and delay the triggering of the positive supportive 
459	reaction of the foot (see 6.1.2) when contacting the floor.

471	It is necessary to take into account the following guidelines for using plyometric exercises:
472	1. The magnitude of the impulsive load is determined by the weight and the height o f its free-fall. The 
473	optimal combination is determined empirically in each specific case; however, preference should be given 
474	to a large height over a heavy weight. Since the resulting force is governed by Newton's Second Law (F = 
475	m.a), a force plate may be used to determine the height of drop to produce the required force.
476	2. The amortisation phase should be of minimal duration, but sufficient to create impulsive contraction of the 
477	muscles. Therefore, the initial posture with respect to the joint angles should correspond to the same 
478	position in which the working movement begins in the sporting exercise.
479	3. The plyometric training should be preceded by a good warmup of the intensively involved muscles.
480	4. As an initial guideline, the dosage of plyometric exercises should not exceed 5-8 repetitions in one set. A 
481	more precise way to determine this is to calculate the force involved (from bodymass and the drop height) 
482	and the athlete’s level of special speed-strength.
483	5. One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or 
484	take-off height.
485	6. Rest periods are crucial for the effective and safe use of plyometrics. The rest interval between sets of 
486	maximal plyomctric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and 
487	speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength 
488	endurance.
489	In those cases where the plyometric method is used for developing jumping power (i.e. explosive strength and the 
490	reactive ability of the extensors of the torso and legs), one can work without an additional load and utilise only 
491	falling bodymass for providing the impulsive stimulation. For example, one may energetically jump upwards, or 
492	upward and forwards, after a depth-jump from some height (Fig 5.10). The optimal depth o f the jump is 
493	determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is 
494	developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved.

683	Many articles on plyometrics describe exercises such as depth jumps and medicine ball drills as suitable 
684	supplementary speed-strength exercises for all sports. This approach, however, fails to distinguish adequately 
685	between the different sports, because some sports require symmetry of joint action and rhythms, while others 
686	display asymmetry and unilateral emphasis. Depth jumps and medicine ball drills using both limbs 
687	simultaneously and symmetrically may be valuable for sports which require this type o f limb action, but are far 
688	less beneficial for sports which involve alternate action of the limbs in different patterns of movement.
689	Therefore, before selecting plyometric drills, it is important to categorize sporting movements as cyclic, 
690	acyclic, unilateral, bilateral, symmetric, asymmetric or as various combinations of the preceding actions. One also 
691	needs to distinguish between dominant and non-dominant limbs, as well as driving leg and swing leg in running, 
692	since the efficiency of movement depends primarily on central nervous factors and not merely indiscriminate

701	longitudinal axis, as determined by one's dominance of hand. For example, a right-handed baseballer, golfer or 
702	shotputter displays anti-clockwise rotational dominance, whereas the left-hander displays clockwise rotational 
703	dominance. Clearly, this has a distinct influence on upper body catching and throwing drills with medicine ball 
704	plyometrics. Yet, it is rare to find any textbook that comments on how jumping, bounding, catching and other 
705	drills should be used to take functional asymmetries and dominances into account in improving neuromuscular 
706	efficiency in given sporting movements.
707	Research has shown that the transfer of strength developed in bilateral training (e.g. using squats or power 
708	cleans) offers specific improvement in performance in bilateral events such as the squat clean and snatch in 
709	weightlifting, while unilateral training (e.g. with dumbbells or split cleans) enhances performances more effectively 
710	in unilateral activity such as running, jumping or karate. Similarly, it should be appreciated that speed-strength 
711	development is influenced by the type of plyometric drill chosen for regular training. That this point is not 
712	sufficiently understood in the West is emphasized by the fact that the chapters on so-called 'sport specific' 
713	plyometrics in the best-known texts make no mention of specificity of explosive exercises with respect to limb or 
714	rotational dominance. Yet, even a rudimentary working knowledge of the principles of neuro-developmcntal 
715	training and PNF reveals that motor performance is determined by how competently one programs the central 
716	nervous computer of the body, taking functional asymmetry into careful consideration when doing so.

1967). With this method, speed of movement increases with and without loads, and experiments have shown that 
the general increase in speed can reach 146% of the initial level. Movements should be executed with maximal 
effort and the apparatus should be accelerated as rapidly as possible.
To promote muscle recruitment in the active state, exercises with light and heavier weights (up to 40% of 
IRM) should be combined (the variable method) and the load should be lifted with the emphasis on acceleration at 
the beginning of the movement. Plyometric exercises (see 5.2.4), as well as exercises where isometric tension is 
generated quickly using 60-80% of 1 RM, should also be included. The optimal combination o f the volume of 
exercises with light weights and relatively heavy weights should be in a ratio of 5:1. Regarding sequencing, it has 
been found that the alternation of exercises is most effective for the ranked athlete.
To develop speed-strength in acyclic movements, plyometric or throwing exercises should be selected on the 
basis of their relevance to the sports activity. For example, to develop strength for the waterpolo throw, better 
results are obtained by throwing a medicine ball of 2 kg weight rather than one of 4 kg, the increases in throwing 
distance being 13.6% and 8.9%, respectively. 
Moreover, throwing a 4 kg ball is detrimental to technique 
(Rogener, 1961).
Training with a light (57 grams) and a heavy (184 gm) baseball for throwing ability results in improvements 
with both of them, where the mass of a regulation ball is about 148 gm. However, the transfer of specific fitness 
is not uniform: throwing the light ball improves precision for throwing the heavier ball, but the reverse effect does 
not occur (Egstrom et al, 1960). The optimal weight for javelin training which does not disrupt technique is 3 kg 
(Matveyev, 1967).
The progressive development o f speed-strength is the result of combining means for exploiting the after- 
ejfect phenomenon of preceding work to increase the effectiveness of subsequent work. In devising training means 
and methods for perfecting sporting performance, modelling is of central importance, where sports modelling 
refers to the formulation of descriptive models of sporting activities on the basis of biomechanical, kinesiological, 
physiological and other scientific measures.
Exercise modelling experiments show that the working effect of an explosive movement, as measured by the 
height to which a load was thrown (Fig 5.4), increases by an average of 38-40% after execution of barbell presses 
for 3 sets of 3 repetitions with 80% of the 1 RM (with a rest interval of 10 minutes between the pressing and the 
throwing). Movement time decreases, there is an increase in the length of the working path, the average speed, the 
driving force and power output (Table 5.3). Thus, the repetition of the same stimulus evokes a more pronounced 
reaction by the body and greater development of strength and speed.
Research shows that speed of movement increases significantly by use of the variation method: for example, by 
putting the shot directly after muscular contraction has been produced by putting a lighter object. 
In one 
experiment, lighter and heavier shots differing in mass by 250 grams were thrown at different velocities. A 
statistically significant difference was not found in the mean results of alternately putting standard shots of 
different mass. However, distances close to the mean were obtained with a difference in mass of 250 grams,

Thus, the transference of throwing speeds from a lighter to a heavier mass (i.e. the normal mass) apparently is 
possible only by alternating the throwing of shots of different mass. The effectiveness of the variable method of 
developing speed of movement was confirmed in the training of hockey players who successively hit a normal and 
a heavier puck. The optimal mass o f the heavier puck was found to be between 0.6-0.8 kg. However, it is 
necessary to select the mass for each player individually, based on the athlete's ability to hit the heavier puck effi­
ciently (Savin, 1974).
It should be pointed out that certain Eastern European and Chinese athletes train with heavier implements in 
their own sports and maintain that this method contributes to their impressive results. For instance, some table 
tennis competitors will eventually train with as much as 2kg bats, which is considerably heavier than typical bats 
of about 100 grams mass. Their coaches stress that this type of training is done only with carefully balanced bats 
by elite athletes about once a week before the competition phase, with less advanced competitors gradually 
increasing the weight of their bats over a prolonged period. 
This method should not be emulated by less 
experienced coaches, as the untutored use of this extraordinary approach can lead to overload injuries and altered 
neural control patterns.
Attempts must be made to resolve the conflict between the magnitude of the load and speed of movement in 
developing speed-strength. In this instance, this may be achieved if strength is used to oppose not the weight 
(gravitational force), but its inertia (acceleration force). Unfortunately this method is very seldom used in practice 
and its potential for enhancing strength is largely unexplored (see Fig 4.4), so that it is difficult to give specific 
recommendations for its application.
The next issue is the rest interval between sets of exercises. This interval is determined by level of fitness, 
the level of special endurance to repeatedly produce maximal tension and the degree of strength exerted. 
Experiments show that, with an optimal pause of 0.5-1 minute, speed-strength output can be maintained at a high 
level for a fairly long period without serious deterioration. The possible gradual decrease of speed-strength with 
exhausting, monotonous work can be largely eliminated by creating a favourable emotional state.
Spced-strength as displayed in rapid cyclical movements is characterised by repetitive contractions 
separated by relaxation phases. Depending on the special exercise, the effect of speed-strcngth can be determined 
by the ability of the neuromuscular apparatus to maintain the strength output for a long period at a specific work 
rate.
Thus, the movement tempo and the duration of work are of great significance in the development of speed- 
strength in speed-cyclic exercises. The resistance and the movement tempo are inversely proportional to one 
another. In other words, an increase in the resistance decreases the movement tempo and promotes the rapid 
onset of fatigue. Therefore, the optimal combination of resistance and tempo should be selected in each specific 
case, based on the kinesiological structure of the given exercise. It should be remembered that speed of movement 
decreases over a long period of training done at a slow tempo and increases through training at the optimal speed 
(Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958).
The ability to correctly execute the full movement cycle, including the appropriate phases of tension and 
muscular relaxation, should serve as a criterion. The movement tempo should gradually approach the tempo of the 
special exercise and even exceed it, while the working time should lengthen (Diachkov, 1961).
All that has been stated concerning the development o f speed-strength is related primarily to exercising 
functionally the relevant muscle groups by means of the special exercise. However, good results are achieved by 
making the special exercise more demanding. Thus, the use of water resistance in rowing or very small loads on
266


######## PDF idx 278 (printed 267)
SUPERTRAINING
the limbs of track-and-field athletes and gymnasts can enhance speed-strength under conditions that are very close 
to those of the special exercise.
In certain cases, power can be increased without using additional loads. For example, with jumps from one leg 
to the other, the push-off displays values of power which are greater than in running. Therefore, these jumps are 
excellent for the special strength training of sprinters. It is only necessary to execute them correctly by not 
accentuating the push-off of the body (which does not happen in sprinting), but by active gathering-in of the 
planted leg (i.e. via hip flexion). These jumps should be executed repetitively over distances of 50-100 meters as 
fast as possible. The addition of small cuffs weighing from 100-150 grams on each thigh can makes such exercises 
more effective in experienced athletes (based on Verkhoshansky’s experience with top Russian sprinters, such as 
Zubov).
Thus, to develop speed-strength one should use exercises, primarily with small resistance (20% of 1 RM) and, 
for acyclic activities of brief duration, a combination of these exercises with weights up to 40% of 1 RM in a ratio 
of 5 to 1. The work regime should correspond to the special exercise (cyclic or acyclic) and take into account the 
initial conditions from which force is developed (i.e. with the muscles relaxed, in a state of preliminary tension or 
stretched).
Perfecting the methods of developing speed-strength is a result of the search for a specific combination of 
means that exploit:
• the positive after-effect of preceding work on the subsequent activity
• the use of exercises in which muscular force opposes the inertia of the load and not its weight.
Fatigue must be avoided when one is trying to develop speed-strength for acyclic movements. However, fatigue is 
a necessary component of training for spced-strength in cyclic movements which require speed-endurance. Precise 
implementation of these findings is possible only under specific training conditions so, for the present, one has to 
rely on empirical methods.
5.2.4 Developm ent of Explosive Strength and R eactive Ability
The development of effective methods to develop explosive strength and reactive ability logically begins with an 
analysis of the speed-strength methods traditionally used for this purpose. For instance, athletes often attempt 
to develop explosive strength in the legs by using heavy barbell squats. In this case the musclcs work very slowly 
(quasi-isometrically) with a relatively constant tension produced by the load. 
Consequently, the muscles 
primarily develop isometric strength, but this does not mean that it is impossible for them to execute fast dynamic 
contractions. It should be added that increase in the weight of the barbell, which is frequently considered a basic 
indicator of special strength fitness, places a large and generally unnecessary load on the spine.
However, to solve the task of speed-strength preparation, athletes use smaller loads. For example, doing 
squat thrusts with a 60kg barbell on the shoulders produces a large dynamic maximum force. Therefore, exercises 
with heavy weights tend to increase the strength potential of the muscles, while fast exercises with light weights 
improve speed. Nevertheless, these means are not the only way of developing explosive strength.
Explosive strength is a motor quality requiring specific movements and training means. The above- 
mentioned means of strength training do not adequately enhance specific components of explosive movements 
such as the rapid excitation of muscles and the rapid changing from eccentric to concentric work.
These and allied skills require a specific training regime which is impossible to imitate with only one 
resistance exercise. Indeed, stimulation of muscular activity with slow resistance movements, and lifting a barbell 
in preparation for squatting or jumping with it, removes the possibility of controlling the mechanisms which are 
crucial to the rapid switching of muscles to the active state. At the same time, a decrease in the resistance 
diminishes the dynamic effort required and creates a vicious cycle from which there is no apparent escape.
Thus, if the athlete successfully develops a high level of explosive strength, then it may be attributed to 
certain means in his training. Consequently, the problem amounts to singling out those means and organising them 
so as to systematise the special strength training.
The Plyometric Method
Prolonged research in the direction discussed above led to the development of the so-called 'shock' (plyometric) 
method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability (see 1.5). Basically it consists of stimulating the 
muscles by means of a sudden stretch preceding any voluntary effort (see 4.2.3). Kinetic energy and not heavy
2 6 7


######## PDF idx 279 (printed 268)
SUPERTRAINING
weights should be used for this, where the kinetic energy may be accumulated by means o f the body or loads 
dropping from a certain height (see 4.2.3). Depth jumps and medicine ball rebounding are two of the exercise 
regimes commonly used in plyometrics.
The increase in popularity of plyometrics in the West deems it necessary that the concept be more rigorously 
defined. Plyometrics or the 'shock method' means precisely that - a method of mechanical shock stimulation to 
force the muscle to produce as much tension as possible. This method is characterised by impulsive action of 
minimal duration between the end of the eccentric braking phase and initiation o f the concentric acceleration 
phase. It relies on the production of a very brief explosive-isometric and eccentric-isometric phase which pre­
cedes the release of the elastic energy stored in the tendons and other components of the scries elastic component 
of the muscle complex during the eccentric deceleration phase (see 1.9, 3.1 and Fig 4.11). If the transition phase 
(or, coupling phase) is prolonged by more than about 0.15 second, the action may be considered to constitute 
ordinary jumping and not classical training plyometrics. A useful visualisation is to imagine that the surface being 
touchcd by the hands or the feet during the plyomctric contact phase is red hot, so that any prolonged contact 
would be dangerous.
It is important to note that the activity is not accurately plyometric if the athlete relies upon ongoing 
feedback processes to control the isometric and concentric actions instead of upon feedforward programmes 
established before any movement begins (see 1.8 and 1.12). True plyometric training usually involves ballistic 
rather than cocontraction processes, a concept discussed earlier (see 1.8).
Plyometrics as a Discrete Training System
A thorough discussion of what is meant by the term plyometrics is essential, bccause one must distinguish clearly 
between plyometric actions, which occur as part of many 
running, jumping, hurdling, striking and other 
rebounding movements in sport, and plyometric training, which applies plyometric actions as a distinct training 
modality according to a definite methodology.
The fairly recent adoption of plyometrics by Western coaches as a so-called 'Russian training secret’ has 
created an unwarranted mystique about a method that has been used extensively in Russia since its scientific 
formalisation in the early 1960s as a discrete training system by Verkhoshansky. In recognising that plyometric 
actions are widespread in most sport, Verkhoshansky has always consistently favoured the use of the term 'shock 
method' instead of'plyometrics' to distinguish between naturally occurring plyometric actions in sport and the 
formal discipline he devised as a discrete training system to develop speed-strength in particular. This is why the 
term powermetrics has been suggested elsewhere in this text to refer to plyometric training, as opposed to 
plyometric actions which occur quite naturally in many natural ballistic movements. The earliest published use of 
the word plyometrics seems to have been in a Soviet publication (Zanon, 1966).
Popular adoption of the term 'plyometrics' in the place of'shock method' has produced this confusion, just as 
popular use of the term 'aerobics' has caused widespread confusion between aerobic (cardiovascular) conditioning 
and acrobics as a form of exercise to music. Consequently, it is probably better to refer to plyometric action as 
stretch-shortening action, as has been done in much of the scientific literature, and to redefine 'plyometrics' as a 
specific training system in its own right, or, powermetrics.
Possibly the easiest way of showing that the shock method can indeed be regarded as a separate, goal-directed 
training system is to examine the concept of resistance training. Resistance to movement is encountered in all 
sport, so the critics of plyometrics as a definite training method should then agree that it is equally logical to 
conclude that resistance training must not be regarded as a distinct training system. On this basis one might also 
conclude that distance running or cycling are resistance training methods, because the athlete certainly experiences 
resistance and produces high levels of muscular tension in these sports.
One might extend this argument further and conclude that all human movement is really resistance training. 
After all, it is somewhat artificial to refer to weight training as resistance training and to ignore other sports that 
also involve work against significant resistance, simply because the loads superficially appear to be heavier in 
weight training. Basic biomechanical analysis of the forces and tensions involved show clcarly that the high levels 
of resistance and muscle tension involved in sports such as gymnastics, swimming, rowing and wrestling easily 
justify any objections to regarding resistance training as a separate training system.
Just as resistance training has adopted means, methods and apparatus from other sports and physical 
activities to create a discrete training discipline, so has plyometric training or powermetrics (as distinct from 
plyometric action) done the same to create its own methodology.
