# Eric's method baseline (draft for Eric's review)

Purpose: this is the step-1 baseline for Flint. It pulls every position, practice, and decision rule out of Eric's own 23-document corpus (Baylor Applied Performance playbook, protocols, assessment manual, professional writing, and HHPR 5355 graduate-course material) so that every future synthesis note comparing an outside source (Landon Evans, TB's Training Info, Old Bull, Harries RTP, SCN/Moyer, etc.) has something of Eric's own to compare against. Date: 2026-09-26. Revised 2026-09-28 with Eric's method interview (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`, 30 of 30 answered).

## Provenance note (read this before the bullets)

Not all 23 documents are Eric's own words, and the two richest sources (the class transcripts) have a diarization problem. Read this once, then use these tags:

- **Eric-authored, high confidence**: the two SportSmith articles, the Performance Playbook Development Plan, the Force Plate Testing V3 and Iso Seated Calf protocols, the Applied Performance Playbook (departmental document under his unit), and the HD ODSF metrics note (adopted practice, though the framework itself is Hawkin Dynamics' own).
- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
- **Both class transcripts (Class 1, Class 3) are diarized entirely under one Fireflies speaker label, "Chris Ruf," for every line, across 100+ minutes combined.** This is true even for Class 3 (Feb. 5), which the syllabus assigns solo to Rash. Fireflies likely defaulted to the meeting organizer's name rather than doing real per-speaker diarization. That means specific sentences in these transcripts cannot be confidently attributed to Rash vs. Ruf vs. Wenger. Bullets drawn from the transcripts are marked **Inferred**, with a citation note, even where the statement itself is a direct, confident, first-person claim in the text. Flint should treat these as "the HHPR 5355 teaching team's shared position, individual speaker unconfirmed" until Eric ratifies them.
  - **Confirmed by Eric, 2026-09-26:** HHPR 5355 is taught each spring by Chris Ruf, Eric and Mike Wenger. The lecture material is split among the three of them. This confirms the course is partly Eric's, but it cannot say who spoke a given transcript line. So transcript bullets stay tagged Inferred and read as **course team positions**. Each one becomes Eric's own only when he claims it, in review or in the interview.
- **Reference material, not Eric's position**: `intencurriculumn.md` is Jason Avedesian's (Clemson) authored curriculum end to end, used by the Development Plan as a benchmark, not as something Eric wrote or necessarily agrees with. The two Unit Goal Programming Standards documents are explicitly staff templates filled in (thinly) by Geyer and Skodinski, not Eric. The AP Assessment Manual V12 and the TechnologyTemplateSOP (TMG) have uncertain/likely-legacy authorship (see Tensions below) and are marked accordingly.

Sections below use **Explicit** (the source states Eric holds this position, with confidence in authorship per the tiers above) and **Inferred** (implied by protocol design, shared course material, or transcript content with unconfirmed speaker attribution).

Tags added 2026-09-28 from the method interview:

- **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric stated or claimed the position in the interview. His words are quoted as "Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Qn):". Q1 claimed exactly four course positions (Vermeil hierarchy, undulating periodization, Dynamic Correspondence, the football energy-system priority stack); other course material stays Inferred.
- **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Qn)**: Eric said the source or practice is not current. The old content is kept and marked, not deleted, so a synthesis note can see what changed.
- **Superseded by interview (Qn)**: a documented position, sometimes from Eric's own slides, that his interview answer replaces.

---

## Philosophy and decision principles

- Applied Performance's stated mission is to "drive elite performance ... by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships," enabling the high-performance team to answer questions, ask better questions, and discover new ones — not to hand down answers unilaterally. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- The department's four operating principles are Athlete Monitoring and Analysis, Athlete Evaluation and Return-to-Performance, Performance Team Collaboration, and Research and Development. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6]
- Institutional framing: "Prepare Champions for Life" across four pillars (academic, athletic, social, spiritual), operationalized through six "One Standard, One Accord" principles. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.3-4]
- Data collection is judged on cost versus insight: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- A test can be scientifically valid and still be the wrong choice operationally: "The lesson wasn't about the test. It was about the infrastructure required to make a test useful ... even a valid test stops being valuable" without staff ownership and consistent collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- General rule for any test or technology, stated as a standing rule rather than a fresh call each time. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)**
- The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)**
- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
- Attribution in practice: outside frameworks are absorbed into the team's own way of working rather than credited to one person. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q27): "We fold it into the mantra of 'this is how we do our business.'" **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q27)** Inference: this is how Eric applies the "we/our" bullet above, so that bullet reads as practice, though the transcript line itself is still unclaimed.
- The "five expectations" culture rules (Golden Rule, Be Disciplined, Be Relentless, Communicate, No Excuses) were presented in the course as absolute [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.1-2]. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q26): "These are more a relic of another coaching era that has held over. I would say none [no deliberate exception], but they are rarely mentioned around here any more." **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q26)**
- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
- Be skeptical of social-media-driven training trends: a viral clip is "just a brief snapshot," stripped of the context that would tell you whether it's sound. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.3]
- Recovery has to be earned by training hard first; a culture of fear grew out of early GPS/load-monitoring work that pushed teams toward under-training in the name of "recovery." **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]

## Department model and roles

- Applied Performance operates inside the Baylor Athletics Health & Wellness department, alongside (not above or below) Athletics Performance, Athletic Medicine, Performance Nutrition, and Mental Health Services. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.5-6]
- Asked whether Applied Performance is a peer discipline that enables Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine and Nutrition, or in-house programming support for Athletic Performance, Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q5): "Both." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q5)** Resolves Tension 2.
- Coach-facing reports are built by whoever supports the team, which for most teams is strength staff. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): "Strength staff will build it most likely; we don't have sport science support for most teams. When applicable, sport science staff would provide it." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q28)**
- The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke — no single discipline owns the athlete's development. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5]
- An Athletic Performance coach is framed in explicit contrast to a narrower "Strength Coach" identity: "we/our" and holistic mind-body-spirit development versus "me/my" and just lifting/running. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5; week1-lecture.md p.13]
- The current Baylor Applied Performance Operations Guide is judged, by Eric's own gap analysis, as missing: an intern/GA curriculum, sport-specific data dictionaries, daily operational checklists, Baylor-specific (not generic-template) technology workflows, and a guiding-principles/policy framework for staff and interns. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 1, 3.2]
- A three-phase roadmap (Foundation, weeks 1-4; Operational Depth, weeks 5-10; Education and Culture, weeks 11-16+) is the stated plan to close those gaps, ending with an annual Playbook review cycle each May. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Some assessments coaches already run inside practice should not be duplicated; use that existing data to triangulate rather than re-testing, and set objective criteria for coach-mandated tests when none exist. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Team Cultures and Assessments"]

## Testing and assessment

- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
- Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ("how you do it in January needs to be the same as how you do it in April") or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6]
- Favor a small number of valid, reliable tests mapped to clear KPI categories over an exhaustive battery — illustrated with a simple baseball profile (bodyweight, 60-yard dash, vertical jump, broad jump, back squat, push-up max). **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.6; week1-lecture.md p.16]
- Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7] (See the cadence bullet below: there is no department-wide cadence.)
- There is no common testing cadence across sports; each sport keeps its own schedule. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q9): "We currently don't have a consistent cadence across all sports. Individual sports have their own unique schedules." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)**
- No sport performs true 1RM testing. Maxes are projected from observation plus the athlete's history. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q10): "things are ballparked based on other information we're grabbing on the athlete: watching them move in real time, then using historical context to make future programming decisions around projected 1RMs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q10)**
- Change of direction is not tested in most sports. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q13): "If the data is captured, it's on an individual sport basis and that information lives with that coach." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q13)** The RTP templates still gate on COD and FMS, run by Athletic Medicine or the sport coach (Tension 18, resolved 2026-10-02).
- The Assessment Manual V12 is not current. A new, more robust manual is in development and will incorporate the NCAA technology and sport-science recommendations. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)** Every bullet below sourced to `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md` is therefore Legacy.
- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
- Reassessment timing is governed by three factors: proximity to competition, the expected magnitude of change for that training phase and athlete level, and current recovery status: "do not reassess an athlete if there is known fatigue." **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md, "Reassessment"]
- 1RM testing is reserved for intermediate/advanced athletes with real exposure to near-maximal loads; novices and most women's-sport testing default to repetition-max protocols, which are described as better tolerated neurologically, psychologically, and physically for smaller-framed lifters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q10)**: no sport tests true 1RM now; was Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- Velocity-based 1RM estimation (linear-displacement transducer, ~10% load increments to 85-90% or a target mean velocity) is preferred over live 1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing, with published target mean velocities at 1RM (squat 0.3 m/s, bench 0.2 m/s, power hang snatch 1.0 m/s, power hang clean 0.8 m/s). **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8, Q10)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md] Inference: Q10 describes projection from observation and history and does not mention a velocity protocol.
- The Baylor Sport Assessment Table (V4) assigns a specific battery per sport (movement screen, anthropometrics, CMJ, broad jump, weighted throw, upper/lower strength estimation, strength endurance, aerobic fitness, repeat sprint ability, linear sprint, change of direction) rather than testing every sport the same way. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)**; was Inferred. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q9): "That assessment schedule was never used." Inference: the table was never practice, not just outdated. [update-baylor-sport-assessment-table-v4.md]
- The current data dictionary is organized by vendor (Catapult, Perch, ForceDecks, Polar), not by sport, which Eric's own gap analysis flags as a real usability problem for staff and a priority to fix with sport-specific, threshold-contextualized dictionaries. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2]

## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring

- Force plates (CMJ testing) were already the department's longitudinal performance-tracking tool well before the 2022-23 wellness-survey experiment, and remained in place after that experiment ended. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
- The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds, not a single cut-off or position-group thresholds. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2): "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized." Individualized against: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)** Inference: "should be" may describe the intended rule rather than a fully running one; no numeric threshold was given. See Tension 12 (daily testing versus a Wednesday read), resolved 2026-10-02: daily jumps build the baseline and SWC, Wednesday is the decision read.
- The dynamic strength index (DSI: CMJ against isometric mid-thigh pull peak force) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q21): "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** This is not the SJ-CMJ gap the question asked about. Evidence check done 2026-09-29 (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`): cite it as Eric's practice, tagged [contested; the ratio tracks IMTP strength; one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data]. See Tension 17.
- The standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks: hands-free squat, squat jump (quarter-squat start, 3s hold), countermovement jump (x3), hop test / repeated CMJ (10 reps total, n=5 pairs), and single-leg CMJ (x3 per leg) — each with a scripted weigh-in, stabilization, and rep protocol. **Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)** [revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
- Metric selection for force-plate reporting follows a disciplined framework: pick 1-2 output metrics (the obvious performance result, e.g. jump height), 1-3 driver metrics (what produces the output, e.g. braking/propulsive force), 1-3 strategy metrics (how the athlete achieved it, e.g. phase durations), optional symmetry metrics (L/R differences), and add "fluffy" metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale. **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** [hd-odsf-metrics.md — origin: Hawkin Dynamics]
- NordBord hamstring testing was retired for roster-wide football monitoring (after starting January 2023) because a 25-30 minute per-group session could not be sustained across 120+ athletes without large, uncontrolled gaps in the data, and staff turnover ended the coordination needed to run it at scale. The decision rule stated: keep a demanding test only where you have "smaller numbers, clear clinical purpose, dedicated oversight" (now used for targeted return-to-play groups paired with joint-specific isometric testing); drop it where you can't guarantee consistent, comparable collection. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]

## Load monitoring and GPS

- The core GPS technology stack is Catapult (device/OpenField software) with Kitman Labs as the central athlete-management system for cross-technology storage, scaling, and visualization. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Core GPS metrics tracked: maximum velocity, total distance, player load, field time, heart-rate bands, velocity/acceleration/deceleration effort bands, and Inertial Movement Analysis (IMA) for indoor sessions without GPS coverage. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.11-13, Data Dictionary]
- A documented step-by-step SOP exists for the full GPS session lifecycle: charging, alarm-setting, activity creation, live period management, post-session sync, data cleaning (spike detection), tagging, and PDF export/reporting. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md pp.9-11]
- No sport-specific or position-specific GPS/load thresholds currently exist in the documented data dictionary; it is generic and vendor-organized, and building contextualized per-sport thresholds is named as unfinished, prioritized work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a gap)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.3, Phase 2] The formal gap is confirmed. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q7): "They do not exist formally." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q7)** The question also asked about informal thresholds; that half was not answered.
- Heavy GPS/load-monitoring data was described as having bred a "culture of fear" in the field broadly (do less, to protect recovery), which the course material argues actually leaves athletes under-prepared for competition. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10]
- Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal. Wellness surveys are still used, deliberately, in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions, where subjective context still adds value objective data can't supply. **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]

## Speed and sprint

- Linear sprint testing uses a 2-point start for team-sport athletes (for reliability), athlete self-selected start timing, at least two maximal-effort reps over 30-40 meters. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)**; was Inferred (author uncertain) [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
- SmartSpeed timing gates are the standard tool for sprint, agility, and reaction-time testing across the department. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity) and is described as harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power, but as the biggest separator between good and great athletes at the elite level. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11]
- Issurin's residual training effects (speed fades fastest, 5 ± 3 days; Block Periodization PDF p. 35, as cited in `docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md`) drive speed programming. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** See the residual-effects bullets under Conditioning and Periodization, and Tension 11.

## Strength and power

- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + shared course material) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
- The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky), matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + slides) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14; week1-lecture.md p.34]
- Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
- Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21] Not claimed in the interview. The in-season dose itself is unknown: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps."
- Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use") [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
- Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block, used consistently across strength and power teaching. **Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.15] Inference: with no true 1RM testing (Q10), any %1RM prescription rests on projected maxes. Kept on that explicit basis (Tension 16, resolved 2026-10-02).
- Strength's residual training effect is treated as roughly 30 days; a minimal retention dose is still trained within that window, even during lower-strength-emphasis blocks. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-25] Inference: consistent with Eric siding with Issurin (Q16), whose strength residual is 30 ± 5 days, though Q16 was about speed and he did not claim this bullet.
- Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21; week1-lecture.md p.46]

## Conditioning and energy systems

- Conditioning is defined two ways: (1) how well an athlete can meet the energy requirements of their specific sport/activity, and (2) how well they sustain strength, speed, and power output across a full competition. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.22]
- All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
- A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once — priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands (e.g., for football: prepared for fall camp first, then the first game). **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31]
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the interview, **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**
- Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
- Anaerobic (lactate) threshold heart-rate zones are assigned by athlete body size rather than a single number: roughly 165 bpm for big/tall athletes, 170 for medium, 175 for small, with Zone 1-4 bands set as percentages of that individual threshold. **Superseded by interview (Q20)**; was Explicit [class-4-2026.md pp.28-29]
- The anaerobic-threshold heart rate in use is the age-based method (the slide deck's max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at about 85% of that [class-4-2026.md p.27]). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q20): "Age-based." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q20)** Resolves Tension 6.
- The traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining; the traits hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest; this ordering is used to sequence what needs the most frequent re-exposure. **Superseded by interview (Q16)**; was Explicit [class-4-2026.md p.47] Eric now sides with Issurin (speed fades fastest). See Tension 11.
- Training intensities between roughly 75-90% of maximal effort are labeled (via Francis) "no man's land" — too fast to build alactic power cleanly, too slow to build real aerobic capacity — and are treated as a zone to generally avoid as a primary training target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.48]
- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
- Joel Jamieson's *Ultimate MMA Conditioning* is recommended as the single best practical resource for energy-system development, on the basis that its methods transfer cleanly to non-combat sports despite the MMA framing. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md pp.49-50; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]

## Periodization and programming

- Macro/meso/microcycle structure is used as the standard planning language, with an explicit reminder that a "training week" does not have to equal 7 calendar days — it can be extended to fit training themes around a real competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.17-18; week1-lecture.md p.39]
- The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
- In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.21]
- Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
- An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.22-23; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.13-15]
- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27] Inference: these are Issurin's figures, and Eric sides with Issurin (interview 2026-09-28, Q16), so the speed half reads as his; the aerobic and strength halves were not asked directly.
- In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
- The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**
- Bye weeks: three practice days, extra rest and recovery, slightly higher practice volume than a game week, a speed and strength top-up, and harder work for players with few game snaps. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q17): "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)**
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

16. **No true 1RM against %1RM prescription.** No sport tests true 1RM (Q10), while Prilepin's chart and the phase bands are written in %1RM [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.19; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]. Inference: loads are percentages of projected maxes, so their error carries into every prescription. Not a contradiction in practice, but worth stating.
    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Keep %1RM and Prilepin prescription, stated explicitly as built on projected maxes (observation plus history, Q10), not tested 1RMs.
17. **DSI as a plyo-vs-strength switch against the evidence.** Eric uses DSI to choose plyometric versus max-strength emphasis (Q21). The evidence check (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`) finds that IMTP PF explains most of DSI's variance, that the 0.60/0.80 cutoffs were never validated, and that the one controlled trial found a benefit only in its strength arm. Inference: keep the test, but decide on CMJ PF and IMTP PF alongside the ratio, and set cutoffs from the roster.
18. **COD and FMS gates in the RTP templates against Q12/Q13.** The LE template gates Evaluation on the 10-5 COD test and on FMS > 14 (`docs/interview/2026-09-28-method-interview.md`), while Q13 says COD is not tested in most sports and Q12 says screens do not change decisions.
    **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** The gates stay in the RTP templates. The baseline names who runs them (Athletic Medicine or the sport coach), not Applied Performance, consistent with "the template answers readiness" (Q22).

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

735	ground or some object. Even in Russia, the birthplace of scientific plyometrics, the emphasis has been almost 
736	entirely on actions which exert some form of impact loading on the body. It may also be stated that all running, 
737	jumping and other ballistic actions involve a phase of plyometric activity, so that shock contact of parts of the 
738	body with some surface would appear to be the common denominator underlying all plyometrics.
739	However, this is not the only way of producing plyomctric action. As discussed earlier, all plyometric drills 
740	so far used in the athletic world are of the impact variety. The existence of the non-impact variety was recognised 
741	when the author used a force plate to analyse biomechanically martial arts movements and the seated fitness 
742	system (Supersitting) developed by his wife, Lisa Ericson of Denver, Colorado. She attracted worldwide attention 
743	for her 'seated aerobics’ classes, which she developed after becoming paralysed. A former professional ice-skatcr 
744	who was determined to explore and expand the range of possibilities for physical activity by spinal cord patients, 
745	she developed a system of exercise rehabilitation which can produce very significant improvements in motor 
746	control, strength and hypertrophy without the use of weights or any other resistance apparatus.
747	After years of experimentation with different training methods, she has managed to gain recognition for her 
748	work and for several years has been teaching her seated fitness class to spinal patients at the renowned Craig 
749	Rehabilitation Hospital in Denver, as well as to regular aerobics clients at other athletic clubs in that city.
750	279
751	
752	
753	######## PDF idx 291 (printed 280)
754	SUPERTRAINING
755	What distinguishes her exercise routines from normal aerobics is that she often uses very rapid widc-rangc 
756	movements choreographed at rates exceeding 240 beats per minute, interspersed with rhythmic transitional PNF- 
757	type patterns, offered over a session which charactcristically lasts for 60 minutes. After an extended warm-up to 
758	ensure that the arms are adequately prepared for the main, high-intensity phase, the subsequent movements arc 
759	initiated and terminated explosively in sets o f uninterrupted sequences which regularly change their form and 
760	direction to avoid excessive fatigue, habituation or injury.
761	This system recruits the myotatic stretch reflex dynamically and powerfully in agonistic and antagonistic 
762	muscles over as large a range of movement as possible. The use of patterns, deliberately deviating in space and 
763	timing from those recommended by PNF and Pilatcs practitioners, cause pronounced overflow to adjacent 
764	muscles and speed up the rehabilitation of spinal patients, a phenomenon that has attracted the attention of 
765	medical specialists.
766	Ericson's system may best be categorised as non-impact plyometrics, (non-impact powermetrics) becausc it 
767	obeys all the requirements of plyometrics as originally conceived by Russian scientists. True plyometric activity 
768	involves a ballistic action which is rapidly terminated by eccentric and explosive isometric muscle contraction, 
769	followed immediately by a powerful conccntric recoil mediated by recruitment of the myotatic stretch reflex and 
770	augmented by the release of elastic energy stored in the connective tissues of the muscle-tendon complex.
771	The system developed by Ericson is reminiscent in many ways of some o f the training methods used in 
772	karate which involve explosive snap punches, blows and kicks, or some boxing training drills such as shadow 
773	boxing or speed ball. In karate, the limbs are thrust powerfully outwards and then drawn back in a whip-likc 
774	action, ready for the next repetition. In the martial arts, the number of repetitions are relatively few in number 
775	and separated by very brief intervals between them, whereas the Ericson system uses many repetitions without 
776	pause. The karate punch is rarely whipped back immediately, but makes contact with its target for a very short 
777	period, which is sufficient to dissipate much of the elastic energy stored in the connectivc tissues. The transition 
778	phase between eccentric and concentric phases in the Ericson system is usually shorter than that in karate and, 
779	therefore, maintains high levels of muscle tension for prolonged periods. The shorter transition phase and the 
780	greater number of continuous repetitions in the Ericson system probably explains the differences in functional and 
781	structural development produced by it compared with the karate system.
782	The implications of the Ericson Supersitting system for sports training are great. Traditional plyometric 
783	drills have often been criticised because they all involve high impact forces produced during explosive contact of 
784	parts of the body with some surfacc or object. The Ericson system eliminates the need for impulsive contact with 
785	a hard surface and drastically diminishes the intensity of shock waves transmitted to the joints and entire 
786	musculoskeletal system by explosive two-way movements.
787	Most of the Ericson movements offered in the average fitness class more accurately would be classed as 
788	submaximal plyomctrics, just like the more usual repetitive rebounding drills over obstacles or with medicinc balls. 
789	Performed in the form of all-out single movements, they become maximal non-impact plyomctrics. Since depth- 
790	jumps involve the projection of the entire mass of the body, maximal impact plyometrics will generally increase 
791	muscle tension to a greater extent than the equivalent non-impact movements for the leg and hip extensors (e.g. the 
792	karate thrust-kick).
793	Nevertheless, maximal non-impact plyometrics, like submaximal impact plyomctrics can serve as a 
794	preparatory tool for maximal impact plyometrics, for enhancing other functional and structural qualities or for 
795	selectively offering plyometric training to certain muscle groups instead of unnecessarily stressing the entire 
796	musculature. These qualities may include strength, musclc hypertrophy, muscle endurance and speed-strcngth 
797	endurance. To date, research into plyometrics has devoted most o f its attention to increases in speed-strcngth 
798	(power), rather than these other qualities, so that preliminary studies executed in 1995 by University of Pretoria 
799	physiotherapy students supervised by Siff and Ericson warrant more detailed expansion.
800	Meanwhile, the significant increases in strength, speed-strength endurance and hypertrophy (which are not 
801	simply a result of propelling their wheelchairs) achieved by Ericson and her wheelchair athletes emphasize that 
802	there is still much more to be discovered about the methods and consequences of the different types of resistance 
803	training. Up till now, it has been considered fairly accurate to state that strength and power are best achieved by 
804	few repetitions of high-intensity exercises, whereas hypertrophy is best produced by medium numbers of 
805	repetitions with 65-85% of one's 1RM. Piyomctric exercise traditionally fits into this scheme as a means of 
806	enhancing speed-strength.
807	280
808	
809	
810	######## PDF idx 292 (printed 281)
811	SUPERTRAINING
812	From the changes observed in Ericson's students, it would appear that even plyomctrics should be examined 
813	in the context of the nature, duration and pattern of sets and repetitions, since it may be used to enhance fitness 
814	qualities other than speed-strength alone. Her system of non-impact plyometrics offers a safe addition to the 
815	fields of sports plyometrics and popular aerobics. It is potentially beneficial to any athletes who require high 
816	levels of upper body power and endurance, and vastly expands the somewhat uninspiring repertoire of arm 
817	rehabilitation techniques generally offered to injured clients or spinal damaged patients in conventional 
818	physiotherapy. The aerobics world has erroneously labelled some rapid landing and jumping movements as 
819	aerobic plyometrics, but the latter, unlike the Ericson movements, in no way comply with the definition of 
820	classical plyomctrics. It is apparent that the aerobics community, as well as strength conditioning coaches, have a 
821	great deal to leam from an innovative non-impact plyometric system developed by a creative athlete in a 
822	wheelchair.
823	Non-Impact Plyometrics in Sports Training
824	Although sports involving explosive non-impact plyometric actions are commonplace in international sport, these 
825	actions had not been used systematically as plyometric training drills prior to the fundamental research conducted 
826	in this field by the author in 1994 (Fig 5.7 was derived from some of this work on upper-body non-impact 
827	plyometrics). 
828	Every Western training book on plyometrics to date seems to have been devoted exclusively to 
829	impact plyometrics using high inertia systems such as the human body, weighted medicine balls or other heavy 
830	objects. This is entirely a consequence of the West, in its quest for 'Russian training secrets', simply applying the 
831	pioneering scientific work earned out by Verkhoshansky to devise an ever expanding repertoire of'plyometric 
832	drills’ and market various high inertia systems for explosive training.
833	In this endeavour, a vast encyclopaedia of non-impact actions from boxing and the martial arts, in particular, 
834	lay largely unutilised. To this we may now add many of the movements developed by Ericson in her SMART 
835	seated fitness system. Low impact plyometric methods using very light objects for activities such as throwing or 
836	kicking may also be included in this low inertia approach to plyometrics. Interestingly, many of the movements 
837	derived from all of these systems share a common denominator in PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular 
838	Facilitation), in that they naturally follow spiral and diagonal paths which move both ways across the midline of 
839	the body. Deliberate deviation from the classical PNF patterns is also encouraged in applying non-impact 
840	plyometrics, since this develops a wider range of more demanding functional motor abilities that typify sport.
841	Thus, from the realm of martial arts alone, one may borrow thrust punches, rising blocks, downward blocks, 
842	knife-hand thrusts, palm-heel strikes, front kicks, side snap kicks, side thrust kicks, front kicks and many other 
843	standard forms in a wide variety of full or limited range movements to offer non-impact plyometric drills. These 
844	actions may be performed solo in a static stance with some of the classical pre-stretching techniques, with 
845	explosive punches terminating in a brief isometrically-hcld end position or with rapid recoil actions which snap 
846	the extremities back to their starting positions.
847	The same movements may be done in fixed routines between opponents standing facing one another, in the 
848	form of kata (prescribed sequences o f movements) or in freestyle sparring (no body contact). These offer a 
849	repertoire, not only of non-impact plyometric drills, but also of many other methods for enhancing explosive 
850	strength, movement speed, quickness, rapid decision-making skill, reaction time, kinaesthetic awareness and other 
851	qualities which are important in sports demanding rapidity of action. The use of martial arts, boxing and Ericson's 
852	SMART methods in explosive sports training was described and demonstrated at the 1994 NSCA (National 
853	Strength & Conditioning Association) Conference by Siff and Ericson (Myths and Facts o f Speed-Strength, 
854	Explosive Power and Plyometric Training June 1994). The advisability of integrating such methods into a 
855	periodised weight training scheme was emphasized to enhance acquisition of the necessary explosive qualities and 
856	minimise the possibility of injury, as was the role of cognitive plyometric processes and asymmetric plyometric 
857	training in ensuring that sport specific motor qualities are developed.
858	Resisted and Water Plyometric Training
859	Plyometric drills may be offered with some form of resistance being imposed during the amortisation phase, 
860	concentric rebound phase or both of these phases. Thus, one may jump and land with light weights or against 
861	resistance offered by elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips. Although both of these 
862	methods increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction, they also 
863	increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even 
864	normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training. No resistance
865	281
866	
867	
868	######## PDF idx 293 (printed 282)
869	SUPERTRAINING
870	methods should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupl’ 
871	time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especia 
872	during the landing or contact phase.
873	A far safer resisted alternative is water or aqua plyometrics, a method used for many decades to decrease the 
874	landing force and increase the resistance during the recoil phase. Although this variant does not offer maximal cf 
875	shock method plyometrics, it can serve as a usual form of preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, especially for 
876	one-legged drills. The depth of water determines the level of resistance, with chest or shoulder high water offering 
877	greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscic activity, smaller impact 
878	forces and enhanced safety. Repeated aqua jumps for developing rebound explosive muscle endurance with one or 
879	both legs are considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the 
880	latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive 
881	sports. Upper body aqua plyomctrics may be offered in varying depths of water by performing suitable non­
882	impact plyometric actions derived from the martial arts or SMART fitness systems, as discussed above.
883	Popular Inform ation on Plyom etrics
884	Most of the popular plyometric textbooks in the West (e.g. Chu, 1992; Radcliffe & Farantinos, 1985) present an 
885	interesting array of jumping and rebound activities, many of which do not constitute true plyometric training as 
886	originally conceived by Russian scientists. Such exercises are often supplementary or preparatory movements 
887	which lead up to or accompany plyomctric training, but they are not really ‘shock method’ plyometric drills. 
888	Most books classify extended range swinging, passing or catching of mcdicine balls or other objects as 
889	'plyometric’, although the amortisation phase is too long to produce classical plyometrics. This is not to say that 
890	these exerciscs are not useful: they can play a useful role in enhancing qualities such as eye-hand coordination, 
891	eccentric strength and starting strength, but they arc not strictly plyometric.
892	Although some of these books, often advertised to be the most complete ever written on plyometrics, claim 
893	to dispel the myths and misinformation about plyometrics, the contents do not confirm these sentiments, for they 
894	often fail to reveal an thorough understanding of the scientific model upon which the original Russian shock 
895	method (“udamiye metod”) is based.
896	This method was refined by identifying many different strength qualities such as strength-speed, speed- 
897	strength, explosive strength, acceleration strength, maximal strength, absolute strength and starting strength. In 
898	particular, it relies on the production of a very brief explosive-isometric and eccentric-isometric phase which 
899	precedes the release of the elastic energy stored in the tendons and other components of the series elastic 
900	component o f the muscle complex during the eccentric deceleration phase. Although most books pay detailed 
901	attention to the myotatic reflex, which comprises a tonic, longer duration reflex and a phasic, rapid reflex, they do 
902	not discuss their relationship to the different types o f plyometric drill. The relevance of positive supportive 
903	reaction, the crossed extensor reflex and other important reflexes is also not covered. The role of correctly phased 
904	breathing, which is vital to maximal plyomctrics and efficient stabilisation of the body, is not mentioned in any 
905	book.
906	Distinction is seldom made between maximal and submaximal plyometrics (and how they are produced), nor 
907	is the concurrent and sequential prescription of plyometric and other forms of training discussed in any depth. 
908	For example, several books advocate sessions with over 100 repetitions of plyomctric movements, sometimes 
909	combined with resistance training. This volume of maximal plyometrics (unlike sub-maximal plyometrics) is 
910	neither productive nor safe for any athlete. Maximal plyometrics, like maximal weight lifting, involves single all- 
911	out repetitions separated by a few minutes of rest. It is extremely demanding on the central nervous system and 
912	imposes great mechanical strain on the tendons, in particular.
913	To ascertain whether an athlete needs plyometric or heavy resistance training depends on measuring the 
914	strength deficit (see Ch 1), prescription of plyometric training remains haphazard, yet plyometric books rarely 
915	mention this concept. The opposition to plyometric training (powermetrics) by some experts is often the result 
916	of this type of guesswork training, which can hinder performance and increase the risk of injury.
917	Some authors rightly criticize the recommendation sometimes put forward that athletes should be able to 
918	squat 1.5-2 times bodymass in order to use certain plyomctric drills, sincc they consider that this criterion is not 
919	based on research evidence and does not apply to all plyometric exercises. This recommendation is a safety 
920	measure based on force plate analysis of maximal plyometrics in the form of depth jum ps, where the ground 
921	reaction force on the lower extremity can easily exceed 6 times bodyweight. This guideline was never intended to
922	282
923	
924	
925	######## PDF idx 294 (printed 283)
926	SUPERTRAINING
927	apply religiously to submaximal plyometrics using small drops, skipping drills or less demanding actions. This 
928	misunderstanding of Russian guidelines is largely a result of an incomplete grasp of the scientific principles on 
929	which the original shock method was based.
930	Coaches would appreciate more what plyometrics really is if they were introduced to some of the facilitation 
931	techniques used in physiotherapeutic PNF (see 7.2). The physical therapist sometimes imposes a short, sharp 
932	jerk on an eccentrically or isometrically contracting muscle to produce strong muscle contraction in a weakened 
933	musclc. Relatively prolonged movements such as many of the drills recommended in most books are used for 
934	other purposes, including the reduction of spasm or increasing functional range of movement. These principles 
935	have preceded sporting plyometrics by several decades, so it is surprising that so much confusion still abounds 
936	over plyomctrics. Certainly, the so-called plyometric drills in current Western texts are known to enhance 
937	performance, but it is not predominantly due to plyometric training, but more to the increased loading o f eccentric 
938	contraction, the conditioning o f connective tissue, the improvement o f voluntary starting strength from the quasi- 
939	isometric state, the use ofprestretch, and enhancement o f acceleration strength by increasing the velocity of 
940	projectiles such as medicine balls.
941	Plyometrics and the Brain
942	Rccent brain research reveals that piyomctric action is not simply a phenomenon that can be adequately explained 
943	on the basis of stored elastic energy and the stretch shortening cycle. The phenomenon of plyometrics involves fa r 
944	more intricate processes than reflexive muscle activities that operate at the level of the spinal column and bypass the 
945	brain. Many of the subtleties and complexities o f plyometrics can be missed if one is preoccupied with the 
946	prescription of so-called piyomctric drills or with laboratory measurement of the stretch-shortening cyclc as a local 
947	musculotendinous phenomenon. In both cases, it is easy to overlook the possibility that activities such as depth- 
948	jumping or medicinc ball throwing may involve non-local events, particularly the enormously complicated computer 
949	programs in the brain.
950	While it is accurate to state that plyometric actions arc extremely rapid and therefore occur at the level of 
951	specific spinal nerves without involving conscious thought processes, it must be remembered that the preparatory 
952	period prior to the piyomctric action can involve higher order mental processing of exceptional intricacy (sec Fig 
953	3.11). In fact, the period prior to execution of any skilled movement involves running mental programmes that have 
954	been stored and refined by repeated rehearsal in the brain of the well-trained athlete.
955	One can distinguish further between a plyometric action produced under conditions in which the athlete 
956	anticipates a particular course of action (cognitive plyometrics) and a plyometric action produced as a purely 
957	reflexive response under unexpected circumstances (non-cognitive plyometrics). The latter type of plyometrics 
958	occur primarily under survival or self-preservation conditions intended to protect a person from injury or death. 
959	The rapidity of the event does not permit any forethought or planning, but relies on primitive reflexes that generally 
960	lend to bypass the brain by acting at the more spontaneous level of the spinal cord. Cognitive plyometrics, though 
961	also a very rapid phenomenon, is preceded by a phase of thinking that prepares the person for a specific course of 
962	action to achieve a definite goal.
963	One should not conclude simplistically that non-cognitivc plyometrics are purely instinctive or automatic 
964	actions which involve no cognitive or learning processes. It should never be forgotten that efficient execution of 
965	piyomctric actions and drills only takes place after a considerable amount o f practice using cognitive processes. In 
966	fact, most athletes do not manage to perfect plyometric skills even after many weeks of practice. The use of 
967	numerous sequential repetitions to imprint these skills may constitute the inappropriate strategy because classical 
968	plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete. 
969	Submaximal plyometrics and pseudo-plyometrics may be performed in a state of advancing fatigue, unlike classical 
970	shock method' plyometrics. The neural and reflexive processes are quite different in each case.
971	Even then, what appears to be quite reflexive still involves a certain degree of cognitive preparation and control. 
972	The lack of adequate mention o f the importance of cognitive and learning processes in plyometrics by all popular 
973	texts on the subject constitutes a major deficit in the field. Reflexes are casually referred to as entirely robotic 
974	actions that elicit or inhibit musclc contraction, but little is mentioned of the fact that reflexes can be trained and 
975	modified, something that the renowned Russian physiologist, Pavlov, had proved some 70 years ago in the form of 
976	his'conditioned reflexes'. Later, Skinner (1938) distinguished between two types of conditioning: which he called 
977	respondent conditioning, in which the response is modified by a preceding stimulus, and operant conditioning, in 
978	which the response is strengthened or weakened by events that follow the response.
979	283
980	
981	
982	######## PDF idx 295 (printed 284)
983	SUPERTRAINING
984	In the plyometric situation, this implies that a stimulus such as an emotion (e.g. fear, excitement) or a men 
985	image (or visualisation) one entertains before an action like a depth jump can shape the subsequent neuromuscJ 
986	reflexes. Likewise, any event (such as the jarring of the body, post-exercise fatigue or an injury) following 
987	plyometric action can modify these reflexes. In fact, it is common for plyometric activity to be associated w' 
988	both respondent and operant conditioning.
989	It has also been shown that if the reflex learning proccss is carried out with the subject in a parti 
990	physiological or psychological state, then the conditioned reflexes are exhibited only when the same state is pre 
991	but not when the state is different. This phenomenon is known as state-dependent learning. Its existence imp!’ 
992	that plyometric proficiency or deficiency learned in a specific training situation may not be reproduced 
993	competitive circumstances which differ from those of the learning situation.
994	What the preceding few paragraphs imply is that it is only partially correct to regard plyometrics as a pr 
995	in which basic reflexes automatically produce a powerful muscle contraction which is accompanicd by elastic energy 
996	released after the muscle has been stretched eccentrically. It is vital to note that the entire plyometric process 
997	involves complex state-dependent learning events which modify the pattern o f reflex activity according to how the 
998	given plyometric drills are executed. This may be one of the reasons why some researchers have carried out 
999	experiments which apparently have shown plyometric training to produce little or no improvement in speed- 
1000	strength or sporting performance. One cannot ignore the neural factors involved in studying the effects of any 
1001	neuromuscular phenomena: study of muscular output alone is incomplete and lack of control over essential neural 
1002	factors affecting the experiment can easily distort the results.
1003	It should be more obvious now that plyometric training is not simply a matter o f dropping from a height or 
1004	throwing an object for a given number of repetitions to improve fitness qualities such as strength-speed or explosive 
1005	strength. 
1006	Sport usually involves the reproduction of a wide variety of technical skills under expected and 
1007	unexpected conditions, so that feedforward training and other 'visualisation' (mental and kinaesthetic imaging) 
1008	techniques must be used to enable the athlete not only to increase explosive strength and strength-specd, but also to 
1009	efficiently manage any plyometric actions under real sporting conditions.
1010	Lest the connection between visualization and movement be oversimplified by sports psychologists, 
1011	neuroscientist. Dr Kensall Wise of the University of Michigan, points out that the part o f the brain which can 
1012	visualise a given action is totally separate from those parts which initiate the muscle contractions to carry out the 
1013	action (Scientific American, Oct 1988: 23). Although fairly modem research has identified some of the connections 
1014	between some regions of the brain and functions such as sight, hearing and motor output, researchers still have only 
1015	a vague idea of how the nervous system initiates and manages any given actions.
1016	The importance of ballistic activity to humankind recently has been shown to extend far beyond the realms of 
1017	sport. Neurophysiologist, William Calvin, has proposed the fascinating hypothesis that the brain's planning of 
1018	ballistic movements may have played a major role in the development of language, music and intelligence over the 
1019	ages (Scientific American, Oct 1994). He makes this proposal, since ballistic movements and language processes 
1020	involve some of the same regions of the brain, in particular those associated with sequencing and planning. In 
1021	reaching this conclusion, he emphasizes that ballistic movements, unlike cocontractive slower movements, require a 
1022	great amount of planning and problem solving. Slow movements may be corrected readily by ongoing feedback 
1023	information, but ballistic movements require the brain to determine every detail of the action in advance by mentally 
1024	planning the exact sequence of neural activation for numerous individual muscles.
1025	Apparently, parts of the language cortex of the brain serve a far more generalised function than previously 
1026	suspected. It is implicated in the production of novel sequences of sensations and movements for both the hands 
1027	and mouth, so that ballistic arm actions may play a role in mental development. Calvin adds that improvements 
1028	in language skills might improve dexterity and vice versa. The emphasis placed by Russian coachcs on athletes 
1029	being able to accurately describe, draw and visualise sporting movements would appear to correlate with this 
1030	proposal. Instead of simply executing entertaining plyometric drills like biological robots, athletes would be well 
1031	advised to integrate cognitive processes more actively into the training programme.
1032	Various Shock M ethods
1033	Plyometrics should not be thought of as the only type of'shock training', even though the term 'shock method' 
1034	was the preferred name given to the plyometric method by Verkhoshansky when he first formalised this category 
1035	of impulsive training. Training plyometrics may be regarded as one of several shock methods that may be used in 
1036	special strength training to provide intense stimulation to compel the body to attain a higher level of functional
1037	284
1038	
1039	
1040	######## PDF idx 296 (printed 285)
1041	SUPERTRAINING
1042	adaptation. The principle of gradual progressive overloading may, after a prolonged period of unvaried use, 
1043	sometimes fail to improve strength or performance, as is commonly the case among elite athletes. 
1044	In this 
1045	situation, it may be necessary to disrupt the persistent state of stagnation by use of one of the following shock 
1046	methods (see 7.1):
1047	• plyometrics 
1048	• forced repetitions
1049	• supramaximal methods 
1050	• electrical stimulation (macrostimulation)
1051	• repeated single I RM training 
1052	• restricted range maxima
1053	• contrast methods 
1054	• maximal eccentrics
1055	The appropriate method, its timing and the duration of its use must be chosen with great care, since lack of 
1056	progress may be due to overtraining rather than long-term stagnation. The use of any shock method under such 
1057	circumstances is potentially harmful and definitely detrimental to performance. These methods arc generally 
1058	unsuitable for novices and should only be employed by experienced athletes with a solid background of special 
1059	strength training.
1060	5.2.5 The D evelopm ent of Strength-Endurance
1061	Strength-endurance involves the production of muscular tension without a decrease in efficiency over a long 
1062	period. Strength-endurance, like explosive strength, has several forms, depending upon the motor pattern of the 
1063	athletic activity, in particular the categories of dynamic and static endurance.
1064	Dynamic strength-endurance is typical of exercises involving repetitive and significant muscular tension at a 
1065	relatively slow speed of movement, as well as repeated cyclic or acyclic exercises requiring speed-strength. In the 
1066	latter case we are referring to the specific endurance to execute special speed-strength and explosive work without 
1067	adecrease in efficiency over a relatively long period. Static strength-endurance is typical of activities associated 
1068	with the maintenance of maximal and near-maximal tension, as well as the moderate tension necessary for holding 
1069	a specific posture (for example, in shooting or speed-skating).
1070	The development of strength-endurance is an inherent characteristic and a fundamental principle of training 
1071	for dev eloping general endurance. Training for strength-endurance is determined predominantly by:
1072	1. The magnitude of the load
1073	2. The tempo of movement
1074	3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements
1075	4. The rest interval between training sessions
1076	5. The length of the training period
1077	6. The initial levels of strength-cndurance of the athlete
1078	7. The kinesiological structure of the movement
1079	8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance.
1080	Repetition work with weights 25-50% of IRM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for 
1081	developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness of strength-endurance development, using equivalent weights 
1082	and movement tempos, will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter 
1083	duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; 
1084	Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961).
1085	Strength-endurance, like the other characteristics of muscular activity, is specific. However, the specificity 
1086	of strength-endurance is expressed to a lesser degree than the specificity of speed, for example, while its carry­
1087	over from one activity to another is greater. When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant 
1088	resistance (exceeding 75-80% of IRM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to 
1089	developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966).
1090	This study by Zatsiorsky showed that isometric endurance increased 84% as a result of exercising 10 times a 
1091	day for 5 weeks with the elbow flexors holding a 60% maximal contraction for as long as possible. Dynamic 
1092	auiurance increased by 93% as a result of performing these arm curls with a weight of 60% of 1 RM at a rate of 
1093	28repetitions per minute until it was impossible to increase the tempo further. At the same time, the ability to 
1094	execute repetitive isometric contractions (60% of maximal strength for 5 seconds of tension and 2 seconds of rest) 
1095	to failure increased by 219%. A similar experiment with 10 dynamic movements executed daily with maximal 
1096	resistance for 5 weeks resulted in increases in both dynamic and static strength, but dynamic and static endurance
