1102	remained almost unchanged (Hansen, 1963). This indicates that it is necessary to optimise the volume of work 
1103	required to develop strength-endurance.
1104	It has been established that an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance 
1105	runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). However, it must be 
1106	emphasized that the magnitude of the strength load used is different if, on the one hand, the key quality required 
1107	is general endurance and, on the other hand, it is strength-endurance.
1108	It should be noted that certain popular strength exercises such as running with a sack of sand weighing 25% of 
1109	the subject's bodyweight, barbell pressing, squats, 'good mornings', and twisting with a barbell not only do not 
1110	enhance, but to a certain degree, will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises 
1111	(Maisuradze, 1960). It some instances the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy, 
1112	which is a by-product of strength training. Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there 
1113	is no correlation between them (Maison & Broekcr, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954).
1114	The lack of a definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in different sports where the key 
1115	quality is endurance has been observed by several authors (Chistyakov, 1965; Chcmyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 
1116	1972). This conccms primarily cyclic sports (middle distance running, skating and skiing). In other cases, for 
1117	example, with gymnasts, a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and 
1118	relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of 
1119	significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results.
1120	The general principles concerning the development of strength-endurance, which were discusscd earlier, arc 
1121	applied differently in each specific case, depending on the characteristics of the sport, for example:
1122	• During the preparatory period, skiers should exercise with weights which are up to 65% of 1RM, in 
1123	combination with simulation exercises on a flat surface, as well as with movements on roller-skis 
1124	(Chistyakov, 1965).
1125	• Middle and long distance runners obtain good results from lifting a barbell of 55-60% of bodymass up to head 
1126	level 8-10 times rhythmically, clean-and-jerks with various weights (60-85% of bodymass); jumps with 
1127	kettlebells from a squat position (using about one-third of bodymass for 18-20 repetitions) and squats with 
1128	55-60% of bodymass until complete fatigue (Likachycvskaya & Kovalchuk, 1963). Exercises with weights 
1129	of 60-80% of 1RM for multiple repetitions, jumping and hard running are also recommended (Popov, 1966).
1130	• Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM), as well as medium and small weights are recommended for 
1131	developing strength-endurance in skaters. Exercises with heavy loads are executed for several sets at a 
1132	moderate tempo for 4-12 repetitions per set until the point of complete fatigue, with 2-4 minutes of rest 
1133	between sets. Exercises with light and moderate weights are executed as rapidly as possible for 15-25 
1134	repetitions per set, for 3-5 sets with rest intervals of 5-8 minutes (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
1135	• Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1 RM and female rowers with loads of 30-40% of 
1136	1RM (Ulrich ct al, 1966). Significant improvement (up to 40% from initial levels) in strength-endurancehzs 
1137	been noted in women rowers working with light weights (18-20kg) for many repetitions (Chumakova, 1964). 
1138	Improvement is greater with these weights than with larger loads (35-50 kg) executed in sets of 2-3 
1139	repetitions, and it is even greater (by 28%) than that produced by a combination of both methods.
1140	It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases. 
1141	The following method is recommended for skaters to develop strength-endurance in the legs: increasing the 
1142	number of barbell squats by 20-30 each week (beginning with 50 squats per set and over a period of 2-3 months 
1143	increasing this to 200-300 repetitions), then increasing the amount of weight and starting a new cycle of strength 
1144	training, but beginning with a smaller number of squats (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975).
1145	For developing strength-endurance it is always appropriate to strive to execute the work under demanding 
1146	conditions, though with movements whose coordination and structure in space and time are close to those of the 
1147	special exercise. For instance, a runner may run with a small parachute resisting him or pull a loaded sled in the 
1148	preparatory phases (Popov, 1966). Similarly, gymnasts may use a heavy belt and vest (Zhilei, 1964) and rowers 
1149	a spccial water-resistancc dcvice attached to the hull of the boat (Chuprun, 1966). In the case of the rowers. 
1150	strength-endurance as measured by the number of pull-ups, the number of arm flexions in the prone position and 
1151	the number of barbell presses in 30 seconds increased by 57.1%, 27.8% and 9.1%, respectively.

1157	Thus, multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for 
1158	developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases 
1159	requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises 
1160	simulating the given sport activity. If the special exercise is associated with the prolonged production of moderate 
1161	force, then it is useful to work with light weights in repeated sets to the point of fatigue or failure.
1162	Strength training should not result in increased muscle mass in those types of sport where the key quality is 
1163	endurance of moderate work output. If strength-endurance is required, especially in those cases where it is 
1164	necessary to overcome a large resistance, a small increase in muscle mass is permissible. In no cases, should the 
1165	training ever produce a decrease in relative strength of any muscle groups in the body.
1166	5.3 Application of Special S trength Training Means
1167	The value of systematic application of the training means has been investigated repeatedly, but the preliminary 
1168	conclusions still need to be extended. Consequently, there have been attempts to devise a rational combination of 
1169	strength, speed and endurance exercises to:
1170	• raise the body's general work capacity (Zimkin, Yakovlev, Korobkov, Zatsiorsky )
1171	• investigate the effectiveness of sequential and concurrent (parallel or complcx) use of the means for 
1172	developing endurance and speed-strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Mikhailov, Volkov ct al)
1173	• study the effect of the sequential use of aerobic and anaerobic exercise on the development of endurance 
1174	(Volkov ct al, Gordon et al)
1175	• investigate the sequential use of strength and speed-strength exercises as one of the schcmes for 
1176	systematically developing explosive strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Vorobyev, Filin, Vcrkhoshansky).
1177	However, research in the area of the systematic use of means is limited and no definitive practical 
1178	recommendations have yet emerged.
1179	The systematic use of means of special strength training over a given period produces a cumulative effect 
1180	which is significantly greater than the separate non-sequential application of these same means. In principle, there 
1181	at two possible variants for the systematic application of means: sequential and concurrent, as mentioned above:
1182	1. The first variant (sequential means) involves the strictly determined, successive introduction of different 
1183	means, each with a higher training effect, into the annual or multi-annual cyclc. The theoretical basis for this 
1184	variant is based upon two observations:
1185	• the training effect of any means diminishes as the body adapts to its influence
1186	• the training effect must be maintained by using a complcx of means to steadily increase the body's special 
1187	work capacity.
1188	In addition, experience and research indicate that the training regime designed to develop a particular motor ability 
1189	is determined largely by the degree of continuity in sequentially changing means with different training effects. 
1190	Because of this, functional changes produced by earlier means should create favourable conditions for achieving 
1191	the training effect of subsequent means. To devise a systematic sequence of the means of special strength 
1192	training, one must:
1193	• assess the quantitative and qualitative components of the training effect
1194	• categorise the means relative to the level of the athlete's special fitness.
1195	This, in effect, is the subject of research aimed at identifying the principles for devising logical systems for 
1196	applying the different means of special strength training effectively. As an example, the sequential development of 
1197	endurance begins by training aerobic (cardiorespiratory) processes, then non-oxidative glycolysis and finally high 
1198	energy phosphagen processes. This sequential introduction of'anaerobic' work creates favourable conditions for 
1199	the training effect of'aerobic'work (Ozolin, 1959, 1970; Volkov, 1963; Yakovlev, 1957; Borisov, 1979).
1200	2. The second variant (concurrent means) involves the parallel use of means (over an extended period) that are 
1201	close to the body’s work regime, but which produce a largely different training effect. This method is based on 
1202	experimental evidence that adaptation elicited by the separate components of the complex of training work is not 
1203	amply a summation of the separate effects, but the synergistic result of the interaction of the effects at each stage 
1204	of training. This interaction produces a new physical state with a significantly greater work potential than would
1205	287
1206	
1207	
1208	######## PDF idx 299 (printed 288)
1209	SUPERTRAINING
1210	have resulted from the separate non-systematic use of these same means, even at increased volume. Experimental 
1211	assessment of the cumulative effects of different variations of the combination of means is necessary for applying 
1212	the complex system of special strength training means.
1213	A number of researchers, including Purvin, FChodykin, Dcniskin, Tatian and Chemousov have studied the 
1214	systematic use of special strength means in speed-strength sports. They have established that the sequence of 
1215	means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real 
1216	significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order.
1217	A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training 
1218	load) occun-ed in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed 
1219	training sessions. This alternation sequence creates the optimal conditions for functional adaptation. This docs 
1220	not ignore the fact that this training regime, with a rest interval between sessions on the same day, also produces a 
1221	positive response of the after-effect phenomenon by use of the strength and speed-strength exercises. On the 
1222	whole, this elicitcd more intense and more stable adaptation. It should be noted that the contrasting of stimuli in 
1223	mixed workouts by alternating training means which are primarily of a strength and speed-strength character 
1224	undoubtedly has a positive effect.
1225	In another experiment one group of novice athletes used weights exercises in the first stage of training and 
1226	plyometric depth jumps in the next stage. A second group did the same exercises in reverse order and a third 
1227	group did these same exercises together in both stages, although not in the same workout. It was established that 
1228	the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength. The concurrent use of exercises (the third 
1229	variant) caused significant improvement in speed-strength in the first stage, but the rate of improvement in speed- 
1230	strength decreased noticeably in the second stage, due to monotonous repetition. The second variant (reversed use 
1231	of these same means) produced significant improvement after the first stage due to the larger training effect of the 
1232	plyometric method. However, the acquired speed-strength qualities were lowest at the end o f the second stage.
1233	Another experiment studied the question of whether the execution of speed-strength exercises in one workout 
1234	against the background of the positive after-effect produced by previous tonic strength work influences the 
1235	effectiveness of speed-strength preparation of novices. One group of athletes executed exercises in this sequence 
1236	(i.e. strength, then speed-strcngth work) during the fundamental stage of their workouts, while another group did 
1237	the reverse. The pauses between exercises were increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after­
1238	effect of the preceding work on the subsequent work. A third group executed depth jumps. The presence of this 
1239	group in the experiment served two purposes: firstly, to study the effectiveness of plyometrics and secondly, to 
1240	compare this effect with the results obtained with a complcx of less effective means. There was no statistically 
1241	significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the 
1242	parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group.
1243	Thus, an increase in the training effect of speed-strength exercises performed against the background of the 
1244	positive after-effect of strength work has not been corroborated in the training of novices. In this experiment, the 
1245	means with a higher training effect (i.e. dcpth-jumps) produced significantly larger improvement in speed-strength 
1246	fitness for a smaller volume of training. In explaining these results, one should take into account that any training 
1247	influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly 
1248	strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training 
1249	stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one 
1250	workout, the traccs of all the training tasks arc summed, which results in the same effect, despite these tasks being 
1251	done in succession.
1252	These findings should not be considered to disprove in general the appropriateness of using a complex of 
1253	means in training, which exploits the positive after-effect of preceding strength work to enhance the training effect 
1254	of the subsequent speed-strength and speed work. Since the experiment was conducted on a group of novice 
1255	athletes, it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this 
1256	phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect 
1257	on the training effect of speed-strength and speed work in a training programme. However, the validity of this 
1258	hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation.
1259	In an experiment with junior class sprinters the specific effect of short jumping exercises and the systematic 
1260	use of combinations of these exercises was investigated. The jumping exercises involved variations of repeated 
1261	jumps on one and two legs, as well as variations of triple and quintuple standing broad jumps and long jumping 
1262	exercises (multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30- 100m). One group of sprinters 
1263	executed mainly short jumps, a second group did mainly long jumping exercises and a third group did both fora

ground or some object. Even in Russia, the birthplace of scientific plyometrics, the emphasis has been almost 
entirely on actions which exert some form of impact loading on the body. It may also be stated that all running, 
jumping and other ballistic actions involve a phase of plyometric activity, so that shock contact of parts of the 
body with some surface would appear to be the common denominator underlying all plyometrics.
However, this is not the only way of producing plyomctric action. As discussed earlier, all plyometric drills 
so far used in the athletic world are of the impact variety. The existence of the non-impact variety was recognised 
when the author used a force plate to analyse biomechanically martial arts movements and the seated fitness 
system (Supersitting) developed by his wife, Lisa Ericson of Denver, Colorado. She attracted worldwide attention 
for her 'seated aerobics’ classes, which she developed after becoming paralysed. A former professional ice-skatcr 
who was determined to explore and expand the range of possibilities for physical activity by spinal cord patients, 
she developed a system of exercise rehabilitation which can produce very significant improvements in motor 
control, strength and hypertrophy without the use of weights or any other resistance apparatus.
After years of experimentation with different training methods, she has managed to gain recognition for her 
work and for several years has been teaching her seated fitness class to spinal patients at the renowned Craig 
Rehabilitation Hospital in Denver, as well as to regular aerobics clients at other athletic clubs in that city.

What distinguishes her exercise routines from normal aerobics is that she often uses very rapid widc-rangc 
movements choreographed at rates exceeding 240 beats per minute, interspersed with rhythmic transitional PNF- 
type patterns, offered over a session which charactcristically lasts for 60 minutes. After an extended warm-up to 
ensure that the arms are adequately prepared for the main, high-intensity phase, the subsequent movements arc 
initiated and terminated explosively in sets o f uninterrupted sequences which regularly change their form and 
direction to avoid excessive fatigue, habituation or injury.
This system recruits the myotatic stretch reflex dynamically and powerfully in agonistic and antagonistic 
muscles over as large a range of movement as possible. The use of patterns, deliberately deviating in space and 
timing from those recommended by PNF and Pilatcs practitioners, cause pronounced overflow to adjacent 
muscles and speed up the rehabilitation of spinal patients, a phenomenon that has attracted the attention of 
medical specialists.
Ericson's system may best be categorised as non-impact plyometrics, (non-impact powermetrics) becausc it 
obeys all the requirements of plyometrics as originally conceived by Russian scientists. True plyometric activity 
involves a ballistic action which is rapidly terminated by eccentric and explosive isometric muscle contraction, 
followed immediately by a powerful conccntric recoil mediated by recruitment of the myotatic stretch reflex and 
augmented by the release of elastic energy stored in the connective tissues of the muscle-tendon complex.
The system developed by Ericson is reminiscent in many ways of some o f the training methods used in 
karate which involve explosive snap punches, blows and kicks, or some boxing training drills such as shadow 
boxing or speed ball. In karate, the limbs are thrust powerfully outwards and then drawn back in a whip-likc

pause. The karate punch is rarely whipped back immediately, but makes contact with its target for a very short

therefore, maintains high levels of muscle tension for prolonged periods. The shorter transition phase and the 
greater number of continuous repetitions in the Ericson system probably explains the differences in functional and 
structural development produced by it compared with the karate system.
The implications of the Ericson Supersitting system for sports training are great. Traditional plyometric 
drills have often been criticised because they all involve high impact forces produced during explosive contact of 
parts of the body with some surfacc or object. The Ericson system eliminates the need for impulsive contact with 
a hard surface and drastically diminishes the intensity of shock waves transmitted to the joints and entire 
musculoskeletal system by explosive two-way movements.
Most of the Ericson movements offered in the average fitness class more accurately would be classed as 
submaximal plyomctrics, just like the more usual repetitive rebounding drills over obstacles or with medicinc balls. 
Performed in the form of all-out single movements, they become maximal non-impact plyomctrics. Since depth- 
jumps involve the projection of the entire mass of the body, maximal impact plyometrics will generally increase 
muscle tension to a greater extent than the equivalent non-impact movements for the leg and hip extensors (e.g. the 
karate thrust-kick).
Nevertheless, maximal non-impact plyometrics, like submaximal impact plyomctrics can serve as a 
preparatory tool for maximal impact plyometrics, for enhancing other functional and structural qualities or for 
selectively offering plyometric training to certain muscle groups instead of unnecessarily stressing the entire 
musculature. These qualities may include strength, musclc hypertrophy, muscle endurance and speed-strcngth 
endurance. To date, research into plyometrics has devoted most o f its attention to increases in speed-strcngth 
(power), rather than these other qualities, so that preliminary studies executed in 1995 by University of Pretoria 
physiotherapy students supervised by Siff and Ericson warrant more detailed expansion.
Meanwhile, the significant increases in strength, speed-strength endurance and hypertrophy (which are not 
simply a result of propelling their wheelchairs) achieved by Ericson and her wheelchair athletes emphasize that 
there is still much more to be discovered about the methods and consequences of the different types of resistance 
training. Up till now, it has been considered fairly accurate to state that strength and power are best achieved by 
few repetitions of high-intensity exercises, whereas hypertrophy is best produced by medium numbers of 
repetitions with 65-85% of one's 1RM. Piyomctric exercise traditionally fits into this scheme as a means of

methods increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction, they also

Plyometrics and the Brain
Rccent brain research reveals that piyomctric action is not simply a phenomenon that can be adequately explained 
on the basis of stored elastic energy and the stretch shortening cycle. The phenomenon of plyometrics involves fa r 
more intricate processes than reflexive muscle activities that operate at the level of the spinal column and bypass the 
brain. Many of the subtleties and complexities o f plyometrics can be missed if one is preoccupied with the 
prescription of so-called piyomctric drills or with laboratory measurement of the stretch-shortening cyclc as a local 
musculotendinous phenomenon. In both cases, it is easy to overlook the possibility that activities such as depth- 
jumping or medicinc ball throwing may involve non-local events, particularly the enormously complicated computer 
programs in the brain.
While it is accurate to state that plyometric actions arc extremely rapid and therefore occur at the level of 
specific spinal nerves without involving conscious thought processes, it must be remembered that the preparatory 
period prior to the piyomctric action can involve higher order mental processing of exceptional intricacy (sec Fig 
3.11). In fact, the period prior to execution of any skilled movement involves running mental programmes that have 
been stored and refined by repeated rehearsal in the brain of the well-trained athlete.
One can distinguish further between a plyometric action produced under conditions in which the athlete 
anticipates a particular course of action (cognitive plyometrics) and a plyometric action produced as a purely 
reflexive response under unexpected circumstances (non-cognitive plyometrics). The latter type of plyometrics 
occur primarily under survival or self-preservation conditions intended to protect a person from injury or death. 
The rapidity of the event does not permit any forethought or planning, but relies on primitive reflexes that generally 
lend to bypass the brain by acting at the more spontaneous level of the spinal cord. Cognitive plyometrics, though 
also a very rapid phenomenon, is preceded by a phase of thinking that prepares the person for a specific course of 
action to achieve a definite goal.
One should not conclude simplistically that non-cognitivc plyometrics are purely instinctive or automatic 
actions which involve no cognitive or learning processes. It should never be forgotten that efficient execution of 
piyomctric actions and drills only takes place after a considerable amount o f practice using cognitive processes. In 
fact, most athletes do not manage to perfect plyometric skills even after many weeks of practice. The use of 
numerous sequential repetitions to imprint these skills may constitute the inappropriate strategy because classical 
plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete. 
Submaximal plyometrics and pseudo-plyometrics may be performed in a state of advancing fatigue, unlike classical 
shock method' plyometrics. The neural and reflexive processes are quite different in each case.
Even then, what appears to be quite reflexive still involves a certain degree of cognitive preparation and control. 
The lack of adequate mention o f the importance of cognitive and learning processes in plyometrics by all popular 
texts on the subject constitutes a major deficit in the field. Reflexes are casually referred to as entirely robotic 
actions that elicit or inhibit musclc contraction, but little is mentioned of the fact that reflexes can be trained and 
modified, something that the renowned Russian physiologist, Pavlov, had proved some 70 years ago in the form of 
his'conditioned reflexes'. Later, Skinner (1938) distinguished between two types of conditioning: which he called 
respondent conditioning, in which the response is modified by a preceding stimulus, and operant conditioning, in 
which the response is strengthened or weakened by events that follow the response.

5.2.5 The D evelopm ent of Strength-Endurance
Strength-endurance involves the production of muscular tension without a decrease in efficiency over a long 
period. Strength-endurance, like explosive strength, has several forms, depending upon the motor pattern of the 
athletic activity, in particular the categories of dynamic and static endurance.
Dynamic strength-endurance is typical of exercises involving repetitive and significant muscular tension at a 
relatively slow speed of movement, as well as repeated cyclic or acyclic exercises requiring speed-strength. In the 
latter case we are referring to the specific endurance to execute special speed-strength and explosive work without 
adecrease in efficiency over a relatively long period. Static strength-endurance is typical of activities associated 
with the maintenance of maximal and near-maximal tension, as well as the moderate tension necessary for holding 
a specific posture (for example, in shooting or speed-skating).
The development of strength-endurance is an inherent characteristic and a fundamental principle of training 
for dev eloping general endurance. Training for strength-endurance is determined predominantly by:
1. The magnitude of the load
2. The tempo of movement
3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements
4. The rest interval between training sessions
5. The length of the training period
6. The initial levels of strength-cndurance of the athlete
7. The kinesiological structure of the movement
8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance.
Repetition work with weights 25-50% of IRM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for 
developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness of strength-endurance development, using equivalent weights 
and movement tempos, will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter 
duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; 
Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961).
Strength-endurance, like the other characteristics of muscular activity, is specific. However, the specificity 
of strength-endurance is expressed to a lesser degree than the specificity of speed, for example, while its carry­
over from one activity to another is greater. When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant 
resistance (exceeding 75-80% of IRM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to 
developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966).
This study by Zatsiorsky showed that isometric endurance increased 84% as a result of exercising 10 times a 
day for 5 weeks with the elbow flexors holding a 60% maximal contraction for as long as possible. Dynamic 
auiurance increased by 93% as a result of performing these arm curls with a weight of 60% of 1 RM at a rate of 
28repetitions per minute until it was impossible to increase the tempo further. At the same time, the ability to 
execute repetitive isometric contractions (60% of maximal strength for 5 seconds of tension and 2 seconds of rest) 
to failure increased by 219%. A similar experiment with 10 dynamic movements executed daily with maximal 
resistance for 5 weeks resulted in increases in both dynamic and static strength, but dynamic and static endurance

5.3 Application of Special S trength Training Means
The value of systematic application of the training means has been investigated repeatedly, but the preliminary 
conclusions still need to be extended. Consequently, there have been attempts to devise a rational combination of 
strength, speed and endurance exercises to:
• raise the body's general work capacity (Zimkin, Yakovlev, Korobkov, Zatsiorsky )
• investigate the effectiveness of sequential and concurrent (parallel or complcx) use of the means for 
developing endurance and speed-strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Mikhailov, Volkov ct al)
• study the effect of the sequential use of aerobic and anaerobic exercise on the development of endurance 
(Volkov ct al, Gordon et al)
• investigate the sequential use of strength and speed-strength exercises as one of the schcmes for 
systematically developing explosive strength (Ozolin, Diachkov, Vorobyev, Filin, Vcrkhoshansky).
However, research in the area of the systematic use of means is limited and no definitive practical

# Sport-Specific Strength-Endurance Prescriptions: Skiers, Distance Runners, Skaters and Rowers

**What it is** — The authors' examples of applying the general strength-endurance principles "differently in each specific case" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286, verified against the page image):
- **Skiers (Chistyakov, 1965):** in the preparatory period, weights "up to 65% of 1RM", combined with simulation exercises on a flat surface and roller-ski movements.
- **Middle and long distance runners (Likachyevskaya & Kovalchuk, 1963):** a barbell of "55-60% of bodymass" lifted to head level "8-10 times rhythmically"; clean-and-jerks with "60-85% of bodymass"; kettlebell jumps from a squat with "about one-third of bodymass for 18-20 repetitions"; squats with "55-60% of bodymass until complete fatigue." Also (Popov, 1966): "60-80% of 1RM for multiple repetitions, jumping and hard running."
- **Skaters (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975):** heavy weights "(80-85% of 1RM)" for "several sets at a moderate tempo for 4-12 repetitions per set until the point of complete fatigue, with 2-4 minutes of rest between sets"; light and moderate weights "as rapidly as possible for 15-25 repetitions per set, for 3-5 sets with rest intervals of 5-8 minutes." Leg progression: "increasing the number of barbell squats by 20-30 each week (beginning with 50 squats per set and over a period of 2-3 months increasing this to 200-300 repetitions), then increasing the amount of weight and starting a new cycle of strength training, but beginning with a smaller number of squats."
- **Rowers:** men "50-80% of 1RM", women "30-40% of 1RM" (Ulrich et al, 1966). Women rowers with light weights "(18-20kg) for many repetitions" improved strength-endurance "up to 40% from initial levels" (Chumakova, 1964), more than with "(35-50 kg) executed in sets of 2-3 repetitions", "and it is even greater (by 28%) than that produced by a combination of both methods."

**Why it works** — The authors present these as applications of the general principles (load set by the dynamics of the sport exercise). No mechanism is given per sport.

**When to apply** — As reference doses when designing strength-endurance work for cyclic athletes. Inference: the skater squat progression (50 to 200-300 reps per set over 2-3 months) is an extreme local-endurance model with no obvious football use; the rower result (light, many reps beating heavy, low-rep sets for strength-endurance) is the transferable point.

**When NOT to apply** — The skaters' 80-85% 1RM conflicts with the 75-80% 1RM ceiling stated a page earlier (see [[heuristic--strength-endurance-load-tempo-and-the-75-80-percent-ceiling]]). Loads mix % of 1RM and % of bodymass. The Chumakova "by 28%" comparison is ambiguous (28 percentage points or 28% relative is not stated). No sample sizes, durations or outcome tests are given. These are Soviet-era single-source prescriptions.

**Example** — The authors' own: the skater squat progression from 50 to 200-300 reps per set before raising the weight and restarting with fewer reps (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).

# Depth Landings Without a Rebound Raised Strength in Dursenev and Raevsky (1978): 1500-3500 kgf in 0.028-0.061 s From Drops up to 3.2 m

**What it is** — "*depth landings* (i.e. depth jumps without the rebound after landing) alone can also have a significant effect on concentric and eccentric strength. This was shown by Dursenev and Raevsky (1978) who investigated the effect of depth landings from heights of 2m or more onto soft gymnastic mats. Under these conditions, the subjects acquired the ability to display brief muscle tension (over periods of between 0.028-0.061 secs) of magnitude 1500-3500 kgf, i.e. over 20 times bodyweight for heights of up to 3.2 metres. The rationale for using this method was that weight training or other similar methods of resistance training cannot produce this intensity of voluntary effort." "the maximum possible height which the athletes could contemplate using produced the greatest increase in strength, although they often hesitated to attempt these extremely stressful jumps" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).

The authors' caveats on the same page: "the drop heights studied were for experimental purposes alone and it would be most inadvisable to use drops of 3.2 metres for training." "It appeared that the main consideration for enhancing strength is not the type of muscle contraction, but the intensity and speed of contraction elicited by the exercise." Increase drop height "gradually from fairly low levels", "limit the number of drops per session", "land on suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces" and attend to landing technique.

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale: intensity of tension that resistance training cannot reach, with intensity and speed of contraction, not contraction type, as "the main consideration." Inference: "over 20 times bodyweight" holds for a 75 kg subject at the low end (1500 kgf / 75 kg = 20); the book gives no subject masses, so the ratio is approximate.

**When to apply** — As evidence that the eccentric landing alone is a strong stimulus, which supports using low-height landing drills as a step before rebound work. Inference: for football, landing drills from modest heights are the safe use of this finding; the experimental heights are not.

**When NOT to apply** — Never use 2-3.2 m drops in training (the authors' own warning). The study is reported second-hand, with no subject numbers, training duration or strength measure given. It used "soft gymnastic mats", which differs from the firm surfaces the authors want for rebound plyometrics (see [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: drops of 2 m or more onto soft mats, with peak tensions of 1500-3500 kgf over 0.028-0.061 s (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

**What it is** — "The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted a total volume of 93 tons!" Two sentences around it: "The training effect of depth-jumps or shock-loading for developing explosive strength is very large, having little equal when compared with the other means of strength training, especially when combined in a complex with other forms of intensive strength training", corroborated by Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974, Dobrovolsky 1972, Savin 1974, Khodykin 1974 and Deniskin 1976 (same page). **When to apply** — Making the case to coaches that a small, well-placed depth-jump dose can do more for reactive ability than a large barbell volume. Inference: the companion sentence (resistance work before plyometrics in the same session) is a direct sequencing rule for combined sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — Unclear points in the source: "all of them did 475 jumps" does not say whether 475 is per athlete or the group total; the experiment has no citation, group sizes, statistics or outcome test named beyond "reactive ability"; the comparison group's "1472 general push-offs" is also unclear per athlete or total. # Heavy Squats Build Strength Potential and Light Fast Lifts Build Speed, but Neither Trains the Rapid Eccentric-to-Concentric Switch

**What it is** — The authors open 5.2.4 by analysing the traditional speed-strength means. In heavy barbell squats "the muscles work very slowly (quasi-isometrically) with a relatively constant tension produced by the load. Consequently, the muscles primarily develop isometric strength". Raising the barbell weight, "frequently considered a basic indicator of special strength fitness, places a large and generally unnecessary load on the spine." For speed-strength, athletes use smaller loads; their example is "squat thrusts with a 60kg barbell on the shoulders", which "produces a large dynamic maximum force". So "exercises with heavy weights tend to increase the strength potential of the muscles, while fast exercises with light weights improve speed." Neither adequately enhances "specific components of explosive movements such as the rapid excitation of muscles and the rapid changing from eccentric to concentric work." These skills need "a specific training regime which is impossible to imitate with only one resistance exercise": slow resistance movements, and lifting a barbell in preparation for squatting or jumping with it, remove "the possibility of controlling the mechanisms which are crucial to the rapid switching of muscles to the active state", while lowering the resistance "diminishes the dynamic effort required and creates a vicious cycle from which there is no apparent escape." This analysis is the authors' stated route to the shock (plyometric) method on the same page. (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267, verified against the page image.)

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the one quoted: the barbell means do not reproduce rapid excitation or the fast eccentric-concentric switch. They give no further physiology here. Inference: the "vicious cycle" is that heavy loads slow the movement and light loads drop the effort, so no single barbell load gives both high effort and a fast switch.

**When to apply** — When a program relies on heavy squats plus light speed squats to develop jumping or cutting explosiveness, this is the authors' argument for adding a means that trains the switch itself (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 104). Inference: this entry is the authors' case for why the jumps in that list are not interchangeable with the squats.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors do not say heavy squats are useless for explosive athletes: "this does not mean that it is impossible for them to execute fast dynamic contractions", and heavy work raises "strength potential". Later in the same section they prefer heavy "brief maximal tension" work where explosive force must overcome large resistance (see [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]]). The 60 kg squat-thrust load is given without athlete bodymass or level, so it is not a prescription.

**Example** — The authors' own example: heavy squats (slow, quasi-isometric) versus squat thrusts with a 60 kg barbell (large dynamic maximum force), with neither training the rapid switch (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267).

# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress, but It Computes a Falling-Body Power, Not Take-Off Power

**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").

**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.

**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.

**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete jumping 0.50 m gives P = 21.693 × 100 × √0.50 ≈ 1,534 W; at 0.55 m, ≈ 1,609 W. This arithmetic is not in the source.

# Plyometric Injury Risk Comes From Prescription (Overload and Overuse), Not the Method; Regularly Impact-Loaded Cartilage Is Reported as Healthier

**What it is** — In "Plyometric Training and Safety" (PDF pp. 280-281 / printed pp. 269-270; p. 280 verified against the page image) the text argues:
- The claim that "plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not been proved experimentally or clinically"; the danger is "inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been measured via force plate research", and an experiment isolating plyometric effects with matched controls "is very difficult to design."
- Opponents imply running and jumping "in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous", and assume joints do not follow SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands).
- Cartilage: "joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from osteoarthritis in old age and ... those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977)." Siff's former colleague Mark Swanepoel (University of the Witwatersrand) noted that fibrillation at any age increases going up from ankle to knee, hip and lumbar spine. Regularly impulse-loaded cartilage is "mechanically much stiffer", while cartilage "heavily loaded infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production" (Swanepoel, 1998).
- "it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the manner in which it is used." Western practice earns much of the criticism: "encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms"; drills often prescribed without regard to "loading imposed by other work or play ... or the use of formal restoration"; and "the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most of the plyometric training that is necessary."
- "overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise)." An "individually appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height)" with "gradual progressive overload" and "adequate restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running or jumping" (PDF pp. 280-281).

Voice: Siff (the passage names "Siff's former colleague").

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is adaptation (SAID) and the cartilage findings cited. Inference: overload maps to drop height and rebound effort, overuse to contacts per session and week, which gives two separate dials to manage.

**When to apply** — Answering "are depth jumps dangerous?" for coaches or medical staff: the text's position is that risk is a dose question. Inference: in football, count the plyometric loading already present in practice (cutting, jumping, sprinting) before adding drills, as the text's "sport alone may offer all or most" warning suggests.

**When NOT to apply** — The text argues mainly from absence of proof and from cartilage studies of everyday joint loading; it cites no controlled study showing plyometric drills are safe. The "heavy impact joints are free from osteoarthritis" sentence compares joints and loading histories, not plyometric training programs, so do not cite it as evidence that depth jumps protect joints. The cited studies were not checked for this entry.

**Example** — The text's own: the Nicol et al (1997) finding, that many repetitions do not improve fatigue resistance in basketball rebounding, as an example of a Western volume habit that is "untrue" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269; see [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]).

# Most "Plyometric" Drills in Popular Western Books Work Through Eccentric Loading, Connective Tissue, Starting Strength and Prestretch, Not the Shock Mechanism

**What it is** — Under "Popular Information on Plyometrics" (PDF pp. 293-294 / printed pp. 282-283; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 294 from the text layer):
- Popular Western texts ("e.g. Chu, 1992; Radcliffe & Farantinos, 1985") present jumping and rebound activities "many of which do not constitute true plyometric training as originally conceived by Russian scientists"; they are "often supplementary or preparatory movements."
- "Most books classify extended range swinging, passing or catching of medicine balls or other objects as 'plyometric', although the amortisation phase is too long to produce classical plyometrics." These drills still help "eye-hand coordination, eccentric strength and starting strength, but they are not strictly plyometric."
- Books omit the tonic versus phasic myotatic reflex in relation to drill types, the positive supportive reaction, the crossed extensor reflex, phased breathing, the maximal-submaximal distinction, and concurrent and sequential prescription.
- "the so-called plyometric drills in current Western texts are known to enhance performance, but it is not predominantly due to plyometric training, but more to the increased loading of eccentric contraction, the conditioning of connective tissue, the improvement of voluntary starting strength from the quasi-isometric state, the use of prestretch, and enhancement of acceleration strength by increasing the velocity of projectiles such as medicine balls" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283).
- The physiotherapy link: in PNF a therapist "sometimes imposes a short, sharp jerk on an eccentrically or isometrically contracting muscle to produce strong muscle contraction in a weakened muscle", principles that "preceded sporting plyometrics by several decades" (same page).
- Related, from the classification passage: *pseudo-plyometrics* such as aerobics "power moves" and many "water plyos" lack "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The text's argument is definitional: long amortisation phases fall outside the shock method, so the benefit must come from the other listed qualities. It gives no study separating these mechanisms.

**When to apply** — Labelling a program's med-ball and jump drills honestly: Inference: a long-amortisation med-ball chest pass or rotational throw is a starting-strength and eccentric drill in the authors' terms, and should not be counted as shock-method volume or dosed with shock-method rest.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the list of "other mechanisms" is the text's assertion, with no data. The criticism of specific books is the author's opinion and was not checked against those books. Not a reason to drop these drills: the text says they "are known to enhance performance."

**Example** — The text's own: extended-range medicine ball swinging and catching, called plyometric in popular books, as an example of a drill whose amortisation is too long for classical plyometrics (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

169	# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress, but It Computes a Falling-Body Power, Not Take-Off Power
170	
171	**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").
172	
173	**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.
174	
175	**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.
176	
177	**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.
178

197	# Plyometric Injury Risk Comes From Prescription (Overload and Overuse), Not the Method; Regularly Impact-Loaded Cartilage Is Reported as Healthier
198	
199	**What it is** — In "Plyometric Training and Safety" (PDF pp. 280-281 / printed pp. 269-270; p. 280 verified against the page image) the text argues:
200	- The claim that "plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not been proved experimentally or clinically"; the danger is "inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been measured via force plate research", and an experiment isolating plyometric effects with matched controls "is very difficult to design."
201	- Opponents imply running and jumping "in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous", and assume joints do not follow SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands).
202	- Cartilage: "joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from osteoarthritis in old age and ... those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977)." Siff's former colleague Mark Swanepoel (University of the Witwatersrand) noted that fibrillation at any age increases going up from ankle to knee, hip and lumbar spine. Regularly impulse-loaded cartilage is "mechanically much stiffer", while cartilage "heavily loaded infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production" (Swanepoel, 1998).
203	- "it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the manner in which it is used." Western practice earns much of the criticism: "encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms"; drills often prescribed without regard to "loading imposed by other work or play ... or the use of formal restoration"; and "the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most of the plyometric training that is necessary."
204	- "overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise)." An "individually appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height)" with "gradual progressive overload" and "adequate restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running or jumping" (PDF pp. 280-281).
205	
206	Voice: Siff (the passage names "Siff's former colleague").
207	
208	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is adaptation (SAID) and the cartilage findings cited. Inference: overload maps to drop height and rebound effort, overuse to contacts per session and week, which gives two separate dials to manage.
209	
210	**When to apply** — Answering "are depth jumps dangerous?" for coaches or medical staff: the text's position is that risk is a dose question. Inference: in football, count the plyometric loading already present in practice (cutting, jumping, sprinting) before adding drills, as the text's "sport alone may offer all or most" warning suggests.
211	
212	**When NOT to apply** — The text argues mainly from absence of proof and from cartilage studies of everyday joint loading; it cites no controlled study showing plyometric drills are safe. The "heavy impact joints are free from osteoarthritis" sentence compares joints and loading histories, not plyometric training programs, so do not cite it as evidence that depth jumps protect joints. The cited studies were not checked for this entry.

268	**What it is** — From 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 297-298 / printed pp. 286-287, verified against the page images):
269	- "an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). In some instances "the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy". "Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there is no correlation between them (Maison & Broeker, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954)."
271	- No definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in cyclic endurance sports (middle distance running, skating, skiing: Chistyakov, 1965; Chernyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 1972). But in gymnasts "a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results."
272	- Closing rules: "Strength training should not result in increased muscle mass in those types of sport where the key quality is endurance of moderate work output. If strength-endurance is required, especially in those cases where it is necessary to overcome a large resistance, a small increase in muscle mass is permissible. In no cases, should the training ever produce a decrease in relative strength of any muscle groups in the body" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).

300	# The "Squat 1.5-2 Times Bodymass" Prerequisite Is a Safety Rule for Maximal Depth Jumps, Not for Submaximal Plyometrics
301	
302	**What it is** — "Some authors rightly criticize the recommendation sometimes put forward that athletes should be able to squat 1.5 - 2 times bodymass in order to use certain plyometric drills, since they consider that this criterion is not based on research evidence and does not apply to all plyometric exercises. This recommendation is a safety measure based on force plate analysis of *maximal plyometrics* in the form of depth jumps, where the ground reaction force on the lower extremity can easily exceed 6 times bodyweight. *This guideline was never intended to apply religiously to submaximal plyometrics using small drops, skipping drills or less demanding actions.* This misunderstanding of Russian guidelines is largely a result of an incomplete grasp of the scientific principles on which the original shock method was based" (PDF pp. 293-294 / printed pp. 282-283; p. 282 verified against the page image, p. 283 from the text layer).
303	
304	Both halves are the authors': they agree the criterion is not research-based ("rightly criticize"), then defend it as a force-plate-based safety measure for maximal depth jumps.
305	
306	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: maximal depth jumps can produce ground reaction forces that "easily exceed 6 times bodyweight", so a strength base is a safety margin. They give no derivation linking a 1.5-2 × bodymass squat to tolerating a 6 × bodyweight landing. Inference: the squat is a slow, bilateral, concentric-eccentric test and the landing is a brief eccentric-isometric impact, so the rule is a proxy, not a matched test.
307	
308	**When to apply** — Deciding whether an athlete may do maximal depth jumps (high box, maximal rebound). Inference: for football, where most players have a lifting base, the rule mainly screens young or newly enrolled athletes before maximal depth jumps; it should not block hops, skips, low drops or bounds, which the authors explicitly exclude.
309	
310	**When NOT to apply** — Not a gate for submaximal plyometrics, "small drops, skipping drills or less demanding actions." The authors do not say whether the squat is a 1RM, a full or partial squat, or how to test it. The book also says readiness for plyometric versus heavy work should be decided by the strength deficit (see [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]]), which is a different question from this safety threshold.
311	
312	**Example** — The authors' own framing: the threshold comes from force plate analysis of maximal depth jumps with ground reaction forces over 6 × bodyweight (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

# Sport-Specific Strength-Endurance Prescriptions: Skiers, Distance Runners, Skaters and Rowers

**What it is** — The authors' examples of applying the general strength-endurance principles "differently in each specific case" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286, verified against the page image):
- **Skiers (Chistyakov, 1965):** in the preparatory period, weights "up to 65% of 1RM", combined with simulation exercises on a flat surface and roller-ski movements.
- **Middle and long distance runners (Likachyevskaya & Kovalchuk, 1963):** a barbell of "55-60% of bodymass" lifted to head level "8-10 times rhythmically"; clean-and-jerks with "60-85% of bodymass"; kettlebell jumps from a squat with "about one-third of bodymass for 18-20 repetitions"; squats with "55-60% of bodymass until complete fatigue." Also (Popov, 1966): "60-80% of 1RM for multiple repetitions, jumping and hard running."
- **Skaters (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975):** heavy weights "(80-85% of 1RM)" for "several sets at a moderate tempo for 4-12 repetitions per set until the point of complete fatigue, with 2-4 minutes of rest between sets"; light and moderate weights "as rapidly as possible for 15-25 repetitions per set, for 3-5 sets with rest intervals of 5-8 minutes." Leg progression: "increasing the number of barbell squats by 20-30 each week (beginning with 50 squats per set and over a period of 2-3 months increasing this to 200-300 repetitions), then increasing the amount of weight and starting a new cycle of strength training, but beginning with a smaller number of squats."
- **Rowers:** men "50-80% of 1RM", women "30-40% of 1RM" (Ulrich et al, 1966). Women rowers with light weights "(18-20kg) for many repetitions" improved strength-endurance "up to 40% from initial levels" (Chumakova, 1964), more than with "(35-50 kg) executed in sets of 2-3 repetitions", "and it is even greater (by 28%) than that produced by a combination of both methods."

**Why it works** — The authors present these as applications of the general principles (load set by the dynamics of the sport exercise). No mechanism is given per sport.

**When to apply** — As reference doses when designing strength-endurance work for cyclic athletes. Inference: the skater squat progression (50 to 200-300 reps per set over 2-3 months) is an extreme local-endurance model with no obvious football use; the rower result (light, many reps beating heavy, low-rep sets for strength-endurance) is the transferable point.

**When NOT to apply** — The skaters' 80-85% 1RM conflicts with the 75-80% 1RM ceiling stated a page earlier (see [[heuristic--strength-endurance-load-tempo-and-the-75-80-percent-ceiling]]). Loads mix % of 1RM and % of bodymass. The Chumakova "by 28%" comparison is ambiguous (28 percentage points or 28% relative is not stated). No sample sizes, durations or outcome tests are given. These are Soviet-era single-source prescriptions.

**Example** — The authors' own: the skater squat progression from 50 to 200-300 reps per set before raising the weight and restarting with fewer reps (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).

# Depth Landings Without a Rebound Raised Strength in Dursenev and Raevsky (1978): 1500-3500 kgf in 0.028-0.061 s From Drops up to 3.2 m

**What it is** — "*depth landings* (i.e. depth jumps without the rebound after landing) alone can also have a significant effect on concentric and eccentric strength. This was shown by Dursenev and Raevsky (1978) who investigated the effect of depth landings from heights of 2m or more onto soft gymnastic mats. Under these conditions, the subjects acquired the ability to display brief muscle tension (over periods of between 0.028-0.061 secs) of magnitude 1500-3500 kgf, i.e. over 20 times bodyweight for heights of up to 3.2 metres. The rationale for using this method was that weight training or other similar methods of resistance training cannot produce this intensity of voluntary effort." "the maximum possible height which the athletes could contemplate using produced the greatest increase in strength, although they often hesitated to attempt these extremely stressful jumps" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).

The authors' caveats on the same page: "the drop heights studied were for experimental purposes alone and it would be most inadvisable to use drops of 3.2 metres for training." "It appeared that the main consideration for enhancing strength is not the type of muscle contraction, but the intensity and speed of contraction elicited by the exercise." Increase drop height "gradually from fairly low levels", "limit the number of drops per session", "land on suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces" and attend to landing technique.

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale: intensity of tension that resistance training cannot reach, with intensity and speed of contraction, not contraction type, as "the main consideration." Inference: "over 20 times bodyweight" holds for a 75 kg subject at the low end (1500 kgf / 75 kg = 20); the book gives no subject masses, so the ratio is approximate.

**When to apply** — As evidence that the eccentric landing alone is a strong stimulus, which supports using low-height landing drills as a step before rebound work. Inference: for football, landing drills from modest heights are the safe use of this finding; the experimental heights are not.

**When NOT to apply** — Never use 2-3.2 m drops in training (the authors' own warning). The study is reported second-hand, with no subject numbers, training duration or strength measure given. It used "soft gymnastic mats", which differs from the firm surfaces the authors want for rebound plyometrics (see [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: drops of 2 m or more onto soft mats, with peak tensions of 1500-3500 kgf over 0.028-0.061 s (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

# Jumpers Doing 475 Depth Jumps in 12 Weeks Gained More Reactive Ability Than a Group Doing 1472 Barbell Push-Offs and 93 Tonnes

**What it is** — "The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted a total volume of 93 tons!" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).

Two sentences around it: "The training effect of depth-jumps or shock-loading for developing explosive strength is very large, having little equal when compared with the other means of strength training, especially when combined in a complex with other forms of intensive strength training", corroborated by Semyenov 1971, Tatyan 1974, Dobrovolsky 1972, Savin 1974, Khodykin 1974 and Deniskin 1976 (same page). And: "Carefully periodised training programmes which combine resistance exercises with plyometrics can develop explosive strength even more effectively than plyometrics alone, provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors give the result as evidence of "economising training"; no mechanism is stated here beyond the shock-method rationale elsewhere in 5.2.4.

**When to apply** — Making the case to coaches that a small, well-placed depth-jump dose can do more for reactive ability than a large barbell volume. Inference: the companion sentence (resistance work before plyometrics in the same session) is a direct sequencing rule for combined sessions.

**When NOT to apply** — Unclear points in the source: "all of them did 475 jumps" does not say whether 475 is per athlete or the group total; the experiment has no citation, group sizes, statistics or outcome test named beyond "reactive ability"; the comparison group's "1472 general push-offs" is also unclear per athlete or total. Supported only as a reported Soviet-era comparison. The result is for track-and-field jumpers in a preparation phase.

**Example** — The authors' own experiment as quoted above (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

# Heavy Squats Build Strength Potential and Light Fast Lifts Build Speed, but Neither Trains the Rapid Eccentric-to-Concentric Switch

**What it is** — The authors open 5.2.4 by analysing the traditional speed-strength means. In heavy barbell squats "the muscles work very slowly (quasi-isometrically) with a relatively constant tension produced by the load. Consequently, the muscles primarily develop isometric strength". Raising the barbell weight, "frequently considered a basic indicator of special strength fitness, places a large and generally unnecessary load on the spine." For speed-strength, athletes use smaller loads; their example is "squat thrusts with a 60kg barbell on the shoulders", which "produces a large dynamic maximum force". So "exercises with heavy weights tend to increase the strength potential of the muscles, while fast exercises with light weights improve speed." Neither adequately enhances "specific components of explosive movements such as the rapid excitation of muscles and the rapid changing from eccentric to concentric work." These skills need "a specific training regime which is impossible to imitate with only one resistance exercise": slow resistance movements, and lifting a barbell in preparation for squatting or jumping with it, remove "the possibility of controlling the mechanisms which are crucial to the rapid switching of muscles to the active state", while lowering the resistance "diminishes the dynamic effort required and creates a vicious cycle from which there is no apparent escape." This analysis is the authors' stated route to the shock (plyometric) method on the same page. (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267, verified against the page image.)

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the one quoted: the barbell means do not reproduce rapid excitation or the fast eccentric-concentric switch. They give no further physiology here. Inference: the "vicious cycle" is that heavy loads slow the movement and light loads drop the effort, so no single barbell load gives both high effort and a fast switch.

**When to apply** — When a program relies on heavy squats plus light speed squats to develop jumping or cutting explosiveness, this is the authors' argument for adding a means that trains the switch itself (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 104). Inference: this entry is the authors' case for why the jumps in that list are not interchangeable with the squats.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors do not say heavy squats are useless for explosive athletes: "this does not mean that it is impossible for them to execute fast dynamic contractions", and heavy work raises "strength potential". Later in the same section they prefer heavy "brief maximal tension" work where explosive force must overcome large resistance (see [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]]). The 60 kg squat-thrust load is given without athlete bodymass or level, so it is not a prescription.

**Example** — The authors' own example: heavy squats (slow, quasi-isometric) versus squat thrusts with a 60 kg barbell (large dynamic maximum force), with neither training the rapid switch (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267).

# Many Sets and Reps of Plyometrics Do Not Build Fatigue Resistance for Repeated Rebounding; Movement Efficiency Does (Nicol et al, 1997)

**What it is** — Stated twice in 5.2.4:
- "Many repetitions of plyometric drills frequently are prescribed for some sports because of assumptions that this sort of training will improve fatigue resistance in repeated actions such as rebounding in basketball, yet research has shown this to be untrue (Nicol et al, 1997)" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269, verified against the page image).
- "The use of many repetitions and sets of plyometric drills in an attempt to facilitate adaptation to cope with exhaustive bouts of stretch-shortening activities such as rebounding in basketball is not supported by research (Nicol et al, 1997). Instead any improvement in such situations is better mediated by the use of training to enhance movement efficiency. This is a very important point which concerns all explosive and ballistic activities: it is futile to rely predominantly on plyometric drills to enhance sport specific explosive strength and power, because efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance" (PDF pp. 288-289 / printed pp. 277-278, verified against the page images).

**Internal conflict, recorded:** the "futile to rely predominantly" sentence is followed on PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278 by "plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes for developing explosive strength and reactive ability." See [[heuristic--brief-maximal-tension-vs-plyometrics-by-resistance-size]].

**Why it works** — The text's stated reason is "efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance." It does not describe the Nicol et al (1997) study design or measures, and the paper was not checked for this entry, so what it measured is unverified here.

**When to apply** — When someone proposes high-rep plyometric circuits to make athletes "fresher" in the fourth quarter. Eric's baseline: "Everything we do is some form of conditioning" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 122). Inference: the text's alternative for repeat-effort tolerance is better movement efficiency in the sport skill itself, not more drill volume; the book also allows "much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 6), so submaximal plyometric endurance work is not ruled out.

**When NOT to apply** — Not evidence against plyometrics for explosive strength; the same section calls the shock method's training effect "very large." The claim rests on one citation the book does not describe.

**Example** — The text's own: basketball rebounding as the repeated stretch-shortening task that high plyometric volume was assumed, wrongly, to prepare (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269).

# The Lewis Formula P = 21.693 x B x √H Tracks Jump Progress, but It Computes a Falling-Body Power, Not Take-Off Power

**What it is** — In the preparatory programme, the authors suggest tracking jump progress this way: "To gain an idea of individual progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P = (21.693) B√H watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, formula read from the page image; the text layer garbles it as "b Vh").

**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation. Inference (physics): 21.693 = 9.8 × √4.9, so the formula is P = B·g·√(g·H/2) with g = 9.8 m/s². A body falling freely from rest through height H reaches √(2gH); its mean speed during the fall is half that, √(gH/2). So the formula is body weight (B·g) times the mean speed of a body falling through H, in watts. It is a fixed function of bodymass and jump height only.

**When to apply** — As the authors use it: a cheap way to see whether an individual's bodymass-scaled jump is improving over time, when only a jump height and a scale are available. Eric's baseline: jumps are tested on ForceDecks force plates (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 77, the CMJ family protocol). Inference: where force plates are available, measured propulsive power replaces this estimate; the formula is only a fallback.

**When NOT to apply** — Inference: because the formula is weight times the mean speed of a free fall through H, it is not the athlete's peak or mean propulsive power during take-off, which depends on how fast force is produced over the push-off distance; two athletes with the same mass and jump height get the same value even if one pushes off much faster. Do not compare its values with force-plate peak power. The book gives no validation data for it.

**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete jumping 0.50 m gives P = 21.693 × 100 × √0.50 ≈ 1,534 W; at 0.55 m, ≈ 1,609 W. This arithmetic is not in the source.

**Related** — [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]]; [[claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power]] (Ch4.3, the authors' own warning about crude power estimates); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
