# Plyometric Injury Risk Comes From Prescription (Overload and Overuse), Not the Method; Regularly Impact-Loaded Cartilage Is Reported as Healthier

**What it is** — In "Plyometric Training and Safety" (PDF pp. 280-281 / printed pp. 269-270; p. 280 verified against the page image) the text argues:
- The claim that "plyometric drills on their own are dangerous and useless has not been proved experimentally or clinically"; the danger is "inferred from the magnitude of the impulsive peak forces which have been measured via force plate research", and an experiment isolating plyometric effects with matched controls "is very difficult to design."
- Opponents imply running and jumping "in the context of normal sport are perfectly safe, but in the context of special plyometric drills are dangerous", and assume joints do not follow SAID (Specific Adaptation to Imposed Demands).
- Cartilage: "joints subjected to heavy impact are relatively free from osteoarthritis in old age and ... those subjected to much lower loading experience a greater incidence of osteoarthritis and cartilage fibrillation (Bullough et al, 1973; Kempson et al, 1975; Seedhom & Swann, 1985; Seedhom & Wright, 1988; Seedhom et al, 1977)." Siff's former colleague Mark Swanepoel (University of the Witwatersrand) noted that fibrillation at any age increases going up from ankle to knee, hip and lumbar spine. Regularly impulse-loaded cartilage is "mechanically much stiffer", while cartilage "heavily loaded infrequently softens due to decrease in proteoglycan production" (Swanepoel, 1998).
- "it is not the inherent nature of plyometrics which may produce injury, but the manner in which it is used." Western practice earns much of the criticism: "encyclopaedic compilations of drills offered in extended, isolated and highly repetitive forms"; drills often prescribed without regard to "loading imposed by other work or play ... or the use of formal restoration"; and "the athlete's sport alone may offer all or most of the plyometric training that is necessary."
- "overtraining comprises two distinct components: overload (the imposition of too great a force at any given time) and overuse (the imposition of too great a volume of exercise)." An "individually appropriate volume and intensity (e.g. via choice of drop height)" with "gradual progressive overload" and "adequate restoration regimes need pose no greater risks than the naturally occurring plyometric actions found in running or jumping" (PDF pp. 280-281).

Voice: Siff (the passage names "Siff's former colleague").

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is adaptation (SAID) and the cartilage findings cited. Inference: overload maps to drop height and rebound effort, overuse to contacts per session and week, which gives two separate dials to manage.

**When to apply** — Answering "are depth jumps dangerous?" for coaches or medical staff: the text's position is that risk is a dose question. Inference: in football, count the plyometric loading already present in practice (cutting, jumping, sprinting) before adding drills, as the text's "sport alone may offer all or most" warning suggests.

**When NOT to apply** — The text argues mainly from absence of proof and from cartilage studies of everyday joint loading; it cites no controlled study showing plyometric drills are safe. The "heavy impact joints are free from osteoarthritis" sentence compares joints and loading histories, not plyometric training programs, so do not cite it as evidence that depth jumps protect joints. The cited studies were not checked for this entry.

**Example** — The text's own: the Nicol et al (1997) finding, that many repetitions do not improve fatigue resistance in basketball rebounding, as an example of a Western volume habit that is "untrue" (PDF p. 280 / printed p. 269; see [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]).

# Most "Plyometric" Drills in Popular Western Books Work Through Eccentric Loading, Connective Tissue, Starting Strength and Prestretch, Not the Shock Mechanism

**What it is** — Under "Popular Information on Plyometrics" (PDF pp. 293-294 / printed pp. 282-283; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 294 from the text layer):
- Popular Western texts ("e.g. Chu, 1992; Radcliffe & Farantinos, 1985") present jumping and rebound activities "many of which do not constitute true plyometric training as originally conceived by Russian scientists"; they are "often supplementary or preparatory movements."
- "Most books classify extended range swinging, passing or catching of medicine balls or other objects as 'plyometric', although the amortisation phase is too long to produce classical plyometrics." These drills still help "eye-hand coordination, eccentric strength and starting strength, but they are not strictly plyometric."
- Books omit the tonic versus phasic myotatic reflex in relation to drill types, the positive supportive reaction, the crossed extensor reflex, phased breathing, the maximal-submaximal distinction, and concurrent and sequential prescription.
- "the so-called plyometric drills in current Western texts are known to enhance performance, but it is not predominantly due to plyometric training, but more to the increased loading of eccentric contraction, the conditioning of connective tissue, the improvement of voluntary starting strength from the quasi-isometric state, the use of prestretch, and enhancement of acceleration strength by increasing the velocity of projectiles such as medicine balls" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283).
- The physiotherapy link: in PNF a therapist "sometimes imposes a short, sharp jerk on an eccentrically or isometrically contracting muscle to produce strong muscle contraction in a weakened muscle", principles that "preceded sporting plyometrics by several decades" (same page).
- Related, from the classification passage: *pseudo-plyometrics* such as aerobics "power moves" and many "water plyos" lack "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The text's argument is definitional: long amortisation phases fall outside the shock method, so the benefit must come from the other listed qualities. It gives no study separating these mechanisms.

**When to apply** — Labelling a program's med-ball and jump drills honestly: Inference: a long-amortisation med-ball chest pass or rotational throw is a starting-strength and eccentric drill in the authors' terms, and should not be counted as shock-method volume or dosed with shock-method rest.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the list of "other mechanisms" is the text's assertion, with no data. The criticism of specific books is the author's opinion and was not checked against those books. Not a reason to drop these drills: the text says they "are known to enhance performance."

**Example** — The text's own: extended-range medicine ball swinging and catching, called plyometric in popular books, as an example of a drill whose amortisation is too long for classical plyometrics (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

# Strength-Endurance Helps Cyclic Endurance, but Some Popular Strength Exercises and Excess Hypertrophy Hinder It; Never Let Relative Strength Fall

**What it is** — From 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 297-298 / printed pp. 286-287, verified against the page images):
- "an increase in strength-endurance contributes to improving endurance in distance runners, skiers and skaters (Popov, 1968; Nabatnikova, 1972; Mikhailov & Panov, 1975). However ... the magnitude of the strength load used is different if, on the one hand, the key quality required is general endurance and, on the other hand, it is strength-endurance."
- "certain popular strength exercises such as running with a sack of sand weighing 25% of the subject's bodyweight, barbell pressing, squats, 'good mornings', and twisting with a barbell not only do not enhance, but to a certain degree, will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises (Maisuradze, 1960)." In some instances "the increase in strength is associated with excessive muscle hypertrophy". "Endurance and hypertrophy do not increase simultaneously and there is no correlation between them (Maison & Broeker, 1941; McMorris & Elkins, 1954)."
- No definite correlation between special strength and muscle mass in cyclic endurance sports (middle distance running, skating, skiing: Chistyakov, 1965; Chernyaev, 1965; Nabatnikova, 1972). But in gymnasts "a positive linear correlation (R = 0.77) is noticed between strength-endurance and relative strength (Zhalei, 1964). Therefore, in those cases where endurance is associated with the display of significant strength, some muscular hypertrophy does not negatively influence training results."
- Closing rules: "Strength training should not result in increased muscle mass in those types of sport where the key quality is endurance of moderate work output. If strength-endurance is required, especially in those cases where it is necessary to overcome a large resistance, a small increase in muscle mass is permissible. In no cases, should the training ever produce a decrease in relative strength of any muscle groups in the body" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).

**Tension with Chapter 4, recorded:** section 4.4 cites research that strength training "contributes more to the largest improvements in distance sports than aerobic training" (PDF pp. 261-262 / printed pp. 250-251; see [[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]]), while 5.2.5 says squats, presses and good mornings "will even hinder the development of endurance in cyclic type exercises" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286). Inference: the two may differ in which strength exercises and loads are meant, but the book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is the hypertrophy by-product and the lack of correlation between endurance and hypertrophy; they give no physiology beyond that.

**When to apply** — Inference: for football the relevant case is the gymnast-like one, endurance "associated with the display of significant strength", where some hypertrophy "does not negatively influence training results." The relative-strength rule applies to every position: Inference: track strength per kg of bodymass when linemen are gaining mass, since the authors say training should never lower relative strength.

**When NOT to apply** — The Maisuradze (1960) list is a single citation without design or loads beyond the 25% bodyweight sandbag. The correlation and hypertrophy statements cite studies from 1941-1972. Not a reason to avoid squats for endurance athletes in general; the authors' own sport prescriptions (skaters, runners) use squats ([[case-study--soviet-sport-specific-strength-endurance-prescriptions]]), which is itself in tension with the Maisuradze sentence.

**Example** — The authors' own: gymnasts, R = 0.77 between strength-endurance and relative strength (Zhalei, 1964), against middle-distance runners, skaters and skiers with no definite strength-mass correlation (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).

# The "Squat 1.5-2 Times Bodymass" Prerequisite Is a Safety Rule for Maximal Depth Jumps, Not for Submaximal Plyometrics

**What it is** — "Some authors rightly criticize the recommendation sometimes put forward that athletes should be able to squat 1.5 - 2 times bodymass in order to use certain plyometric drills, since they consider that this criterion is not based on research evidence and does not apply to all plyometric exercises. This recommendation is a safety measure based on force plate analysis of *maximal plyometrics* in the form of depth jumps, where the ground reaction force on the lower extremity can easily exceed 6 times bodyweight. *This guideline was never intended to apply religiously to submaximal plyometrics using small drops, skipping drills or less demanding actions.* This misunderstanding of Russian guidelines is largely a result of an incomplete grasp of the scientific principles on which the original shock method was based" (PDF pp. 293-294 / printed pp. 282-283; p. 282 verified against the page image, p. 283 from the text layer).

Both halves are the authors': they agree the criterion is not research-based ("rightly criticize"), then defend it as a force-plate-based safety measure for maximal depth jumps.

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: maximal depth jumps can produce ground reaction forces that "easily exceed 6 times bodyweight", so a strength base is a safety margin. They give no derivation linking a 1.5-2 × bodymass squat to tolerating a 6 × bodyweight landing. Inference: the squat is a slow, bilateral, concentric-eccentric test and the landing is a brief eccentric-isometric impact, so the rule is a proxy, not a matched test.

**When to apply** — Deciding whether an athlete may do maximal depth jumps (high box, maximal rebound). Inference: for football, where most players have a lifting base, the rule mainly screens young or newly enrolled athletes before maximal depth jumps; it should not block hops, skips, low drops or bounds, which the authors explicitly exclude.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a gate for submaximal plyometrics, "small drops, skipping drills or less demanding actions." The authors do not say whether the squat is a 1RM, a full or partial squat, or how to test it. The book also says readiness for plyometric versus heavy work should be decided by the strength deficit (see [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]]), which is a different question from this safety threshold.

**Example** — The authors' own framing: the threshold comes from force plate analysis of maximal depth jumps with ground reaction forces over 6 × bodyweight (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

85	# How Long a Prestretch Helps Varies From About 0.25 s to About 4 s by Task, and the Book's Own Figure Attribution Conflicts
86	
87	**What it is** — After stating the about 0.15 s coupling guide, the authors say it "requires some qualification" and list conflicting results (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271; Figs 5.6 and 5.7 verified against the page image):
88	- Wilson et al (1990), bench press: "the benefits of prior stretch may endure for as long as 4 seconds, at which stage it is suggested that all stored elastic energy is lost (see Fig 5.6)."
89	- Chapman and Caldwell (1985), forearm movement: benefits "dissipated within 0.25 second, a figure which agrees with Siff's analysis of explosive rebound elbow flexion without additional loading (Fig 5.7)."
90	- Wilson et al (1991), rebound action of the chest and arms: "no benefits of prior stretching are evident after 0.37 second."
91	
92	Summary in the text: "delays of as long as a second or two can still produce significant augmentation of the subsequent concentric phase for some activities, but delays as short as 0.2 second are sufficient to dissipate the benefits of prior stretch during other activities."
93	
94	Figure readings (approximate, from the image). Fig 5.6, "% decay" against delay 0-5 s: rises steeply from 0 near 0.1-0.2 s, roughly half decayed near 1 s, about 80% by 2 s, near 100% at about 4 s. Fig 5.7, unloaded elbow flexion, delay 0.1-0.25 s: close to linear from 0% at 0.1 s to 100% at 0.25 s.
95	
96	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the Fig 5.6 caption reads "based on the data of Wilson et al, 1991", but the text gives the 4 s bench-press result to Wilson et al (1990) and the 0.37 s chest/arms result to Wilson et al (1991) (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271). The curve's near-total decay at about 4 s matches the text's 1990 sentence, not the 0.37 s result. Which year is right is not resolvable from the book.
97	
98	The authors' partial resolutions:
99	- Fibre type (Bosco et al, 1982a): high-FT individuals show the maximum plyometric effect with a short eccentric phase, small range and brief coupling; high-ST individuals jump best with a longer eccentric phase, greater range and longer coupling, "since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration" (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
100	- Joint-specific maximum delays "probably" exist, but the body has many reflexes acting "at different rates"; tonic (static) and phasic (dynamic) stretch reflexes differ (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
101	- The weightlifters' "pre-stretch principle" (hold an intense stretch "for a couple of seconds and then thrust") "would seem" to involve the more tonic reflex with longer coupling, and "could certainly not be called plyometric", while phasic reflexes are "more likely" behind classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
102	
103	**Why it works** — The authors offer fibre type and tonic versus phasic reflexes as explanations, with hedges ("partial solution", "would seem", "more likely"). They do not test either against the conflicting delay data.
104	
105	**When to apply** — When someone quotes one fixed "the stretch benefit is gone after X ms" number: the book shows the window depends on the task (unloaded elbow about 0.25 s; loaded bench press up to about 4 s). Inference: for loaded lifts a paused rep still keeps some prestretch benefit for a second or more, per Fig 5.6, while for unloaded fast rebounds the benefit is gone within a few tenths of a second, per Fig 5.7.
106	
107	**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Fig 5.6 under a single Wilson year without noting the caption-text conflict. The figure values are read from small plots and are approximate. Fig 5.7 is Siff's own analysis: the book says it "was derived from some of this work on upper-body non-impact plyometrics", the research "conducted in this field by the author in 1994" (PDF p. 292 / printed p. 281), and gives no subject numbers or publication for it. The fibre-type and reflex explanations are proposals, not demonstrated here.
108	
109	**Example** — The authors' own: unloaded explosive elbow flexion loses its prestretch benefit over 0.1-0.25 s (Fig 5.7), while the bench-press benefit decays over about 4 s (Fig 5.6).
110

126	
127	# The Five Phases of a Plyometric Action (Fig 5.5), With Coupling Time as the Explosive-Isometric Interval
128	
129	**What it is** — Under "The Fundamental Theory of Plyometrics" the authors list five phases (PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270; Fig 5.5 verified against the page image):
130	1. **Initial momentum phase:** the body or limb moves "because of kinetic energy (KE) it has accumulated from a preceding action."
131	2. **Electromechanical delay phase:** contact with a surface stops the limb and "provokes the muscles to contract"; the delay is "the time elapsing between the onset of the action potential in the motor nerves and the onset of the muscle contraction." The authors note some workers include lengthening of the SEC (series elastic component) in this phase, but "electromechanical" was coined for the electrical-to-mechanical interval, "which does not include the passive stretching of connective tissue."
132	3. **Amortisation phase:** the KE "produces a powerful myotatic stretch reflex which leads to eccentric muscle contraction accompanied by explosive isometric contraction" and stretching of the SEC (e.g. tendons). "The explosive isometric phase between the end of the eccentric action and the beginning of the concentric action lasts for a period known as the *coupling time*."
133	4. **Rebound phase:** release of elastic energy from the SEC, with involuntary concentric contraction evoked by the stretch reflex, "as well as possible local change in the muscle fibre mechanics"; it "may include the contribution added by voluntary concentric contraction."
134	5. **Final momentum phase:** after the concentric contraction, the body or limb continues on the KE imparted by contraction and elastic recoil.
135	
136	Fig 5.5, as drawn: boxes for initial momentum, amortisation, rebound and final momentum phases; between them, bars for "EM delay", "eccentric contraction" and "concentric contraction", joined at the bottom by a box "explosive isometrics" labelled "Coupling Time".
137	
138	The caption defines EM delay differently from the numbered text: "Electromechanical delay between signal to terminate initial momentum phase and instant when eccentric contraction begins" (caption), against "between the onset of the action potential in the motor nerves and the onset of the muscle contraction" (text item 2). Both are on PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270; the book does not reconcile them.
139	
140	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is in the phase descriptions: stretch reflex plus SEC elastic energy, released in the rebound. Elsewhere they add that the process is not only spinal reflex and elastic recoil (see [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]).
141	
142	**When to apply** — As a shared vocabulary for coaching and for reading a force-time trace of a depth jump or rebound: the coupling interval is the part the authors' 0.15 s guide applies to (see [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]). Inference: on a force plate, the eccentric (braking) and concentric (propulsive) phases of a drop jump map onto phases 3 and 4; the authors do not give a force-plate method for isolating the isometric coupling interval.
143	
144	**When NOT to apply** — The phase list is a descriptive model, not measured timing; the book gives no durations for phases 1, 2, 4 or 5. Do not quote the EM delay definition without noting the caption and text differ. The rebound phase's "possible local change in the muscle fibre mechanics" is stated as possible, not shown.
145	
146	**Example** — Inference: in a depth jump from a box, phase 1 is the fall, phases 2-3 are the first instants of ground contact through the lowest point, phase 4 is the push-off, and phase 5 is the flight. The authors' own illustration is Fig 5.5.
147

164	# Classes of Plyometric (Powermetric) Training: Impact or Non-Impact, Maximal to Non-Plyometric, Functional or Non-Functional (Fig 5.8)
165	
166	**What it is** — The authors replace the "classically plyometric or not" argument with a classification (PDF pp. 283-284 / printed pp. 272-273; Fig 5.8 verified against the page image):
167	- **Impact versus non-impact.** In impact plyometrics "the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object"; in non-impact plyometrics the recoil "is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement not terminated by contact with a surface." Depth jumps are impact; "snap kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts" are non-impact, which "may also be maximal or submaximal."
168	- **Maximal, submaximal, non-plyometric.** *Maximal plyometrics* are "low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced." *Sub-maximal plyometrics* "do not produce maximal muscular tension, although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase": "lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound height"; "rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot" are other examples. The three are drawn in one box "as a reminder that there is really a continuum of intensities."
169	- **Classical, supplementary, preparatory.** Classical plyometric exercises are *functional* ("matched as closely as possible to the specific explosive actions of the particular sport with respect to movement pattern, muscle involvement, timing and direction of motion") or *non-functional* ("general training of the explosive qualities"). Functional examples: forward bounding for long jump, backward rebounds for shot put, one-legged forward hopping for jumping, and for basketball "both short and relatively long amortisation phases in vertical rebounds." Preparatory or supplementary drills are weight training for muscular strength ("especially eccentric strength") and connective tissue, plus jumping, swinging, throwing and catching drills "with longer duration transition phases"; "Most of the drills described in popular books on plyometrics in the West are actually supplementary exercises."
170	- **Pseudo-plyometrics.** Drills "incorrectly labelled as plyometric because they include a sudden stop or some form of jump", e.g. "'power moves' (involving quick landings and delayed jumps in a semi-squat position)" and many "'water plyos'" in aerobics classes; lacking "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time", they serve as "preparatory non-plyometrics."
171	
172	Fig 5.8 as drawn: Plyometric training splits into impact and non-impact; below these sit maximal plyometrics, submaximal plyometrics and non-plyometrics; under maximal sits "classical plyometrics" (split into functional and non-functional); under submaximal sits "supplementary plyometrics"; under non-plyometrics sits "preparatory/supplementary activities" (split into weight training and "jumps throws etc"). The text lists classical, supplementary and preparatory as three flat categories; the figure ties each to one intensity level.
173	
174	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for classifying rather than arguing definitions: the definitional debate "becomes complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272). Intensity is graded by the momentum at contact (see [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]).
175	
176	**When to apply** — Labelling every jump, bound, hop and med-ball drill in a plan by class, so volume and rest rules are applied to the right class: the authors' low-rep, long-rest rules are for maximal plyometrics, while submaximal and preparatory drills tolerate more volume (see [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]). Inference: in football, a vertical depth jump is classical non-functional, while a bound or single-leg hop that matches a cut or drive phase in direction and timing would be the authors' "functional" class.
177	
178	**When NOT to apply** — The text and figure place "supplementary" differently (a flat list of three versus a level under submaximal; and "preparatory or supplementary drills" in the text against "supplementary plyometrics" as its own box in the figure). The class boundaries are a continuum by the authors' own statement, so the labels are not sharp cut-offs.
179	
180	**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps (impact, maximal when performed for maximal rebound), low box depth jumps without striving for height (submaximal), karate snap kicks (non-impact), "power moves" in aerobics (pseudo-plyometric).
181

198	# Non-Impact Plyometrics: Explosive Eccentric Recoil Without Surface Contact (Ericson's Seated System, Martial Arts Snaps)
199	
200	**What it is** — Siff's section (he refers to "the author" doing force-plate analysis and to "his wife, Lisa Ericson") argues that plyometric action does not need impact (PDF pp. 290-292 / printed pp. 279-281, text layer):
201	- Western and even Russian practice treats "shock contact of parts of the body with some surface" as the common denominator of plyometrics, but "this is not the only way of producing plyometric action." The non-impact variety was recognised when Siff analysed martial arts movements and Ericson's seated fitness system (called Supersitting, and on p. 281 the "SMART seated fitness system").
202	- Ericson's system: "very rapid wide-range movements choreographed at rates exceeding 240 beats per minute, interspersed with rhythmic transitional PNF-type patterns", over sessions of about 60 minutes, movements "initiated and terminated explosively in sets of uninterrupted sequences" that change form and direction "to avoid excessive fatigue, habituation or injury."
203	- It counts as non-impact plyometrics "because it obeys all the requirements of plyometrics as originally conceived": "a ballistic action which is rapidly terminated by eccentric and explosive isometric muscle contraction, followed immediately by a powerful concentric recoil mediated by recruitment of the myotatic stretch reflex and augmented by the release of elastic energy."
204	- Comparison with karate: karate uses few repetitions with brief intervals, and the punch often contacts its target briefly, "sufficient to dissipate much of the elastic energy"; Ericson's transition is "usually shorter" with many continuous repetitions, which "probably explains the differences in functional and structural development."
205	- Intensity: most class movements are submaximal plyometrics; "Performed in the form of all-out single movements, they become maximal non-impact plyometrics." "maximal impact plyometrics will generally increase muscle tension to a greater extent than the equivalent non-impact movements for the leg and hip extensors (e.g. the karate thrust-kick)."
206	- Uses: maximal non-impact plyometrics, like submaximal impact plyometrics, "can serve as a preparatory tool for maximal impact plyometrics", for other qualities ("strength, muscle hypertrophy, muscle endurance and speed-strength endurance"), or to train selected muscle groups "instead of unnecessarily stressing the entire musculature."
207	- Sport sources (PNF-like spiral and diagonal paths are a common feature): thrust punches, blocks, knife-hand thrusts, palm-heel strikes, front, side snap and side thrust kicks, done solo with pre-stretch, ending in "a brief isometrically-held end position" or "rapid recoil actions", in kata, or in non-contact sparring. Low-impact throwing or kicking of very light objects is included as "low inertia" plyometrics.
208	
209	**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is the same reflex-plus-elastic recoil as impact plyometrics, produced by the muscles' own explosive eccentric braking. Evidence offered: Siff's force-plate analysis (no data shown), changes in Ericson's wheelchair students, and "preliminary studies executed in 1995 by University of Pretoria physiotherapy students supervised by Siff and Ericson" that "warrant more detailed expansion."
210	
211	**When to apply** — Inference: upper-body rebound work for linemen's hand strikes, or plyometric exposure for an athlete who cannot yet tolerate landing impact, are the obvious fits; the authors name "athletes who require high levels of upper body power and endurance" and arm rehabilitation.
212	
213	**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: no data are reported, the source is the author's own and his wife's system, and the text says research so far has studied speed-strength, not these other qualities. Siff himself says maximal impact plyometrics produce more leg and hip extensor tension than non-impact equivalents, so non-impact work does not replace depth jumps for lower-body reactive strength.
214	
215	**Example** — The text's own: a karate snap kick, thrust out and whipped back (non-impact), compared with a punch that briefly hits its target (PDF p. 291 / printed p. 280).
216

272	
273	**What it is** — The authors' rules for choosing drop height in training (all on pages verified against the page image):
274	- "The optimal depth of the jump is determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
275	- "The optimal height of a depth jump does not result in a landing where the heel is forced to the ground by momentum" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 8).
276	- "One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or take-off height" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 5).
277	- "One should begin at a relatively low height and increase it gradually to the optimal height. It makes sense to begin by jumping upward and forward and only after sufficient training, to jump strictly upward" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1).
278	- Height is preferred over added weight, and a force plate can find the height for a required force (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1).
279	- For jumping power "one can work without an additional load and utilise only falling bodymass" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274). Fig 5.10 (Verkhoshansky, 1977) shows three variants: two under "Horizontal Projection" (after the drop, the athlete rebounds forward over low objects drawn on the ground) and one under "Vertical Projection" (rebound upward toward a hanging marker) (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, read from the image; the drawings are small, so the object details are approximate).

Eric's baseline: the department reads reactive ability through mRSI, which "was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74). Inference: a drop-jump RSI (jump height over contact time) taken at stepped heights is the direct test of the authors' "without slowing down the transition" rule, but Eric's baseline names CMJ-based mRSI, not drop jumps.

305	# Depth-Jump Execution Cues: Step Off Relaxed, Land on the Balls of the Feet With Shallow Amortisation, Eyes Up, Breath Held Through Contact
306	
307	**What it is** — The authors' execution rules for depth jumps and plyometric drills (pages verified against the page images unless marked):
308	- **Leaving the box:** "Depth-jumping necessitates falling in a relaxed state, but not jumping, off the box" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 10).
309	- **Landing:** "land with the legs slightly flexed, muscles mildly tensed and on the balls of the feet in order to avoid an excessive shock. The depth of amortisation should not be great and the subsequent take-off needs to be executed very quickly with an energetic throwing upwards of the arms" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).
310	- **Target:** "strive with the hands or head to reach some height indicated by some marker if the take-off is executed upward, or to land at some point if it is directed upward and forward"; a gain in height or distance "clearly indicates improvement in special fitness, which always has a positive effect on the athlete's emotional state" (same page).
311	- **Starting posture:** the amortisation "should be of minimal duration, but sufficient to create impulsive contraction of the muscles. Therefore, the initial posture with respect to the joint angles should correspond to the same position in which the working movement begins in the sporting exercise" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 2).
312	- **Range of motion** in the Fig 5.9 resistance-apparatus exercises "should be somewhat greater than the required coordination range of the exercise in order to enhance shock absorption by the soft tissues and thereby avoid impact injury" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
313	- **Head and gaze:** "Flexing the head downward to look at the floor before take-off may result in spurious muscle contraction or altered timing. Similarly if the head is not thrust upwards during the take-off, maximal height will not be reached" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 9).
314	- **Warm-up:** plyometric training "should be preceded by a good warmup of the intensively involved muscles" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 3).
315	- **Breathing:** "It is vital that the athlete holds the breath during the amortisation and early propulsion phase to stabilise the body, offer pneumatic shock absorption and to increase the rebound force. Forced exhalation may accompany the remainder of the propulsion phase" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273). Item 12: "the breath should be held and never released during the contact phase or any phase where maximal effort is to be produced. Exhalation during any landing phase reduces overall stability and increases the loading on the spine during depth-jumping" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).
316	
317	**Why it works** — Reasons given by the authors are in the quotes: avoiding excessive shock (landing posture), stability and "pneumatic shock absorption" (breath), timing (gaze), and shock absorption by soft tissues (range). They cite no study for these cues.
318	
319	**When to apply** — Coaching any depth-jump or rebound session; the cues are concrete and observable. Inference: the starting-posture rule (item 2) gives a way to make a depth jump more specific to a football stance or a block-start angle by matching the landing knee and hip angle to the sport's start position.
320	
321	**When NOT to apply** — The two breathing statements differ in detail: p. 273 allows "forced exhalation" during the remainder of the propulsion phase, which is still ground contact in a rebound, while item 12 says the breath is "never released during the contact phase." Inference: read together, the cautious reading is breath held through landing and early push-off. Item 2's "minimal duration but sufficient" depth and the Fig 5.9 "somewhat greater" range are not quantified. Inference: maximal breath-holding effort raises blood pressure; the book does not discuss this for athletes with cardiovascular conditions.
322	
323	**Example** — The authors' own: jumping up to touch a marker with the hands or head after the depth jump (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).
324	
325	**Related** — [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]; [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]]; [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]] (Ch1.7, limiting joint angle to keep the "shock" loading); [[framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines]]
326

340	
341	# Large Resistance Calls for the Brief Maximal Tension Method, Small Resistance and Reactive Demand Call for Plyometrics; the Book Disagrees With Itself on Whether Plyometrics Should Be the Main Method
342	
343	**What it is** — The authors' method-selection rules (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image unless marked):
344	- "In those cases where explosive force is associated with the overcoming of large resistance, preference should be given to the brief maximal tension method, as used commonly in Olympic weightlifting. In situations where the resistance is small and the working effect depends upon the reactive ability of the muscles, plyometric methods should be given preference."
345	- Staging: "Although it should form an integral part of the training programme, plyometrics should not be combined in the beginning stages with resistance exercises such as the brief maximal tension method." "In subsequent stages, plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes for developing explosive strength and reactive ability."
346	- Concentric explosive work: "exercises with maximum effort and mixed regimes using weights equal to 40% of 1RM, or 30% of 1RM (Verkhoshansky, 1963; Papysheva, 1966). Explosive-isometric tension up to 80% of maximum should be used in conjunction with this routine."
347	- In combined sessions, resistance work goes first: combined programmes beat plyometrics alone "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).
348	- Testing decides: "To ascertain whether an athlete needs plyometric or heavy resistance training depends on measuring the *strength deficit* ... Without such testing, prescription of plyometric training tends to remain hit-and-miss" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273; repeated at PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282 in a grammatically broken sentence).
349	
350	**Internal conflict, recorded:** "plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes" (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278) against, half a page earlier, "it is futile to rely predominantly on plyometric drills to enhance sport specific explosive strength and power, because efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance" (PDF pp. 288-289 / printed pp. 277-278). The second follows a Nicol et al (1997) citation. Inference: the first reads like the original shock-method programme and the second like a later addition, but the book marks neither passage by author. The book does not reconcile them.
351	
352	**Why it works** — The authors tie each method to the force demand: heavy brief tension for large resistance, reactive shock loading for small resistance. The strength deficit decides which an individual needs (Ch1; see [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]], which records that the book also states the deficit rule two ways).
353	
354	**When to apply** — Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q21; `docs/method-baseline.md` line 76). Inference: DSI plays the role the authors give the strength deficit (both compare a fast expression of force with a maximal one to choose plyometric versus heavy work), but they are different measures; Eric's baseline Tension 17 records that the DSI cutoffs were never validated and that IMTP peak force drives most of the ratio (line 261). Inference: for linemen, whose sport force is against large resistance, the authors' rule favours brief maximal tension; for skill positions, whose force is against bodymass, it favours plyometrics.
355	
356	**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Supertraining as saying plyometrics should be the main method without the "futile to rely predominantly" sentence, or the reverse. "Beginning stages" and "highly qualified" are not defined. The 40% and 30% of 1RM loads and the 80% explosive-isometric tension are given without sets, reps or rest.
357	
358	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: Olympic weightlifting (large resistance, brief maximal tension) versus jumping from depth (small resistance, reactive ability) (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278).
359

# Plyometric Action Is Not Only Spinal Reflex and Elastic Recoil: It Is Planned, Conditionable and State-Dependent

**What it is** — Under "Plyometrics and the Brain" (PDF pp. 294-295 / printed pp. 283-284, text layer):
- "plyometric action is not simply a phenomenon that can be adequately explained on the basis of stored elastic energy and the stretch shortening cycle." Although the action itself is fast and spinal, "the preparatory period prior to the plyometric action can involve higher order mental processing of exceptional intricacy."
- **Cognitive versus non-cognitive plyometrics:** a plyometric action "under conditions in which the athlete anticipates a particular course of action (*cognitive plyometrics*)" versus "a purely reflexive response under unexpected circumstances (*non-cognitive plyometrics*)", the latter mainly in self-protection.
- **Practice:** "most athletes do not manage to perfect plyometric skills even after many weeks of practice. The use of numerous sequential repetitions to imprint these skills may constitute the inappropriate strategy because classical plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete. Submaximal plyometrics and pseudo-plyometrics may be performed in a state of advancing fatigue, unlike classical 'shock method' plyometrics."
- **Conditioning:** reflexes "can be trained and modified" (Pavlov's conditioned reflexes; Skinner, 1938, respondent and operant conditioning). An emotion such as fear or excitement, or a mental image, before a depth jump "can shape the subsequent neuromuscular reflexes"; events after it ("the jarring of the body, post-exercise fatigue or an injury") can modify them too.
- **State-dependent learning:** conditioned reflexes learned in a particular physiological or psychological state "are exhibited only when the same state is present", so "plyometric proficiency or deficiency learned in a specific training situation may not be reproduced in competitive circumstances." The text suggests this "may be one of the reasons" some experiments found little or no benefit from plyometric training.
- Visualisation caveat: Kensall Wise (Scientific American, Oct 1988) is cited that the brain region that visualises an action is separate from those that initiate it. Calvin's hypothesis (Scientific American, Oct 1994) links planning of ballistic movement to language and intelligence.

Voice: the passage cites no author by name; it reads as Siff's (it continues the Siff-voiced material on either side), but the book does not mark it, so "the text" is used here.

**Why it works** — The text's mechanism is that ballistic movements must be fully planned in advance ("ballistic movements require the brain to determine every detail of the action in advance"), so the planning state, emotions and the learning context become part of the skill.

**When to apply** — Inference: run plyometrics in states closer to competition (with reactive cues, under some arousal, sometimes unplanned) if the aim is transfer to football, since the text warns that drills learned in one state may not reproduce in another. The text recommends feedforward and visualisation techniques "to efficiently manage any plyometric actions under real sporting conditions."

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: no plyometric study is cited for state-dependent learning or for the conditioning claims; the supports are general psychology and two popular-science articles. Do not cite it as evidence that a given plyometric study failed for this reason (the text says only "may be").

**Example** — The text's own: fear or excitement before a depth jump shaping the reflexes, and a jarring landing afterwards modifying them (PDF p. 295 / printed p. 284).

# Endurance Training at 60% Raised Isometric Endurance 84%, Dynamic Endurance 93% and Repeated-Isometric Endurance 219%, While Maximal-Resistance Training Left Endurance Unchanged

**What it is** — Two experiments reported in 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 296-297 / printed pp. 285-286, verified against the page images):
- **Zatsiorsky (1966), elbow flexors, 5 weeks:** "isometric endurance increased 84% as a result of exercising 10 times a day for 5 weeks with the elbow flexors holding a 60% maximal contraction for as long as possible. Dynamic endurance increased by 93% as a result of performing these arm curls with a weight of 60% of 1RM at a rate of 28 repetitions per minute until it was impossible to increase the tempo further. At the same time, the ability to execute repetitive isometric contractions (60% of maximal strength for 5 seconds of tension and 2 seconds of rest) to failure increased by 219%."
- **Hansen (1963):** "A similar experiment with 10 dynamic movements executed daily with maximal resistance for 5 weeks resulted in increases in both dynamic and static strength, but dynamic and static endurance remained almost unchanged."
- The authors' conclusion: "This indicates that it is necessary to optimise the volume of work required to develop strength-endurance."

Reading note: in the image the "28" sits in the shaded page gutter; the first digit is faint but reads as 2.

**Why it works** — The authors give the results without a mechanism beyond the 75-80% ceiling statement that heavy work trains "strength predominantly" (see [[heuristic--strength-endurance-load-tempo-and-the-75-80-percent-ceiling]]). Inference: the text's sentence "At the same time, the ability to execute repetitive isometric contractions ... increased by 219%" does not say which training group (isometric or dynamic) showed the 219%; the passage is ambiguous.

**When to apply** — As the authors' evidence that endurance gains come from submaximal, long-duration work and not from maximal-resistance training. Inference: a maximal-strength block will not by itself raise local muscular endurance, per Hansen's result.

**When NOT to apply** — Single-muscle-group (elbow flexor) studies with no subject numbers or populations given. Inference: percentage gains in time-to-failure tests are not on the same scale as strength percentages, so do not compare them directly. Which group produced the 219% is unclear. Do not generalise to whole-body or sport endurance.

**Example** — The authors' own: Zatsiorsky's 60% elbow flexor protocols versus Hansen's 10 daily maximal movements (PDF pp. 296-297 / printed pp. 285-286).

**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-endurance-load-tempo-and-the-75-80-percent-ceiling]]; [[framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial]]; [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]]; [[claim--isometric-endurance-limits-and-recovery-phases]]

# How Long a Prestretch Helps Varies From About 0.25 s to About 4 s by Task, and the Book's Own Figure Attribution Conflicts

**What it is** — After stating the about 0.15 s coupling guide, the authors say it "requires some qualification" and list conflicting results (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271; Figs 5.6 and 5.7 verified against the page image):
- Wilson et al (1990), bench press: "the benefits of prior stretch may endure for as long as 4 seconds, at which stage it is suggested that all stored elastic energy is lost (see Fig 5.6)."
- Chapman and Caldwell (1985), forearm movement: benefits "dissipated within 0.25 second, a figure which agrees with Siff's analysis of explosive rebound elbow flexion without additional loading (Fig 5.7)."
- Wilson et al (1991), rebound action of the chest and arms: "no benefits of prior stretching are evident after 0.37 second."

Summary in the text: "delays of as long as a second or two can still produce significant augmentation of the subsequent concentric phase for some activities, but delays as short as 0.2 second are sufficient to dissipate the benefits of prior stretch during other activities."

Figure readings (approximate, from the image). Fig 5.6, "% decay" against delay 0-5 s: rises steeply from 0 near 0.1-0.2 s, roughly half decayed near 1 s, about 80% by 2 s, near 100% at about 4 s. Fig 5.7, unloaded elbow flexion, delay 0.1-0.25 s: close to linear from 0% at 0.1 s to 100% at 0.25 s.

**Internal conflict, recorded:** the Fig 5.6 caption reads "based on the data of Wilson et al, 1991", but the text gives the 4 s bench-press result to Wilson et al (1990) and the 0.37 s chest/arms result to Wilson et al (1991) (PDF pp. 281-282 / printed pp. 270-271). The curve's near-total decay at about 4 s matches the text's 1990 sentence, not the 0.37 s result. Which year is right is not resolvable from the book.

The authors' partial resolutions:
- Fibre type (Bosco et al, 1982a): high-FT individuals show the maximum plyometric effect with a short eccentric phase, small range and brief coupling; high-ST individuals jump best with a longer eccentric phase, greater range and longer coupling, "since the actin-myosin cross-bridging attachment time is of greater duration" (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
- Joint-specific maximum delays "probably" exist, but the body has many reflexes acting "at different rates"; tonic (static) and phasic (dynamic) stretch reflexes differ (PDF p. 282 / printed p. 271).
- The weightlifters' "pre-stretch principle" (hold an intense stretch "for a couple of seconds and then thrust") "would seem" to involve the more tonic reflex with longer coupling, and "could certainly not be called plyometric", while phasic reflexes are "more likely" behind classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors offer fibre type and tonic versus phasic reflexes as explanations, with hedges ("partial solution", "would seem", "more likely"). They do not test either against the conflicting delay data.

**When to apply** — When someone quotes one fixed "the stretch benefit is gone after X ms" number: the book shows the window depends on the task (unloaded elbow about 0.25 s; loaded bench press up to about 4 s). Inference: for loaded lifts a paused rep still keeps some prestretch benefit for a second or more, per Fig 5.6, while for unloaded fast rebounds the benefit is gone within a few tenths of a second, per Fig 5.7.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Fig 5.6 under a single Wilson year without noting the caption-text conflict. The figure values are read from small plots and are approximate. Fig 5.7 is Siff's own analysis: the book says it "was derived from some of this work on upper-body non-impact plyometrics", the research "conducted in this field by the author in 1994" (PDF p. 292 / printed p. 281), and gives no subject numbers or publication for it. The fibre-type and reflex explanations are proposals, not demonstrated here.

**Example** — The authors' own: unloaded explosive elbow flexion loses its prestretch benefit over 0.1-0.25 s (Fig 5.7), while the bench-press benefit decays over about 4 s (Fig 5.6).

**Related** — [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]] (Ch1.7, the same Bosco et al 1982 fibre-type finding); [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]; [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

# The Five Phases of a Plyometric Action (Fig 5.5), With Coupling Time as the Explosive-Isometric Interval

**What it is** — Under "The Fundamental Theory of Plyometrics" the authors list five phases (PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270; Fig 5.5 verified against the page image):
1. **Initial momentum phase:** the body or limb moves "because of kinetic energy (KE) it has accumulated from a preceding action."
2. **Electromechanical delay phase:** contact with a surface stops the limb and "provokes the muscles to contract"; the delay is "the time elapsing between the onset of the action potential in the motor nerves and the onset of the muscle contraction." The authors note some workers include lengthening of the SEC (series elastic component) in this phase, but "electromechanical" was coined for the electrical-to-mechanical interval, "which does not include the passive stretching of connective tissue."
3. **Amortisation phase:** the KE "produces a powerful myotatic stretch reflex which leads to eccentric muscle contraction accompanied by explosive isometric contraction" and stretching of the SEC (e.g. tendons). "The explosive isometric phase between the end of the eccentric action and the beginning of the concentric action lasts for a period known as the *coupling time*."
4. **Rebound phase:** release of elastic energy from the SEC, with involuntary concentric contraction evoked by the stretch reflex, "as well as possible local change in the muscle fibre mechanics"; it "may include the contribution added by voluntary concentric contraction."
5. **Final momentum phase:** after the concentric contraction, the body or limb continues on the KE imparted by contraction and elastic recoil.

Fig 5.5, as drawn: boxes for initial momentum, amortisation, rebound and final momentum phases; between them, bars for "EM delay", "eccentric contraction" and "concentric contraction", joined at the bottom by a box "explosive isometrics" labelled "Coupling Time".

The caption defines EM delay differently from the numbered text: "Electromechanical delay between signal to terminate initial momentum phase and instant when eccentric contraction begins" (caption), against "between the onset of the action potential in the motor nerves and the onset of the muscle contraction" (text item 2). Both are on PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270; the book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is in the phase descriptions: stretch reflex plus SEC elastic energy, released in the rebound. Elsewhere they add that the process is not only spinal reflex and elastic recoil (see [[claim--plyometric-skill-is-cognitive-and-state-dependent]]).

**When to apply** — As a shared vocabulary for coaching and for reading a force-time trace of a depth jump or rebound: the coupling interval is the part the authors' 0.15 s guide applies to (see [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]). Inference: on a force plate, the eccentric (braking) and concentric (propulsive) phases of a drop jump map onto phases 3 and 4; the authors do not give a force-plate method for isolating the isometric coupling interval.

**When NOT to apply** — The phase list is a descriptive model, not measured timing; the book gives no durations for phases 1, 2, 4 or 5. Do not quote the EM delay definition without noting the caption and text differ. The rebound phase's "possible local change in the muscle fibre mechanics" is stated as possible, not shown.

**Example** — Inference: in a depth jump from a box, phase 1 is the fall, phases 2-3 are the first instants of ground contact through the lowest point, phase 4 is the push-off, and phase 5 is the flight. The authors' own illustration is Fig 5.5.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]]; [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]]; [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

# Classes of Plyometric (Powermetric) Training: Impact or Non-Impact, Maximal to Non-Plyometric, Functional or Non-Functional (Fig 5.8)

**What it is** — The authors replace the "classically plyometric or not" argument with a classification (PDF pp. 283-284 / printed pp. 272-273; Fig 5.8 verified against the page image):
- **Impact versus non-impact.** In impact plyometrics "the rebound is stimulated by contact with a surface or object"; in non-impact plyometrics the recoil "is mediated by explosive eccentric action of the muscles that produce a movement not terminated by contact with a surface." Depth jumps are impact; "snap kicks or rapidly-retracted blows in boxing or the martial arts" are non-impact, which "may also be maximal or submaximal."
- **Maximal, submaximal, non-plyometric.** *Maximal plyometrics* are "low-repetition activities where the intensity of the depth jump or rebound exercise is such that maximal or near-maximal rebound tension is produced." *Sub-maximal plyometrics* "do not produce maximal muscular tension, although they are still performed with a minimally long contact phase": "lower box heights are used for depth jumps and the athlete does not strive to reach maximal rebound height"; "rapid double-footed bouncing or low skipping on the spot" are other examples. The three are drawn in one box "as a reminder that there is really a continuum of intensities."
- **Classical, supplementary, preparatory.** Classical plyometric exercises are *functional* ("matched as closely as possible to the specific explosive actions of the particular sport with respect to movement pattern, muscle involvement, timing and direction of motion") or *non-functional* ("general training of the explosive qualities"). Functional examples: forward bounding for long jump, backward rebounds for shot put, one-legged forward hopping for jumping, and for basketball "both short and relatively long amortisation phases in vertical rebounds." Preparatory or supplementary drills are weight training for muscular strength ("especially eccentric strength") and connective tissue, plus jumping, swinging, throwing and catching drills "with longer duration transition phases"; "Most of the drills described in popular books on plyometrics in the West are actually supplementary exercises."
- **Pseudo-plyometrics.** Drills "incorrectly labelled as plyometric because they include a sudden stop or some form of jump", e.g. "'power moves' (involving quick landings and delayed jumps in a semi-squat position)" and many "'water plyos'" in aerobics classes; lacking "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time", they serve as "preparatory non-plyometrics."

Fig 5.8 as drawn: Plyometric training splits into impact and non-impact; below these sit maximal plyometrics, submaximal plyometrics and non-plyometrics; under maximal sits "classical plyometrics" (split into functional and non-functional); under submaximal sits "supplementary plyometrics"; under non-plyometrics sits "preparatory/supplementary activities" (split into weight training and "jumps throws etc"). The text lists classical, supplementary and preparatory as three flat categories; the figure ties each to one intensity level.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for classifying rather than arguing definitions: the definitional debate "becomes complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272). Intensity is graded by the momentum at contact (see [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]).

**When to apply** — Labelling every jump, bound, hop and med-ball drill in a plan by class, so volume and rest rules are applied to the right class: the authors' low-rep, long-rest rules are for maximal plyometrics, while submaximal and preparatory drills tolerate more volume (see [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]). Inference: in football, a vertical depth jump is classical non-functional, while a bound or single-leg hop that matches a cut or drive phase in direction and timing would be the authors' "functional" class.

**When NOT to apply** — The text and figure place "supplementary" differently (a flat list of three versus a level under submaximal; and "preparatory or supplementary drills" in the text against "supplementary plyometrics" as its own box in the figure). The class boundaries are a continuum by the authors' own statement, so the labels are not sharp cut-offs.

**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps (impact, maximal when performed for maximal rebound), low box depth jumps without striving for height (submaximal), karate snap kicks (non-impact), "power moves" in aerobics (pseudo-plyometric).

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]; [[framework--non-impact-plyometrics-ericson-and-martial-arts]]; [[claim--popular-plyometric-drills-work-through-other-mechanisms]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]

# Non-Impact Plyometrics: Explosive Eccentric Recoil Without Surface Contact (Ericson's Seated System, Martial Arts Snaps)

**What it is** — Siff's section (he refers to "the author" doing force-plate analysis and to "his wife, Lisa Ericson") argues that plyometric action does not need impact (PDF pp. 290-292 / printed pp. 279-281, text layer):
- Western and even Russian practice treats "shock contact of parts of the body with some surface" as the common denominator of plyometrics, but "this is not the only way of producing plyometric action." The non-impact variety was recognised when Siff analysed martial arts movements and Ericson's seated fitness system (called Supersitting, and on p. 281 the "SMART seated fitness system").
- Ericson's system: "very rapid wide-range movements choreographed at rates exceeding 240 beats per minute, interspersed with rhythmic transitional PNF-type patterns", over sessions of about 60 minutes, movements "initiated and terminated explosively in sets of uninterrupted sequences" that change form and direction "to avoid excessive fatigue, habituation or injury."
- It counts as non-impact plyometrics "because it obeys all the requirements of plyometrics as originally conceived": "a ballistic action which is rapidly terminated by eccentric and explosive isometric muscle contraction, followed immediately by a powerful concentric recoil mediated by recruitment of the myotatic stretch reflex and augmented by the release of elastic energy."
- Comparison with karate: karate uses few repetitions with brief intervals, and the punch often contacts its target briefly, "sufficient to dissipate much of the elastic energy"; Ericson's transition is "usually shorter" with many continuous repetitions, which "probably explains the differences in functional and structural development."
- Intensity: most class movements are submaximal plyometrics; "Performed in the form of all-out single movements, they become maximal non-impact plyometrics." "maximal impact plyometrics will generally increase muscle tension to a greater extent than the equivalent non-impact movements for the leg and hip extensors (e.g. the karate thrust-kick)."
- Uses: maximal non-impact plyometrics, like submaximal impact plyometrics, "can serve as a preparatory tool for maximal impact plyometrics", for other qualities ("strength, muscle hypertrophy, muscle endurance and speed-strength endurance"), or to train selected muscle groups "instead of unnecessarily stressing the entire musculature."
- Sport sources (PNF-like spiral and diagonal paths are a common feature): thrust punches, blocks, knife-hand thrusts, palm-heel strikes, front, side snap and side thrust kicks, done solo with pre-stretch, ending in "a brief isometrically-held end position" or "rapid recoil actions", in kata, or in non-contact sparring. Low-impact throwing or kicking of very light objects is included as "low inertia" plyometrics.

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is the same reflex-plus-elastic recoil as impact plyometrics, produced by the muscles' own explosive eccentric braking. Evidence offered: Siff's force-plate analysis (no data shown), changes in Ericson's wheelchair students, and "preliminary studies executed in 1995 by University of Pretoria physiotherapy students supervised by Siff and Ericson" that "warrant more detailed expansion."

**When to apply** — Inference: upper-body rebound work for linemen's hand strikes, or plyometric exposure for an athlete who cannot yet tolerate landing impact, are the obvious fits; the authors name "athletes who require high levels of upper body power and endurance" and arm rehabilitation.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: no data are reported, the source is the author's own and his wife's system, and the text says research so far has studied speed-strength, not these other qualities. Siff himself says maximal impact plyometrics produce more leg and hip extensor tension than non-impact equivalents, so non-impact work does not replace depth jumps for lower-body reactive strength.

**Example** — The text's own: a karate snap kick, thrust out and whipped back (non-impact), compared with a punch that briefly hits its target (PDF p. 291 / printed p. 280).

**Related** — [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--resisted-and-water-plyometrics]] (upper-body aqua plyometrics use the same actions); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]

# Eight "Shock Methods" for Breaking Long-Term Stagnation in Experienced Athletes, Used Only After Ruling Out Overtraining

**What it is** — Under "Various Shock Methods" (PDF pp. 295-296 / printed pp. 284-285; p. 296 verified against the page image) the text widens "shock" beyond plyometrics: "Training plyometrics may be regarded as one of several shock methods that may be used in special strength training to provide intense stimulation to compel the body to attain a higher level of functional adaptation." Because "The principle of gradual progressive overloading may, after a prolonged period of unvaried use, sometimes fail to improve strength or performance, as is commonly the case among elite athletes", it "may be necessary to disrupt the persistent state of stagnation" with one of:
- plyometrics
- forced repetitions
- supramaximal methods
- electrical stimulation (macrostimulation)
- repeated single 1RM training
- restricted range maxima
- contrast methods
- maximal eccentrics

Cautions: "The appropriate method, its timing and the duration of its use must be chosen with great care, since lack of progress may be due to overtraining rather than long-term stagnation. The use of any shock method under such circumstances is potentially harmful and definitely detrimental to performance. These methods are generally unsuitable for novices and should only be employed by experienced athletes with a solid background of special strength training." The text notes "shock method" was Verkhoshansky's name for the plyometric method when he first formalised it.

**Why it works** — The stated rationale is "intense stimulation to compel the body to attain a higher level of functional adaptation" after adaptation to unvaried progressive overload stalls. No study is cited here; the text refers to 7.1 (not yet ingested).

**When to apply** — An experienced athlete whose strength or power has stalled for a long period despite progressive loading, after overtraining has been excluded. Inference: in a collegiate setting, the check for "overtraining rather than long-term stagnation" would draw on the readiness data already collected (for Eric, mRSI trends, `docs/method-baseline.md` lines 74-75) before choosing a shock method.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for novices, and not when the plateau may be fatigue (the text says a shock method is then "potentially harmful and definitely detrimental"). The list gives no dosing; the methods are described elsewhere (7.1). The text gives no rule for distinguishing stagnation from overtraining.

**Example** — Inference: a senior lifter whose squat has not moved for months on steady linear loading, with stable readiness markers, might get a short block of maximal eccentrics or contrast work from this list. The text gives no worked example.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]; [[heuristic--plan-variation-to-avoid-restrictive-neural-patterns]]; [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]; [[framework--clinical-physiological-effects-of-electrostimulation]]

# Set Depth-Jump Height by Strength Fitness: Too High Once the Transition Slows or the Heels Are Driven to the Ground; Raise Speed Before Height

**What it is** — The authors' rules for choosing drop height in training (all on pages verified against the page image):
- "The optimal depth of the jump is determined by the athlete's strength fitness, while the athlete should ensure that significant dynamic force is developed without slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work by the muscles involved" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
- "The optimal height of a depth jump does not result in a landing where the heel is forced to the ground by momentum" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 8).
- "One should aim to increase the speed and acceleration of movement before increasing the drop height or take-off height" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 5).
- "One should begin at a relatively low height and increase it gradually to the optimal height. It makes sense to begin by jumping upward and forward and only after sufficient training, to jump strictly upward" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1).
- Height is preferred over added weight, and a force plate can find the height for a required force (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1).
- For jumping power "one can work without an additional load and utilise only falling bodymass" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274). Fig 5.10 (Verkhoshansky, 1977) shows three variants: two under "Horizontal Projection" (after the drop, the athlete rebounds forward over low objects drawn on the ground) and one under "Vertical Projection" (rebound upward toward a hanging marker) (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, read from the image; the drawings are small, so the object details are approximate).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the transition: height is only useful while it raises dynamic force without "slowing down the transition from eccentric to concentric work". Heels forced to the ground is their visible sign that momentum has overwhelmed the athlete. Inference: a heel strike means the ankle has been driven through its range, which lengthens the amortisation the authors want kept short; the book states only the rule.

**When to apply** — Inference: with a force plate or contact mat, find each athlete's height by stepping the box up until contact time rises or rebound height falls, and stop below that point; on the field, watch for heels hitting the ground. This individual approach is consistent with the authors' "determined by the athlete's strength fitness." Eric's baseline: the department reads reactive ability through mRSI, which "was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 74). Inference: a drop-jump RSI (jump height over contact time) taken at stepped heights is the direct test of the authors' "without slowing down the transition" rule, but Eric's baseline names CMJ-based mRSI, not drop jumps.

**When NOT to apply** — The Ch4.2.3 figures put the optimum for advanced jumpers at 0.75-1.15 m ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]); the rules here give no number, and the authors stress starting "considerably lower" for anyone unused to the training. The heel rule is a coaching sign, not a measured threshold. Upward-and-forward before strictly upward is the authors' order; they give no reason.

**Example** — The authors' own: the three Fig 5.10 depth-jump variants, and the progression from upward-and-forward to strictly upward jumps (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]; [[heuristic--rate-plyometric-intensity-by-contact-momentum-from-drop-height]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]; [[heuristic--match-plyometric-prescription-to-joint-angle-and-fiber-type]]

# Depth-Jump Execution Cues: Step Off Relaxed, Land on the Balls of the Feet With Shallow Amortisation, Eyes Up, Breath Held Through Contact

**What it is** — The authors' execution rules for depth jumps and plyometric drills (pages verified against the page images unless marked):
- **Leaving the box:** "Depth-jumping necessitates falling in a relaxed state, but not jumping, off the box" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 10).
- **Landing:** "land with the legs slightly flexed, muscles mildly tensed and on the balls of the feet in order to avoid an excessive shock. The depth of amortisation should not be great and the subsequent take-off needs to be executed very quickly with an energetic throwing upwards of the arms" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).
- **Target:** "strive with the hands or head to reach some height indicated by some marker if the take-off is executed upward, or to land at some point if it is directed upward and forward"; a gain in height or distance "clearly indicates improvement in special fitness, which always has a positive effect on the athlete's emotional state" (same page).
- **Starting posture:** the amortisation "should be of minimal duration, but sufficient to create impulsive contraction of the muscles. Therefore, the initial posture with respect to the joint angles should correspond to the same position in which the working movement begins in the sporting exercise" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 2).
- **Range of motion** in the Fig 5.9 resistance-apparatus exercises "should be somewhat greater than the required coordination range of the exercise in order to enhance shock absorption by the soft tissues and thereby avoid impact injury" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274).
- **Head and gaze:** "Flexing the head downward to look at the floor before take-off may result in spurious muscle contraction or altered timing. Similarly if the head is not thrust upwards during the take-off, maximal height will not be reached" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 9).
- **Warm-up:** plyometric training "should be preceded by a good warmup of the intensively involved muscles" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 3).
- **Breathing:** "It is vital that the athlete holds the breath during the amortisation and early propulsion phase to stabilise the body, offer pneumatic shock absorption and to increase the rebound force. Forced exhalation may accompany the remainder of the propulsion phase" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273). Item 12: "the breath should be held and never released during the contact phase or any phase where maximal effort is to be produced. Exhalation during any landing phase reduces overall stability and increases the loading on the spine during depth-jumping" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).

**Why it works** — Reasons given by the authors are in the quotes: avoiding excessive shock (landing posture), stability and "pneumatic shock absorption" (breath), timing (gaze), and shock absorption by soft tissues (range). They cite no study for these cues.

**When to apply** — Coaching any depth-jump or rebound session; the cues are concrete and observable. Inference: the starting-posture rule (item 2) gives a way to make a depth jump more specific to a football stance or a block-start angle by matching the landing knee and hip angle to the sport's start position.

**When NOT to apply** — The two breathing statements differ in detail: p. 273 allows "forced exhalation" during the remainder of the propulsion phase, which is still ground contact in a rebound, while item 12 says the breath is "never released during the contact phase." Inference: read together, the cautious reading is breath held through landing and early push-off. Item 2's "minimal duration but sufficient" depth and the Fig 5.9 "somewhat greater" range are not quantified. Inference: maximal breath-holding effort raises blood pressure; the book does not discuss this for athletes with cardiovascular conditions.

**Example** — The authors' own: jumping up to touch a marker with the hands or head after the depth jump (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).
