# Large Resistance Calls for the Brief Maximal Tension Method, Small Resistance and Reactive Demand Call for Plyometrics; the Book Disagrees With Itself on Whether Plyometrics Should Be the Main Method

**What it is** — The authors' method-selection rules (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image unless marked):
- "In those cases where explosive force is associated with the overcoming of large resistance, preference should be given to the brief maximal tension method, as used commonly in Olympic weightlifting. In situations where the resistance is small and the working effect depends upon the reactive ability of the muscles, plyometric methods should be given preference."
- Staging: "Although it should form an integral part of the training programme, plyometrics should not be combined in the beginning stages with resistance exercises such as the brief maximal tension method." "In subsequent stages, plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes for developing explosive strength and reactive ability."
- Concentric explosive work: "exercises with maximum effort and mixed regimes using weights equal to 40% of 1RM, or 30% of 1RM (Verkhoshansky, 1963; Papysheva, 1966). Explosive-isometric tension up to 80% of maximum should be used in conjunction with this routine."
- In combined sessions, resistance work goes first: combined programmes beat plyometrics alone "provided the resistance movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).
- Testing decides: "To ascertain whether an athlete needs plyometric or heavy resistance training depends on measuring the *strength deficit* ... Without such testing, prescription of plyometric training tends to remain hit-and-miss" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273; repeated at PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282 in a grammatically broken sentence).

**Internal conflict, recorded:** "plyometrics should be the main method in the training of highly qualified athletes" (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278) against, half a page earlier, "it is futile to rely predominantly on plyometric drills to enhance sport specific explosive strength and power, because efficiency of motor control is fundamental to all skilled sporting performance" (PDF pp. 288-289 / printed pp. 277-278). The second follows a Nicol et al (1997) citation. Inference: the first reads like the original shock-method programme and the second like a later addition, but the book marks neither passage by author. The book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors tie each method to the force demand: heavy brief tension for large resistance, reactive shock loading for small resistance. The strength deficit decides which an individual needs (Ch1; see [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]], which records that the book also states the deficit rule two ways).

**When to apply** — Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q21; `docs/method-baseline.md` line 76). Inference: DSI plays the role the authors give the strength deficit (both compare a fast expression of force with a maximal one to choose plyometric versus heavy work), but they are different measures; Eric's baseline Tension 17 records that the DSI cutoffs were never validated and that IMTP peak force drives most of the ratio (line 261). Inference: for linemen, whose sport force is against large resistance, the authors' rule favours brief maximal tension; for skill positions, whose force is against bodymass, it favours plyometrics.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite Supertraining as saying plyometrics should be the main method without the "futile to rely predominantly" sentence, or the reverse. "Beginning stages" and "highly qualified" are not defined. The 40% and 30% of 1RM loads and the 80% explosive-isometric tension are given without sets, reps or rest.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: Olympic weightlifting (large resistance, brief maximal tension) versus jumping from depth (small resistance, reactive ability) (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278).

**Related** — [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]]; [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]; [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]; [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]]; [[claim--heavy-squats-and-light-fast-lifts-miss-the-eccentric-concentric-switch]]

16	# Depth Jumps: Once or Twice a Week, Kept 3-4 Days From Technique Sessions, Every 10-14 Days In Season and Not Within 10 Days of Competition
17	
18	**What it is** — From the authors' depth-jump recommendations (PDF pp. 286-287 / printed pp. 275-276, verified against the page images):
19	- **Weekly frequency (item 3):** depth jumps "in the volume indicated should be done once or twice a week in training sessions devoted to special strength training", which can also include "localised exercises for other muscle groups and general developmental exercises executed with a small volume." But "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training in the particular sport."
20	- **Spacing from technique (item 4):** "Depth-jumps strongly excite the nervous system. Therefore, they should be used not less than 3-4 days before a technique training session. Sessions devoted to general physical preparation with a small volume of work should be done after depth-jump workouts."
21	- **Season (item 5):** "Depth-jumps occupy a fundamental place in the second half of the preparatory period of the yearly cycle. However, they can function as a means of maintaining the achieved level of special strength fitness in the competition period. During the competition period they should be included once every 10-14 days, but no later than 10 days before a competition."
22	- **Delayed effect (item 15):** integration "depends on not disrupting the delayed training effect of prior strength work. It should be noted that the use of depth-jumps as a means of stimulation can delay this effect for 5-6 days."
23	
24	**Internal conflict, recorded:** item 4 keeps depth jumps at least 3-4 days before a technique session, while item 3 allows well-conditioned athletes three depth-jump sessions a week placed "at the completion of technical training." Three sessions a week tied to technical training cannot all sit 3-4 days before the next technique session. Both are on PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the book does not reconcile them.
25	
26	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons: strong excitation of the nervous system (item 4) and a 5-6 day delay of the training effect of prior strength work (item 15). Neither cites a study. Inference: the in-season 10-day cut-off before competition is consistent with item 15's 5-6 day delayed effect plus a margin; the book does not make that link.
27	
28	**When to apply** — Placing depth jumps in a football week or year. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105). Inference: the authors' in-season rule (one exposure every 10-14 days, none in the 10 days before a game) is far sparser than a weekly game schedule allows; read literally, a team playing every 7 days would have no legal in-season depth-jump day. That is a reason to treat the 10-day rule as written for track-and-field competition calendars, which the book does not say.
29	
30	**When NOT to apply** — These are experience-based rules with no population, drop height or study given. They are written for an annual cycle with a long preparatory period and spaced competitions (the authors' examples elsewhere in 5.2.4 are track-and-field jumpers). Do not quote the 3-4 day spacing without the item 3 exception. The 5-6 day delay applies to depth jumps used "as a means of stimulation"; the book does not say how it scales with volume.
31	
32	**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps central in the second half of the preparatory period, then once every 10-14 days in the competition period, last one at least 10 days out (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

50	# Depth-Jump and Maximal-Plyometric Volume and Rest: The Book Gives Two Incompatible Dosing Models
51	
52	**What it is** — Section 5.2.4 gives the following dosing statements. They do not agree, so all are listed with locators.
53	
54	**Model 1: maximal plyometrics dosed like a maximal lift.**
55	- "*Maximal plyometrics* essentially are low-repetition activities ... Just like maximal strength training with weights, these powerful impulses are not meant to be imposed on the musculature every workout, nor are multiple repetitions even possible or advisable. Moreover, a rest interval of 2-4 minutes is recommended between successive repetitions and as much as 10-12 minutes between sets" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
56	- Prescription item 6: "The rest interval between sets of maximal plyometric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
57	- "several books advocate sessions with over 100 repetitions of plyometric movements ... This volume of *maximal plyometrics* (unlike sub-maximal plyometrics) is neither productive nor safe for any athlete. Maximal plyometrics, like maximal weight lifting, involves single all-out repetitions separated by a few minutes of rest" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282, verified against the page image).
58	- "classical plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283, text layer).
59	
60	**Model 2: depth jumps in sets of 5-10 (credited to "prolific experience").**
61	- Prescription item 4: "As an initial guideline, the dosage of plyometric exercises should not exceed 5-8 repetitions in one set" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
62	- Depth-jump item 1: with a complex of vertical jumps (Fig 5.11), "Each exercise is executed in sets of 10 repetitions, with 1-15 minutes of rest between sets" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the page image prints "1-15", recorded as printed).
63	- Depth-jump item 2: "The optimal dosage of depth-jumps with an energetic vertical take-off in one training session should not exceed 4 sets of 10 jumps for well-conditioned athletes and 2-3 sets of 5-8 jumps for lesser conditioned athletes. Easy running and relaxation exercises for a period of 10-15 minutes should be done between sets" (same page, verified against the page image).
64	- Depth-jump item 3: "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training" (same page, verified against the page image).
65	
66	**The conflict.** Model 1 says multiple repetitions of maximal plyometrics are not "possible or advisable" and separates single reps by 2-4 minutes. Model 2 prescribes sets of 10 energetic depth jumps, up to 40 per session, with rest given only between sets. Inference: Model 2 might be read as submaximal work, but depth-jump item 2 specifies "an energetic vertical take-off", and the 0.75-1.15 m heights in Ch4 are for advanced jumpers. Rest between sets also varies: about 10 min (p. 274), 10-12 min (p. 272), 10-15 min of easy running (p. 275), and "1-15 minutes" (p. 275). The book does not reconcile them.
67	
68	**Why it works** — Model 1's stated reasons: maximal plyometrics are "extremely demanding on the central nervous system" and impose "great mechanical strain on the tendons, in particular" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282). Model 2's stated basis is "prolific experience with depth-jumps for developing jumping power" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275). Neither gives fatigue or recovery data.
69	
70	**When to apply** — Inference: one way to use both is to treat Model 1 as the rule for truly maximal efforts (maximal height, rebound to a marker, near-maximal tension) and Model 2 as an upper volume cap for depth-jump sessions, keeping per-session counts at or under 2-3 × 5-8 for less-conditioned athletes and 4 × 10 for well-conditioned ones. The book does not make this split. For any athlete, the authors' quality rule holds: "It is the quality of the plyometric exercises, not the quantity, which is important" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 11). Eric's baseline: in-season the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105). Inference: Model 1's low-rep, long-rest structure fits that rule more directly than Model 2's sets of 10.

92	# Classical Plyometric Training: Coupling Under About 0.15 s, Feedforward Control, and a Shock Force-Time Pattern, Not Coupling Time Alone
93	
94	**What it is** — The authors give three tests for whether a drill is classical "training plyometrics" rather than ordinary jumping:
95	1. **Coupling time.** The method "is characterised by impulsive action of minimal duration between the end of the eccentric braking phase and initiation of the concentric acceleration phase". "If the transition phase (or, coupling phase) is prolonged by more than about 0.15 second, the action may be considered to constitute ordinary jumping and not classical training plyometrics." The coaching image: imagine the contact surface "is red hot, so that any prolonged contact would be dangerous." (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268, verified against the page image.)
96	2. **Feedforward control.** "The activity is not accurately plyometric if the athlete relies upon ongoing feedback processes to control the isometric and concentric actions instead of upon feedforward programmes established before any movement begins"; true plyometric training "usually involves ballistic rather than cocontraction processes" (same page).
97	3. **Force-time pattern.** Later the 0.15 s rule "requires some qualification" (PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270). "One cannot simply distinguish between plyometric and non-plyometric solely on the basis of coupling times, otherwise one would have to classify jogging or even brisk walking as classical plyometrics, because the time taken for the ground reaction force to reach a maximum can be less than 0.15 second. One also has to take the force-time pattern and the rate of force development (RFD) into account" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
98	
99	The same pages separate *plyometric actions*, which "occur as part of many running, jumping, hurdling, striking and other rebounding movements in sport", from *plyometric training*, "which applies plyometric actions as a distinct training modality according to a definite methodology" (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268). Siff writes this passage (it names Verkhoshansky in the third person: "Verkhoshansky has always consistently favoured the use of the term 'shock method'"). He suggests calling the action "stretch-shortening action" and the training system "powermetrics", and writes that "The earliest published use of the word plyometrics seems to have been in a Soviet publication (Zanon, 1966)." He then concludes that arguing whether an action is "classically plyometric or not becomes complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training", and that it is better to recognise types of plyometric training (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272; see [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]).
100	
101	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: the method "relies on the production of a very brief explosive-isometric and eccentric-isometric phase which precedes the release of the elastic energy stored in the tendons and other components of the series elastic component" (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268). For why the time limit varies, see [[claim--prestretch-benefit-decay-time-differs-by-task]] (tonic versus phasic reflexes, fibre type). Inference: jogging passes the 0.15 s test but has a low, unhurried force-time curve, which is why the authors add the force-time and RFD test.
102	
103	**When to apply** — Auditing a "plyo" block: check (1) ground or implement contact, eccentric to concentric, short enough to meet the about 0.15 s guide, (2) a pre-planned ballistic action rather than a corrected one, and (3) a sharp force rise. Eric's baseline: speed is taught "as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 96). Inference: those sprint contacts sit under the authors' 0.15 s coupling guide, though contact time and coupling time are not the same interval (coupling is only the eccentric-to-concentric transition); a force plate contact time over 0.15 s does not by itself show a coupling over 0.15 s.
104	
105	**When NOT to apply** — The 0.15 s figure is "about" and is qualified by the authors themselves; it is not a hard cut-off. Do not use coupling time alone (the jogging counter-example). Do not read "not classical plyometrics" as "not useful": the authors say longer-coupling drills train other qualities (see [[claim--popular-plyometric-drills-work-through-other-mechanisms]]). The authors give no method for measuring coupling time in the field.
106	
107	**Example** — The authors' own: jogging and brisk walking reach peak ground reaction force in under 0.15 s yet are not classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272). The "red hot" surface is their cue (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268).
108	
109	**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the original definition and "powermetrics"); [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]; [[framework--five-phases-of-a-plyometric-action]]; [[claim--prestretch-benefit-decay-time-differs-by-task]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/claim--reversible-muscular-action-is-a-trainable-skill-not-automatic]]

193	# Grade Plyometric Intensity by Momentum at Contact (Set by Drop Height), Since a 1RM Does Not Exist; Prefer Height Over Added Weight
194	
195	**What it is** — The authors propose "a *powermetrics intensity scale* similar to that used in weightlifting, where exercises are ranked in terms of percentages of one's 1RM." Because "the concept of 1RMs is meaningless in plyometric training", one must use estimates of muscle tension or of "the impulse ... produced during the contact phase". "Impulse is equivalent to the change of momentum (m.ΔV) during the amortisation phase, so that its magnitude for a falling body depends on the height from which the body drops. Thus, the momentum just before contact (estimated from height of the drop jump or distance fallen by the object) may serve as a measure of intensity." At the top of the scale is maximal plyometrics, "the equivalent of the emotionally demanding competitive maximum, CFmax"; at the bottom, preparatory non-impact plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
196	
197	The prescription list adds: "The magnitude of the impulsive load is determined by the weight and the height of its free-fall. The optimal combination is determined empirically in each specific case; however, preference should be given to a large height over a heavy weight. Since the resulting force is governed by Newton's Second Law (F = m.a), a force plate may be used to determine the height of drop to produce the required force" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1, verified against the page image). Item 4 says rep dosage can be set more precisely "to calculate the force involved (from bodymass and the drop height) and the athlete's level of special speed-strength" (same page).
198	
199	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the impulse-momentum statement quoted. Inference (physics): for a body falling from rest through height h, speed at contact is √(2gh), so momentum at contact is m·√(2gh). Momentum therefore rises with the square root of drop height, not in proportion to it: doubling the drop height raises contact momentum by a factor of √2, about 41%, and quadrupling it doubles momentum. Inference (physics): the peak force on landing is not fixed by drop height alone; for the same momentum, a shorter, stiffer arrest gives a higher average force (average net force = change in momentum divided by contact time). That is why the authors' force plate step is needed to find the height that gives a target force.
200	
201	**When to apply** — Progressing depth jumps or rebounds: rank drills by drop height and bodymass rather than counting all "plyos" as equal, and raise height before adding external load. Inference: with ForceDecks, a drop jump from a known box gives landing force and contact time for each athlete, which is the measurement the authors' item 1 asks for.
202	
203	**When NOT to apply** — Momentum at contact is an intensity proxy for impact drills with a fall; it does not grade non-impact or ground-based bounding drills where there is no measured drop. The authors give no numeric scale bands (no "% of CFmax" per height). Item 1's "F = m.a" sentence does not on its own let you compute landing force from height (see the Inference above). Height also has an upper limit: past the optimum the transition slows (see [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] and [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]).
204	
205	**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete stepping off a 0.5 m box lands at about √(2 × 9.81 × 0.5) ≈ 3.1 m/s, about 313 kg·m/s of momentum; from a 1.0 m box about 4.4 m/s and about 443 kg·m/s, roughly 41% more, not double. This calculation is not in the source.
206	
207	**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] (Ch4.2.3, the 0.75-1.15 m range); [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements]]

223	# Before Depth Jumps: Months of Barbell, Jumping, Sprint and Skipping Work, Eccentric and Explosive-Isometric Strength, Static-Start Jumps, Then Low Hops
224	
225	**What it is** — The authors' preparation rules (pages verified against the page images):
226	- "Depth-jumps require special preliminary preparation such as a significant volume of barbell exercises and traditional jumping, short sprints and skipping over a period of several months" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1). Contra-indications: "Muscle or tendon fatigue, pain or soreness, as well as incompletely healed injuries" (same item).
227	- "depth-jumping is not a basic type of training to be indulged in lightly by athletes who are relatively unused to explosive or strongly resisted movements. For anyone who is not accustomed to movements such as weightlifting cleans, jerks, squats or hurdling, it is highly advisable that a preparatory programme using submaximal plyometrics, non-impact and non-plyometrics be followed" first (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).
228	- **Eccentric and explosive-isometric strength first:** "a primary requirement for anyone contemplating the use of classical plyometrics is a high level of eccentric strength and explosive isometric strength. Herein lies the value of small-range squats, power cleans, power snatches, cleans from the hang, snatches from the hang, push presses or jerks, push presses or jerks from racks, and the descent of flights of stairs." Front and back squats both, "since they each model different types of jump (directly upwards versus forwards and upwards)." "Slow quasi-isometric squats over a moderate range with heavy weights should later lead to more rapid dips over a shallower range with lighter weights" (PDF pp. 287-288 / printed pp. 276-277).
229	- **Static start before dynamic start:** "it is initially useful to improve jumping ability from a static start, without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start": standing broad and vertical jumps without a dip, then the vertical jump test "progressing from a static flexed knee start to a dynamic dip start with arms flung vigorously upwards" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). Progress can be tracked with the Lewis formula ([[claim--lewis-formula-estimates-jump-power-from-bodymass-and-height]]).
230	- **Low hops:** "hopping on the spot at a frequency which feels most comfortable for the athlete, using a few sets of about 25 repetitions", then small forward, backward, sideward, forward-backward and zig-zag hops, then vertical hops "as rapidly as possible, again using a few sets of about 20 repetitions" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 6). Rope skipping is useful, but "long periods of skipping are not the appropriate form of preparatory drill" because the aim is speed-strength, not endurance (item 7).
231	- **Technique and complexity:** learn normal jumping first, with "the correct lumbar-pelvic rhythm, as is also used during clean pulls or power cleans from the ground" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 13). "Great caution" with depth jumps involving "one-legged thrusts, changes of direction or complex variations, since the injury risk is significantly higher" (item 14).
232	- Then integrate: "As eccentric, isometric and concentric strength increases ... the athlete may progress to actions which more rapidly integrate all three aspects of plyometric movement"; the same principles apply to upper-body work (medicine ball catching and throwing, plyometric press-ups and bench presses) (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

258	# Resisted Plyometrics Only Occasionally and Never With Heavy Weights or Stiff Cords in Depth Jumps; Water Plyometrics Are a Safer Submaximal Option
259	
260	**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 292 from the text layer):
261	- Resistance can be imposed in the amortisation phase, the concentric rebound or both: light weights, or "elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips." Both "increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction", but "also increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training."
262	- Resistance methods "should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase."
263	- Water or "aqua plyometrics" decrease landing force and increase resistance in the recoil. They do "not offer maximal or shock method plyometrics" but serve as preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, "especially for one-legged drills." Water depth sets the resistance: "chest or shoulder high water offering greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscle activity, smaller impact forces and enhanced safety." Repeated aqua jumps for "rebound explosive muscle endurance" are "considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive sports."
264	
265	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are stated: heavy load lengthens the coupling time (taking the drill out of classical plyometrics) and loads spine and tendons; water reduces impact and eccentric intensity.
266	
267	**When to apply** — Inference: aqua jumps suit early return-to-training or single-leg plyometric progressions where impact must be limited, consistent with the authors' "especially for one-legged drills." Light loads during running or hurdling are already loaded plyometrics, per the authors, so they belong in the plyometric count.
268	
269	**When NOT to apply** — Not a replacement for land plyometrics for explosive sport (the authors' own limit). "Light" and "heavy" weights and "stiff" cords are not quantified. The "water plyos" in aerobics classes the authors call pseudo-plyometric (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273) differ from these structured aqua drills; do not conflate them.
270	
271	**Example** — The authors' own: chest- or shoulder-high water for one-legged preparatory jumps (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

289	# Strength-Endurance: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 Reps per Minute, Ideally to Fatigue; Above 75-80% 1RM Trains Strength Instead (but the Book Also Prescribes 80-85%)

291	**What it is** — Section 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 296-298 / printed pp. 285-287; pp. 296-298 verified against the page images):
292	- **Eight determinants.** Training for strength-endurance "is determined predominantly by: 1. The magnitude of the load 2. The tempo of movement 3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements 4. The rest interval between training sessions 5. The length of the training period 6. The initial levels of strength-endurance of the athlete 7. The kinesiological structure of the movement 8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance" (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).
293	- **Basic prescription.** "Repetition work with weights 25-50% of 1RM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness ... will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961)" (same page).
294	- **Ceiling.** "When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant resistance (exceeding 75-80% of 1RM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966)" (same page).
295	- **Progression.** "It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).
296	- **Summary rule.** "multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises simulating the given sport activity. If the special exercise is associated with the prolonged production of moderate force, then it is useful to work with light weights in repeated sets to the point of fatigue or failure" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).
297	
298	**Internal conflict, recorded:** the 75-80% ceiling (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285) conflicts with the sport examples a page later: "Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM) ... are recommended for developing strength-endurance in skaters", 4-12 reps per set to complete fatigue with 2-4 min rest (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975), and "Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1RM" (Ulrich et al, 1966) (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286). The summary rule on p. 287 ("an optimally heavy weight ... together with light weights" where intense effort is needed) sits closer to the examples than to the ceiling. The book does not reconcile them.
299	
300	**Why it works** — The ceiling's stated reason: above 75-80% the work is "constrained to developing strength predominantly." The load-to-fatigue advantage is reported from the cited Soviet studies, without a stated mechanism.
301	
302	**When to apply** — Inference: for football, where strength-endurance means repeated forceful efforts (blocking, pushing a sled), the summary rule fits better than the 25-50% band: a heavy-enough load mixed with lighter or sport-simulating work. The 60-120 reps per minute tempo describes cyclic-sport endurance work more than gridiron work. Eric's baseline: for football the priority stack is alactic and aerobic capacity and power, with glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed through camp and practice (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 116). Inference: to-fatigue strength-endurance sets would add glycolytic load the department deliberately does not program.
303	
304	**When NOT to apply** — Do not quote the 75-80% ceiling as a firm rule without the 80-85% skater and 50-80% rower examples. The determinants list has no weightings. "60% of the maximal work capacity time" is not defined further (Inference: 60% of the time to failure is the plain reading).
305	
306	**Example** — The authors' own: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 reps per minute to fatigue, or to 60% of the maximal work time (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).
307	
308	**Related** — [[framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial]] (Ch3.2.2, the dynamic/static and absolute/partial distinctions this section restates); [[claim--zatsiorsky-and-hansen-show-strength-endurance-training-specificity]]; [[case-study--soviet-sport-specific-strength-endurance-prescriptions]]; [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]] (Ch1 Table 1.1, endurance at 40-60% 1RM)
309

323	
324	# Train Strength-Endurance Under Demanding Conditions With Movements Close to the Sport: Parachutes, Sleds, Weighted Vests, Boat Drag
325	
326	**What it is** — "For developing strength-endurance it is always appropriate to strive to execute the work under demanding conditions, though with movements whose coordination and structure in space and time are close to those of the special exercise. For instance, a runner may run with a small parachute resisting him or pull a loaded sled in the preparatory phases (Popov, 1966). Similarly, gymnasts may use a heavy belt and vest (Zhilei, 1964) and rowers a special water-resistance device attached to the hull of the boat (Chuprun, 1966). 329	
330	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that the loaded work keeps the coordination and space-time structure of the sport movement. Inference: this is the dynamic-correspondence criteria applied to endurance work; the passage does not cite 4.3.
331	
332	**When to apply** — Inference: in football, sled pushes and pulls, resisted sprints and weighted-vest movement drills are the direct analogue, provided the load does not change the movement's structure. The rower test results show the gains can appear in general tests too.
333	
334	**When NOT to apply** — "Demanding" is not quantified; the authors' Ch4.3 parachute material warns that resistance can distort mechanics (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). Note the gymnast citation is spelled "Zhilei, 1964" here and "Zhalei, 1964" a few lines earlier on the same page; probably the same source, but the book does not say. The rower percentages have no sample size or duration given.

# Depth Jumps: Once or Twice a Week, Kept 3-4 Days From Technique Sessions, Every 10-14 Days In Season and Not Within 10 Days of Competition

**What it is** — From the authors' depth-jump recommendations (PDF pp. 286-287 / printed pp. 275-276, verified against the page images):
- **Weekly frequency (item 3):** depth jumps "in the volume indicated should be done once or twice a week in training sessions devoted to special strength training", which can also include "localised exercises for other muscle groups and general developmental exercises executed with a small volume." But "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training in the particular sport."
- **Spacing from technique (item 4):** "Depth-jumps strongly excite the nervous system. Therefore, they should be used not less than 3-4 days before a technique training session. Sessions devoted to general physical preparation with a small volume of work should be done after depth-jump workouts."
- **Season (item 5):** "Depth-jumps occupy a fundamental place in the second half of the preparatory period of the yearly cycle. However, they can function as a means of maintaining the achieved level of special strength fitness in the competition period. During the competition period they should be included once every 10-14 days, but no later than 10 days before a competition."
- **Delayed effect (item 15):** integration "depends on not disrupting the delayed training effect of prior strength work. It should be noted that the use of depth-jumps as a means of stimulation can delay this effect for 5-6 days."

**Internal conflict, recorded:** item 4 keeps depth jumps at least 3-4 days before a technique session, while item 3 allows well-conditioned athletes three depth-jump sessions a week placed "at the completion of technical training." Three sessions a week tied to technical training cannot all sit 3-4 days before the next technique session. Both are on PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons: strong excitation of the nervous system (item 4) and a 5-6 day delay of the training effect of prior strength work (item 15). Neither cites a study. Inference: the in-season 10-day cut-off before competition is consistent with item 15's 5-6 day delayed effect plus a margin; the book does not make that link.

**When to apply** — Placing depth jumps in a football week or year. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume"" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105). Inference: the authors' in-season rule (one exposure every 10-14 days, none in the 10 days before a game) is far sparser than a weekly game schedule allows; read literally, a team playing every 7 days would have no legal in-season depth-jump day. That is a reason to treat the 10-day rule as written for track-and-field competition calendars, which the book does not say.

**When NOT to apply** — These are experience-based rules with no population, drop height or study given. They are written for an annual cycle with a long preparatory period and spaced competitions (the authors' examples elsewhere in 5.2.4 are track-and-field jumpers). Do not quote the 3-4 day spacing without the item 3 exception. The 5-6 day delay applies to depth jumps used "as a means of stimulation"; the book does not say how it scales with volume.

**Example** — The authors' own: depth jumps central in the second half of the preparatory period, then once every 10-14 days in the competition period, last one at least 10 days out (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

# Depth-Jump and Maximal-Plyometric Volume and Rest: The Book Gives Two Incompatible Dosing Models

**What it is** — Section 5.2.4 gives the following dosing statements. They do not agree, so all are listed with locators.

**Model 1: maximal plyometrics dosed like a maximal lift.**
- "*Maximal plyometrics* essentially are low-repetition activities ... Just like maximal strength training with weights, these powerful impulses are not meant to be imposed on the musculature every workout, nor are multiple repetitions even possible or advisable. Moreover, a rest interval of 2-4 minutes is recommended between successive repetitions and as much as 10-12 minutes between sets" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).
- Prescription item 6: "The rest interval between sets of maximal plyometric exercises should be about 10 minutes for power development (strength-speed and speed-strength) and much shorter intervals with submaximal plyometrics to develop explosive-strength endurance" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
- "several books advocate sessions with over 100 repetitions of plyometric movements ... This volume of *maximal plyometrics* (unlike sub-maximal plyometrics) is neither productive nor safe for any athlete. Maximal plyometrics, like maximal weight lifting, involves single all-out repetitions separated by a few minutes of rest" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282, verified against the page image).
- "classical plyometrics are 1 RM movements which require as much as several minutes of rest before recovery is complete" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283, text layer).

**Model 2: depth jumps in sets of 5-10 (credited to "prolific experience").**
- Prescription item 4: "As an initial guideline, the dosage of plyometric exercises should not exceed 5-8 repetitions in one set" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, verified against the page image).
- Depth-jump item 1: with a complex of vertical jumps (Fig 5.11), "Each exercise is executed in sets of 10 repetitions, with 1-15 minutes of rest between sets" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275; the page image prints "1-15", recorded as printed).
- Depth-jump item 2: "The optimal dosage of depth-jumps with an energetic vertical take-off in one training session should not exceed 4 sets of 10 jumps for well-conditioned athletes and 2-3 sets of 5-8 jumps for lesser conditioned athletes. Easy running and relaxation exercises for a period of 10-15 minutes should be done between sets" (same page, verified against the page image).
- Depth-jump item 3: "Well-conditioned athletes can execute depth-jumps 3 times per week for 2 sets of 10 jumps at the completion of technical training" (same page, verified against the page image).

**The conflict.** Model 1 says multiple repetitions of maximal plyometrics are not "possible or advisable" and separates single reps by 2-4 minutes. Model 2 prescribes sets of 10 energetic depth jumps, up to 40 per session, with rest given only between sets. Inference: Model 2 might be read as submaximal work, but depth-jump item 2 specifies "an energetic vertical take-off", and the 0.75-1.15 m heights in Ch4 are for advanced jumpers. Rest between sets also varies: about 10 min (p. 274), 10-12 min (p. 272), 10-15 min of easy running (p. 275), and "1-15 minutes" (p. 275). The book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — Model 1's stated reasons: maximal plyometrics are "extremely demanding on the central nervous system" and impose "great mechanical strain on the tendons, in particular" (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282). Model 2's stated basis is "prolific experience with depth-jumps for developing jumping power" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275). Neither gives fatigue or recovery data.

**When to apply** — Inference: one way to use both is to treat Model 1 as the rule for truly maximal efforts (maximal height, rebound to a marker, near-maximal tension) and Model 2 as an upper volume cap for depth-jump sessions, keeping per-session counts at or under 2-3 × 5-8 for less-conditioned athletes and 4 × 10 for well-conditioned ones. The book does not make this split. For any athlete, the authors' quality rule holds: "It is the quality of the plyometric exercises, not the quantity, which is important" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 11). Eric's baseline: in-season the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 105). Inference: Model 1's low-rep, long-rest structure fits that rule more directly than Model 2's sets of 10.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not cite "4 × 10 depth jumps" as Supertraining's recommendation without the Model 1 statements beside it, or the reverse. "1-15 minutes" may be a misprint (Inference: 1.5 or 10-15 are possible readings), but the page prints 1-15, so do not quote a corrected value. None of these numbers comes with a cited study, population or drop height (except the Ch4 heights for advanced jumpers). The "over 100 repetitions" warning targets maximal plyometrics; the authors say submaximal plyometrics differ.

**Example** — The authors' own figures: lesser-conditioned athletes 2-3 sets of 5-8 energetic depth jumps with 10-15 minutes of easy running between sets (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275), against maximal rebounds as single reps 2-4 minutes apart with 10-12 minutes between sets (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272).

**Related** — [[heuristic--depth-jump-weekly-frequency-and-seasonal-placement]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[claim--high-volume-plyometrics-do-not-build-rebound-fatigue-resistance]]; [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]]

# Classical Plyometric Training: Coupling Under About 0.15 s, Feedforward Control, and a Shock Force-Time Pattern, Not Coupling Time Alone

**What it is** — The authors give three tests for whether a drill is classical "training plyometrics" rather than ordinary jumping:
1. **Coupling time.** The method "is characterised by impulsive action of minimal duration between the end of the eccentric braking phase and initiation of the concentric acceleration phase". "If the transition phase (or, coupling phase) is prolonged by more than about 0.15 second, the action may be considered to constitute ordinary jumping and not classical training plyometrics." The coaching image: imagine the contact surface "is red hot, so that any prolonged contact would be dangerous." (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268, verified against the page image.)
2. **Feedforward control.** "The activity is not accurately plyometric if the athlete relies upon ongoing feedback processes to control the isometric and concentric actions instead of upon feedforward programmes established before any movement begins"; true plyometric training "usually involves ballistic rather than cocontraction processes" (same page).
3. **Force-time pattern.** Later the 0.15 s rule "requires some qualification" (PDF p. 281 / printed p. 270). "One cannot simply distinguish between plyometric and non-plyometric solely on the basis of coupling times, otherwise one would have to classify jogging or even brisk walking as classical plyometrics, because the time taken for the ground reaction force to reach a maximum can be less than 0.15 second. One also has to take the force-time pattern and the rate of force development (RFD) into account" (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).

The same pages separate *plyometric actions*, which "occur as part of many running, jumping, hurdling, striking and other rebounding movements in sport", from *plyometric training*, "which applies plyometric actions as a distinct training modality according to a definite methodology" (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268). Siff writes this passage (it names Verkhoshansky in the third person: "Verkhoshansky has always consistently favoured the use of the term 'shock method'"). He suggests calling the action "stretch-shortening action" and the training system "powermetrics", and writes that "The earliest published use of the word plyometrics seems to have been in a Soviet publication (Zanon, 1966)." He then concludes that arguing whether an action is "classically plyometric or not becomes complex and academic, with no real benefit to the prescription of plyometric training", and that it is better to recognise types of plyometric training (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272; see [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: the method "relies on the production of a very brief explosive-isometric and eccentric-isometric phase which precedes the release of the elastic energy stored in the tendons and other components of the series elastic component" (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268). For why the time limit varies, see [[claim--prestretch-benefit-decay-time-differs-by-task]] (tonic versus phasic reflexes, fibre type). Inference: jogging passes the 0.15 s test but has a low, unhurried force-time curve, which is why the authors add the force-time and RFD test.

**When to apply** — Auditing a "plyo" block: check (1) ground or implement contact, eccentric to concentric, short enough to meet the about 0.15 s guide, (2) a pre-planned ballistic action rather than a corrected one, and (3) a sharp force rise. Eric's baseline: speed is taught "as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand (~0.08s male, ~0.10s female at max velocity)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 96). Inference: those sprint contacts sit under the authors' 0.15 s coupling guide, though contact time and coupling time are not the same interval (coupling is only the eccentric-to-concentric transition); a force plate contact time over 0.15 s does not by itself show a coupling over 0.15 s.

**When NOT to apply** — The 0.15 s figure is "about" and is qualified by the authors themselves; it is not a hard cut-off. Do not use coupling time alone (the jogging counter-example). Do not read "not classical plyometrics" as "not useful": the authors say longer-coupling drills train other qualities (see [[claim--popular-plyometric-drills-work-through-other-mechanisms]]). The authors give no method for measuring coupling time in the field.

**Example** — The authors' own: jogging and brisk walking reach peak ground reaction force in under 0.15 s yet are not classical plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272). The "red hot" surface is their cue (PDF p. 279 / printed p. 268).

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the original definition and "powermetrics"); [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]]; [[framework--five-phases-of-a-plyometric-action]]; [[claim--prestretch-benefit-decay-time-differs-by-task]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/claim--reversible-muscular-action-is-a-trainable-skill-not-automatic]]

# Match Plyometric Drills to the Sport's Symmetry, Limb Dominance and Rotational Dominance (Asymmetric Plyometrics)

**What it is** — Under "Asymmetric Plyometrics" (PDF pp. 289-290 / printed pp. 278-279; p. 289 verified against the page image, p. 290 from the text layer):
- Bilateral depth jumps and medicine ball drills "may be valuable for sports which require this type of limb action, but are far less beneficial for sports which involve alternate action of the limbs in different patterns of movement."
- "before selecting plyometric drills, it is important to categorize sporting movements as cyclic, acyclic, unilateral, bilateral, symmetric, asymmetric or as various combinations", and distinguish "dominant and non-dominant limbs, as well as driving leg and swing leg in running, since the efficiency of movement depends primarily on central nervous factors." "all activity of the legs in sport is related in specific spatio-temporal patterns to motion in the arms."
- Rotational dominance: "a right-handed baseballer, golfer or shotputter displays anti-clockwise rotational dominance, whereas the left-hander displays clockwise rotational dominance", which bears on medicine ball catching and throwing drills.
- "Research has shown that the transfer of strength developed in bilateral training (e.g. using squats or power cleans) offers specific improvement in performance in bilateral events such as the squat clean and snatch in weightlifting, while unilateral training (e.g. with dumbbells or split cleans) enhances performances more effectively in unilateral activity such as running, jumping or karate" (no citation given).
- Named methods: the *alternate-asymmetric method* ("strength and jumping exercises alternately with each leg, rather than with both legs simultaneously") and the *limb-synchronisation method* (each leg synchronised with the opposite arm or both arms, "depending on the given activity (e.g. sprinting vs volleyball, basketball or trampolining)").
- Siff's own laboratory work at the University of the Witwatersrand ("research by the author", Siff writing): drill time, peak force, RFD and distance from a dominant versus non-dominant limb start "reveal that it may be relevant to individualise plyometric drills to match the functional asymmetry and limb dominance characteristics of the athlete."

**Why it works** — The stated reason is central nervous control: "motor performance is determined by how competently one programs the central nervous computer of the body, taking functional asymmetry into careful consideration." No data are given.

**When to apply** — Inference: football movements are mostly unilateral and alternating (sprinting, cutting, a lineman's drive step), so by this rule bilateral depth jumps would be general (non-functional) work and alternate-leg bounds and hops the more specific choice; for rotational throwing (quarterbacks), medicine ball work would account for the thrower's rotational dominance.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the bilateral-unilateral transfer claim has no citation in the passage, and the Witwatersrand study gives no numbers or subjects ("may be relevant"). The book's other position on symmetry warns against chasing perfect bilateral symmetry (see [[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]]); this entry is about matching drills to a sport's asymmetry, not correcting it.

**Example** — The text's own: a right-handed shot putter's anti-clockwise rotational dominance, and sprinting (leg with opposite arm) versus volleyball or basketball (leg with both arms) for limb synchronisation (PDF p. 290 / printed p. 279).

**Related** — [[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]]; [[claim--pursuing-perfect-bilateral-symmetry-can-be-counterproductive]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]

# Plyometric Surfaces and Footwear: Not Too Soft for Rebounds, Yet Sand and Soft Mats Have Their Uses; Swings and Pogo Sticks as Cheap Powermetric Tools

**What it is** — Surface and apparatus statements in 5.2.4:
- "Footwear or the floor covering should not be very soft or excessively shock absorbent, since this may impair ankle stability, diminish the storage of elastic energy in the SEC (e.g. tendons) and delay the triggering of the positive supportive reaction of the foot (see 6.1.2) when contacting the floor" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273, verified against the page image).
- The surface "can also have a significant effect on the outcome of the exercise, as alluded to earlier in comments made about the alterations in motor skill and proprioceptive sensitivity associated with the use of soft-soled shoes and very resilient jumping surfaces. A little known finding is that plyometric and jumping drills performed according to carefully planned progressive patterns in sand can significantly enhance jumping skills in a short period, even as short as 5 days in duration (Montagni & Cardinale, 1996)" (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image).
- For depth landings: Dursenev and Raevsky used "soft gymnastic mats", and the authors advise landing "on suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277, verified against the page image).
- Simple apparatus: a children's swing near a wall, where the feet push off the wall after swinging from "a suitable height", progressed by raising the backswing; longer ropes give a slower repetition rate; uprights in front allow upper-body rebounds. The "Pogo-Stick", with intensity "determined by the height of rebound", and boxers' skipping are also offered as "powermetric" tools (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278, verified against the page image).

**Internal tension, recorded:** p. 273 warns against very soft, shock-absorbent surfaces for plyometrics, while p. 278 reports fast jumping-skill gains from progressive drills in sand, and p. 277 pairs a soft-mat landing study with advice to land on "suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces." The book does not reconcile these. Inference: they may refer to different aims (sand for skill and lower impact; firm surfaces for maximal shock rebounds), but the book does not say so.

**Why it works** — The p. 273 reasons are stated (ankle stability, SEC elastic storage, the foot's positive supportive reaction). No mechanism is given for the sand result. The swing physics is stated by the authors as rope length setting the oscillation time.

**When to apply** — Choosing where to run maximal rebound work: a firm, not very soft surface and non-cushioned footwear, per p. 273. Inference: sand is an option for early-phase or high-volume submaximal jumping, consistent with the p. 278 finding, but not for maximal depth jumps.

**When NOT to apply** — The Montagni & Cardinale (1996) result is cited without design or measures; "jumping skills" is not defined. The swing and pogo stick suggestions are the text's ideas, with no data.

**Example** — The text's own: beach volleyball and beach handball as examples of the value of sand training (PDF p. 289 / printed p. 278).

# Grade Plyometric Intensity by Momentum at Contact (Set by Drop Height), Since a 1RM Does Not Exist; Prefer Height Over Added Weight

**What it is** — The authors propose "a *powermetrics intensity scale* similar to that used in weightlifting, where exercises are ranked in terms of percentages of one's 1RM." Because "the concept of 1RMs is meaningless in plyometric training", one must use estimates of muscle tension or of "the impulse ... produced during the contact phase". "Impulse is equivalent to the change of momentum (m.ΔV) during the amortisation phase, so that its magnitude for a falling body depends on the height from which the body drops. Thus, the momentum just before contact (estimated from height of the drop jump or distance fallen by the object) may serve as a measure of intensity." At the top of the scale is maximal plyometrics, "the equivalent of the emotionally demanding competitive maximum, CFmax"; at the bottom, preparatory non-impact plyometrics (PDF p. 283 / printed p. 272, verified against the page image).

The prescription list adds: "The magnitude of the impulsive load is determined by the weight and the height of its free-fall. The optimal combination is determined empirically in each specific case; however, preference should be given to a large height over a heavy weight. Since the resulting force is governed by Newton's Second Law (F = m.a), a force plate may be used to determine the height of drop to produce the required force" (PDF p. 285 / printed p. 274, item 1, verified against the page image). Item 4 says rep dosage can be set more precisely "to calculate the force involved (from bodymass and the drop height) and the athlete's level of special speed-strength" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the impulse-momentum statement quoted. Inference (physics): for a body falling from rest through height h, speed at contact is √(2gh), so momentum at contact is m·√(2gh). Momentum therefore rises with the square root of drop height, not in proportion to it: doubling the drop height raises contact momentum by a factor of √2, about 41%, and quadrupling it doubles momentum. Inference (physics): the peak force on landing is not fixed by drop height alone; for the same momentum, a shorter, stiffer arrest gives a higher average force (average net force = change in momentum divided by contact time). That is why the authors' force plate step is needed to find the height that gives a target force.

**When to apply** — Progressing depth jumps or rebounds: rank drills by drop height and bodymass rather than counting all "plyos" as equal, and raise height before adding external load. Inference: with ForceDecks, a drop jump from a known box gives landing force and contact time for each athlete, which is the measurement the authors' item 1 asks for.

**When NOT to apply** — Momentum at contact is an intensity proxy for impact drills with a fall; it does not grade non-impact or ground-based bounding drills where there is no measured drop. The authors give no numeric scale bands (no "% of CFmax" per height). Item 1's "F = m.a" sentence does not on its own let you compute landing force from height (see the Inference above). Height also has an upper limit: past the optimum the transition slows (see [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]] and [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]).

**Example** — Inference: a 100 kg athlete stepping off a 0.5 m box lands at about √(2 × 9.81 × 0.5) ≈ 3.1 m/s, about 313 kg·m/s of momentum; from a 1.0 m box about 4.4 m/s and about 443 kg·m/s, roughly 41% more, not double. This calculation is not in the source.

**Related** — [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]] (Ch4.2.3, the 0.75-1.15 m range); [[framework--kinetic-energy-stimulation-mechanical-basis-and-advantages]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements]]

# Before Depth Jumps: Months of Barbell, Jumping, Sprint and Skipping Work, Eccentric and Explosive-Isometric Strength, Static-Start Jumps, Then Low Hops

**What it is** — The authors' preparation rules (pages verified against the page images):
- "Depth-jumps require special preliminary preparation such as a significant volume of barbell exercises and traditional jumping, short sprints and skipping over a period of several months" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 1). Contra-indications: "Muscle or tendon fatigue, pain or soreness, as well as incompletely healed injuries" (same item).
- "depth-jumping is not a basic type of training to be indulged in lightly by athletes who are relatively unused to explosive or strongly resisted movements. For anyone who is not accustomed to movements such as weightlifting cleans, jerks, squats or hurdling, it is highly advisable that a preparatory programme using submaximal plyometrics, non-impact and non-plyometrics be followed" first (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276).
- **Eccentric and explosive-isometric strength first:** "a primary requirement for anyone contemplating the use of classical plyometrics is a high level of eccentric strength and explosive isometric strength. Herein lies the value of small-range squats, power cleans, power snatches, cleans from the hang, snatches from the hang, push presses or jerks, push presses or jerks from racks, and the descent of flights of stairs." Front and back squats both, "since they each model different types of jump (directly upwards versus forwards and upwards)." "Slow quasi-isometric squats over a moderate range with heavy weights should later lead to more rapid dips over a shallower range with lighter weights" (PDF pp. 287-288 / printed pp. 276-277).
- **Static start before dynamic start:** "it is initially useful to improve jumping ability from a static start, without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start": standing broad and vertical jumps without a dip, then the vertical jump test "progressing from a static flexed knee start to a dynamic dip start with arms flung vigorously upwards" (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277). Progress can be tracked with the Lewis formula ([[claim--lewis-formula-estimates-jump-power-from-bodymass-and-height]]).
- **Low hops:** "hopping on the spot at a frequency which feels most comfortable for the athlete, using a few sets of about 25 repetitions", then small forward, backward, sideward, forward-backward and zig-zag hops, then vertical hops "as rapidly as possible, again using a few sets of about 20 repetitions" (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275, item 6). Rope skipping is useful, but "long periods of skipping are not the appropriate form of preparatory drill" because the aim is speed-strength, not endurance (item 7).
- **Technique and complexity:** learn normal jumping first, with "the correct lumbar-pelvic rhythm, as is also used during clean pulls or power cleans from the ground" (PDF p. 287 / printed p. 276, item 13). "Great caution" with depth jumps involving "one-legged thrusts, changes of direction or complex variations, since the injury risk is significantly higher" (item 14).
- Then integrate: "As eccentric, isometric and concentric strength increases ... the athlete may progress to actions which more rapidly integrate all three aspects of plyometric movement"; the same principles apply to upper-body work (medicine ball catching and throwing, plyometric press-ups and bench presses) (PDF p. 288 / printed p. 277).

**Why it works** — The authors derive the preparation from the action itself: because plyometric actions involve "a powerful eccentric amortisation phase terminating in an explosive isometric contraction", eccentric and explosive-isometric strength come first; because the concentric phase is reflex-assisted, static-start jumping builds the concentric part "without exposing oneself to the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start" (PDF pp. 287-288 / printed pp. 276-277).

**When to apply** — Freshmen, return-to-training athletes, or anyone without a lifting and jumping base. Eric's baseline: the Vermeil hierarchy (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, "each level a required foundation for the next") is the department's programming "compass" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 101). Inference: the authors' sequence (strength base, static jumps, low hops, then depth jumps) is the same ordering applied inside the power level. Inference: single-leg and change-of-direction depth jumps, the most football-like variants, are the ones the authors flag as highest risk, so they come last.

**When NOT to apply** — "Several months" is not quantified, and no strength threshold is given here (for the 1.5-2 × bodymass squat rule, see [[claim--squat-1-5-to-2-bodymass-rule-applies-to-maximal-depth-jumps-only]]). Inference: athletes with a long sporting history of running, jumping and lifting may already meet much of this preparation; the authors also say an athlete's sport may already supply most plyometric loading ([[claim--plyometric-injury-risk-comes-from-prescription-not-the-method]]).

**Example** — The authors' own: hopping on the spot in a few sets of about 25, moving to multi-directional hops, then fast vertical hops in sets of about 20 (PDF p. 286 / printed p. 275).

**Related** — [[heuristic--depth-jump-height-set-by-transition-speed-and-heel-contact]]; [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]; [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]]; [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]

# Resisted Plyometrics Only Occasionally and Never With Heavy Weights or Stiff Cords in Depth Jumps; Water Plyometrics Are a Safer Submaximal Option

**What it is** — Under "Resisted and Water Plyometric Training" (PDF pp. 292-293 / printed pp. 281-282; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 292 from the text layer):
- Resistance can be imposed in the amortisation phase, the concentric rebound or both: light weights, or "elastic cords attached to a harness located near the waist or hips." Both "increase the landing impact and ostensibly increase the strength of reflex muscle contraction", but "also increase the risk of impact and overload injuries and should be applied occasionally with great caution. Even normal running or hurdling with very light weights constitutes a form of loaded plyometric training."
- Resistance methods "should not use heavy weights or stiff elastic cords during depth jumps, since this increases the coupling time and imposes unnecessarily large loads on the spine and the tendons of the lower extremities, especially during the landing or contact phase."
- Water or "aqua plyometrics" decrease landing force and increase resistance in the recoil. They do "not offer maximal or shock method plyometrics" but serve as preparatory or submaximal plyometrics, "especially for one-legged drills." Water depth sets the resistance: "chest or shoulder high water offering greater resistance during the landing and take-off phases, less intense eccentric muscle activity, smaller impact forces and enhanced safety." Repeated aqua jumps for "rebound explosive muscle endurance" are "considerably safer than their land-based equivalents, though they should not completely replace the latter, since they do not adequately develop the specific neuromuscular patterns or functional needs of explosive sports."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are stated: heavy load lengthens the coupling time (taking the drill out of classical plyometrics) and loads spine and tendons; water reduces impact and eccentric intensity.

**When to apply** — Inference: aqua jumps suit early return-to-training or single-leg plyometric progressions where impact must be limited, consistent with the authors' "especially for one-legged drills." Light loads during running or hurdling are already loaded plyometrics, per the authors, so they belong in the plyometric count.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a replacement for land plyometrics for explosive sport (the authors' own limit). "Light" and "heavy" weights and "stiff" cords are not quantified. The "water plyos" in aerobics classes the authors call pseudo-plyometric (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273) differ from these structured aqua drills; do not conflate them.

**Example** — The authors' own: chest- or shoulder-high water for one-legged preparatory jumps (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

**Related** — [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[claim--thrown-load-height-decreases-with-load-increases-with-drop-height]] (Ch4.2.3, heavier loads not beneficial for kinetic-energy work); [[heuristic--plyometric-surface-footwear-and-simple-apparatus]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]

# Strength-Endurance: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 Reps per Minute, Ideally to Fatigue; Above 75-80% 1RM Trains Strength Instead (but the Book Also Prescribes 80-85%)

**What it is** — Section 5.2.5 (PDF pp. 296-298 / printed pp. 285-287; pp. 296-298 verified against the page images):
- **Eight determinants.** Training for strength-endurance "is determined predominantly by: 1. The magnitude of the load 2. The tempo of movement 3. The duration of each movement and each phase of the movements 4. The rest interval between training sessions 5. The length of the training period 6. The initial levels of strength-endurance of the athlete 7. The kinesiological structure of the movement 8. The relative involvement of static and dynamic strength-endurance" (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).
- **Basic prescription.** "Repetition work with weights 25-50% of 1RM at a moderate tempo (from 60-120 repetitions/minute) is used for developing strength-endurance. The effectiveness ... will be higher if the work is executed to complete fatigue, although work of shorter duration (60% of the maximal work capacity time) also will yield satisfactory results (Agolinsky, 1953; Korobkov, 1953; Monogarov, 1958; Diachkov, 1961)" (same page).
- **Ceiling.** "When the activity involves repetitively overcoming significant resistance (exceeding 75-80% of 1RM), one cannot enhance endurance, since one becomes constrained to developing strength predominantly (Zatsiorsky, 1966)" (same page).
- **Progression.** "It is necessary to increase the amount of weight and the number of repetitions as strength-endurance increases" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).
- **Summary rule.** "multiple repetition exercises with various weights should be considered the fundamental method for developing strength-endurance, with the load being determined by the dynamics of the given exercise. In cases requiring intense effort, an optimally heavy weight should be used together with light weights or with exercises simulating the given sport activity. If the special exercise is associated with the prolonged production of moderate force, then it is useful to work with light weights in repeated sets to the point of fatigue or failure" (PDF p. 298 / printed p. 287).

**Internal conflict, recorded:** the 75-80% ceiling (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285) conflicts with the sport examples a page later: "Exercises with heavy weights (80-85% of 1RM) ... are recommended for developing strength-endurance in skaters", 4-12 reps per set to complete fatigue with 2-4 min rest (Mikhailov & Panov, 1975), and "Male rowers obtain good results with weights of 50-80% of 1RM" (Ulrich et al, 1966) (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286). The summary rule on p. 287 ("an optimally heavy weight ... together with light weights" where intense effort is needed) sits closer to the examples than to the ceiling. The book does not reconcile them.

**Why it works** — The ceiling's stated reason: above 75-80% the work is "constrained to developing strength predominantly." The load-to-fatigue advantage is reported from the cited Soviet studies, without a stated mechanism.

**When to apply** — Inference: for football, where strength-endurance means repeated forceful efforts (blocking, pushing a sled), the summary rule fits better than the 25-50% band: a heavy-enough load mixed with lighter or sport-simulating work. The 60-120 reps per minute tempo describes cyclic-sport endurance work more than gridiron work. Eric's baseline: for football the priority stack is alactic and aerobic capacity and power, with glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed through camp and practice (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 116). Inference: to-fatigue strength-endurance sets would add glycolytic load the department deliberately does not program.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not quote the 75-80% ceiling as a firm rule without the 80-85% skater and 50-80% rower examples. The determinants list has no weightings. "60% of the maximal work capacity time" is not defined further (Inference: 60% of the time to failure is the plain reading).

**Example** — The authors' own: 25-50% 1RM at 60-120 reps per minute to fatigue, or to 60% of the maximal work time (PDF p. 296 / printed p. 285).

**Related** — [[framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial]] (Ch3.2.2, the dynamic/static and absolute/partial distinctions this section restates); [[claim--zatsiorsky-and-hansen-show-strength-endurance-training-specificity]]; [[case-study--soviet-sport-specific-strength-endurance-prescriptions]]; [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]] (Ch1 Table 1.1, endurance at 40-60% 1RM)

# Train Strength-Endurance Under Demanding Conditions With Movements Close to the Sport: Parachutes, Sleds, Weighted Vests, Boat Drag

**What it is** — "For developing strength-endurance it is always appropriate to strive to execute the work under demanding conditions, though with movements whose coordination and structure in space and time are close to those of the special exercise. For instance, a runner may run with a small parachute resisting him or pull a loaded sled in the preparatory phases (Popov, 1966). Similarly, gymnasts may use a heavy belt and vest (Zhilei, 1964) and rowers a special water-resistance device attached to the hull of the boat (Chuprun, 1966). In the case of the rowers, strength-endurance as measured by the number of pull-ups, the number of arm flexions in the prone position and the number of barbell presses in 30 seconds increased by 57.1%, 27.8% and 9.1%, respectively" (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286, verified against the page image).

The same idea appears earlier for speed-strength: "good results are achieved by making the special exercise more demanding", e.g. "water resistance in rowing or very small loads on the limbs of track-and-field athletes and gymnasts" (PDF pp. 277-278 / printed pp. 266-267; that passage belongs to 5.2.3).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that the loaded work keeps the coordination and space-time structure of the sport movement. Inference: this is the dynamic-correspondence criteria applied to endurance work; the passage does not cite 4.3.

**When to apply** — Inference: in football, sled pushes and pulls, resisted sprints and weighted-vest movement drills are the direct analogue, provided the load does not change the movement's structure. The rower test results show the gains can appear in general tests too.

**When NOT to apply** — "Demanding" is not quantified; the authors' Ch4.3 parachute material warns that resistance can distort mechanics (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). Note the gymnast citation is spelled "Zhilei, 1964" here and "Zhalei, 1964" a few lines earlier on the same page; probably the same source, but the book does not say. The rower percentages have no sample size or duration given.

**Example** — The authors' own: rowers training with a water-resistance device on the hull improved pull-ups by 57.1%, prone arm flexions by 27.8% and 30-second barbell presses by 9.1% (PDF p. 297 / printed p. 286).
